  dot or slash (a file target) only when declared `.PHONY`. No `make -pn` run: reading the file
  is instant and works without make installed (a Makefile that includes others or generates
  targets shows only what it writes out).
- tasks.json labels still win over detected ones; `task.autoDetect` ("on" / "off", VS Code's
  name) turns detection off. Configure default build / test task on a detected task writes a
  shell task with its command, `options.cwd` and problem matcher (D200's `entryForDetected`).
- Tested: `src/extensions/tasks/detect.test.ts`; IO in `detectFolders.ts`.

**Testing: continuous run** (feature-gaps §2 Testing "Continuous run")
- VS Code's "Turn on continuous run": the eye in the Testing view's filter row (whole run), an
  eye on a file's or test's row (that item), `tests.toggleContinuousRun {file?, test?, on?}`,
  `tests.stopContinuousRun`; the status bar shows an eye while it's on; `ide://tests` has
  `continuous` (all, files, tests, runs, last run).
- What a save runs (no module graph, so a guess from names and folders): a test file runs its
  own tests; a source file the tests named after it in its project (`util.ts` → `util.test.ts`,
  `test_util.py`, `util_test.go`), and for Go and Rust also the tests in its folder; when nothing
  matches by name, its project's tests. Files that aren't code (Markdown, images) run nothing.
  Per item: the item runs when the save affects it (a single test whose file runs anyway isn't
  run twice).
- Saves are collected for 800 ms (several files saved at once run once); runs never overlap:
  saves during any run wait for it and then run once; turning it off (every item off) stops a
  run it started. Turning it on asks for workspace trust; saves never ask (without trust nothing
  runs). Runs are quiet (no notification): the view, the margin and the status bar show results.
  Not kept across restarts or folder changes (VS Code doesn't keep it either).
- Tested: `src/extensions/testing/continuous.test.ts`.

**Agent background commands** (feature-gaps §2 Agent "Background processes")
- Claude Code's `run_in_background` / BashOutput / KillShell. `run_command` with
  `background: true` (or a command that looks like a server, as before) starts the command in the
  background with an id (`bg1`, `bg2`… unique while the IDE runs), waits up to 12 s for its first
  output or server address (as before; a server address still opens in the browser tab with
  `agent.openServers`), and returns that output with the id and how to read and stop it.
- New tools: `process_output { id, filter? }` (read-only, so also in Ask and Plan): what it printed
  since the last read; `filter` keeps only the new lines matching a regular expression (plain
  text when it isn't one) and skips the rest, like BashOutput; dropped output is counted; without
  `id` it lists the chat's background commands. `kill_process { id }` ends it and what it started
  (the process group / taskkill /T). A chat can only read and kill its own. Claude Code agent
  files' `BashOutput`, `KillShell` (and `KillBash`) map to these.
- **Changed from D117:** background commands no longer run in a terminal tab; they run through
  the exec plumbing like foreground commands (no pty, stdin closed, `CI=1`, `NO_COLOR=1`), with
  their output in a 1 MB buffer per command (`processOutput.ts`, tested: read cursor, escape
  sequences and progress redraws cleaned). Reading "the new output since the last read" needs our
  own buffer, and a terminal tab per agent server crowded the panel; the user now sees them in
  the chat. Limit: a command that needs a terminal (asks for input, draws a TUI) won't work in
  the background; the terminal is still there for the user (`terminal.start` is unchanged).
- The chat lists its background commands above the message box while one runs (status, id,
  command, server address, Output → a read-only tab, Stop). Commands: `agent.listProcesses
  {session?}`, `agent.killProcess {id}`, `agent.showProcessOutput {id}`; state
  `ide://agent/processes`.
- Lifetime: killed when the chat is deleted, when the folder closes (or another opens) and when
  the IDE ends (Rust's job object, D180) or the page reloads (D163). **Stop doesn't kill them**
  (Claude Code's behaviour: a dev server started in an earlier step keeps running); Stop while
  one is starting kills that one (D161). At most 8 running per chat (a model starting servers in
  a loop is stopped there); the last 10 ended ones per chat stay readable.
- Rust: `exec_run`'s timeout clamp went from 1 hour to 7 days (a background command runs until
  killed); the foreground `run_command` caps `timeoutMs` at 1 hour itself.
- Limits: the processes aren't kept across a restart (nothing to reattach to); a chat closed with
  `/clear` keeps its processes running but the new chat doesn't list them (they show in
  `ide://agent/processes` and are killed with the folder); ACP agents use their own tools.

**Usage**
- **What providers give back** (there is no cross-provider standard; OpenAI's `usage` object is
  the shape compatible servers copy, and OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions —
  `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens` / `output_tokens` — are the nearest thing to one for logs):
  - Anthropic Messages: `usage.input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `cache_read_input_tokens`,
    `cache_creation_input_tokens` (in `message_start` / `message_delta`); headers
    `anthropic-ratelimit-{requests,tokens,input-tokens,output-tokens}-{limit,remaining,reset}`
    (reset: an RFC 3339 time) and `retry-after` on 429. No cost in the response; the cost and
    usage reports need an admin key, which the IDE doesn't ask for.
  - OpenAI Chat Completions (with `stream_options.include_usage`): `prompt_tokens`,
    `completion_tokens`, `prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`,
    `completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens` (inside the output count); headers
    `x-ratelimit-{limit,remaining,reset}-{requests,tokens}` (reset: a duration, "6m0s"). No cost;
    the organization's usage and costs API needs an admin key.
  - OpenRouter: the OpenAI shape plus `usage.cost` (dollars actually billed) and cached tokens;
    `GET /api/v1/key` gives the key's `limit`, `usage`, `limit_remaining`, `usage_daily` /
    `usage_weekly` / `usage_monthly`, `limit_reset` and `is_free_tier`. No rate-limit headers on
    ordinary responses.
  - Groq, xAI, DeepSeek and other compatible servers: the OpenAI usage shape (DeepSeek also
    `prompt_cache_hit_tokens`); Groq and xAI send `x-ratelimit-*` headers.
  - Ollama (local and cloud): `prompt_eval_count`, `eval_count` (and durations). No cost, no
    limits; Ollama's cloud plan limits aren't in its API.
  - External ACP agents (Claude Code, Codex, Copilot…) don't report tokens to the IDE; their
    use isn't in the log. Subscription windows (Claude's five-hour and weekly limits, Cursor's
    plan) aren't reachable with an API key either, so the page shows none.
- **What the IDE keeps**: one record per model request — time, chat id, provider id,
  `provider/model`, input (cached included), output, cache read, cache write, cost and where the
  cost came from (`provider`: OpenRouter's own figure; `price`: `agent.prices`, the provider's
  listing or the built-in list; `local`: an Ollama model on this computer, $0), and what asked:
  `chat`, `subagent` (explore, delegated and background subagents, the reviewer), `summary`
  (compaction), `edit`, `completion`, `nextEdit`, `commit`, `memory`. A request whose provider
  reported no tokens isn't logged (no guesses). `core/agent/usageLog.ts` (DOM-free, tested) builds
  and sums the records.
- **Where**: Rust appends JSON lines to `<appData>/agent/usage/<n>.jsonl`, one file per 10 days
  (`agent/usage.rs`). Plain `O_APPEND` writes of whole lines rather than the store's atomic rewrite
  (that would copy the file on every request); a line cut short by a crash is skipped on reading
  and the next append starts on a new line. Kept: 90 days and 20 MB at most (older files go when
  a new one starts and on each read). Batched in the webview (400 ms) so a burst of completions is
  one write. Never sent anywhere; `agent.usage.keepHistory: false` stops logging.
- **Limits**: Rust reads the rate-limit headers of every OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic chat
  response (also a 429's) and keeps the last ones per provider id in memory (`ai/limits.rs`,
  `ai_rate_limits`); OpenRouter's key credits are one `GET /key` with the key on Rust's side
  (`ai_provider_limits`, the key's label left out because it shows part of the key). The page
  shows "N of M left · resets in …" with a meter per bucket, OpenRouter's credits and its billed
  today / this week / this month; otherwise "Limits: not reported" (local: "runs locally"; hosted:
  "not reported yet — they show after its next request, if it sends them"). Nothing is invented.
- **Cost**: OpenRouter's reported `usage.cost` now rides on the done event (`cost`) and wins over
  prices, for the log and for the chat's cost and budget (D199).
- **The Usage page** (dock view `agent.usage`, the AI pages' layout): tiles for today, the last 7
  and 30 days (cost, requests, tokens, how many had no price); a bar per day (plain DOM, cost or
  tokens, 7 / 30 / 90 days); models and features with share bars; providers with their limits;
  the chats that cost the most (click opens the chat; a deleted chat is shown, not clickable);
  this chat (cost, requests, input with cache, output, the history's total with its subagents and
  summaries) and the per-chat budget field with a meter; "Clear usage history". One column of
  tiles under 520 px.
- **Commands and state**: `agent.showUsage`, `agent.clearUsageHistory` (destructive; asks the
  user), `agent.refreshUsageLimits` (network; agents may use it); `ide://agent/usage/history`
  (`?days=7|30|90`: totals, days with use, by model / provider / feature, top chats with titles)
  and `ide://agent/usage/limits` (no network). `ide://agent/usage` is unchanged (this window's
  sessions).
- **Entry points**: three buttons under the Chats view's search box — Agents (the Agents page),
  Settings (Settings → Agent), Usage — icon and label, labels hidden under 210 px; "Usage" in the
  chat's ⋯ menu (after Configure agents…); Settings → Agent: a "Usage" row above the first
  section (like Models and providers) and a ↗ link in the navigation.
- **Left as is**: subagents' requests are in the log (and the page's "this chat" total) but not
  in the chat's own cost and budget, as before; the chat cost shown under answers is unchanged.

**From the release audit**
- `process_output`'s filter runs on the UI thread: a pattern over 200 characters, or one that can
  backtrack badly (a quantified group with a quantifier or `|` inside, a backreference), matches
  as plain text, and only a line's first 2 000 characters are tested.
- Clear chats stops the deleted chats' background commands, as Delete chat does.
- `ide://agent/processes` leaves the output out (agents read state, and a chat mustn't read
  another's output); `agent.listProcesses` (not for agents) still has its end.
- An ended command keeps the last 200 000 characters of its output; a failed one counts toward
  the 10 kept per chat too. The chat's list registers its listeners in a store.
- The Usage page reads the whole log on opening and after it's cleared only; new records are
  added as they're written, and a redraw waits while the budget field has focus.
- A change bar's diff uses the bars' base (`git.quickDiffBase` HEAD or merge base, through a
  `quickDiffBase:` content source); revealing a line in an open diff with no changes no longer
  leaves a jump pending.
- File nesting looks names without `*` up instead of testing every file (5 000 files: tens of ms).
- gulp and grunt task names with spaces, quotes or shell characters aren't listed.
- The usage log skips a bad record instead of the whole batch, ignores times more than a day
  ahead, and rotates under the write lock; a failed write is logged in the console.
- Task detection is reused for 4 s (a burst of task commands lists the folders once).
- Not changed: the explorer's nest maps keep stale entries until the folder reloads (harmless:
  expanding checks children).

### D202 — m7.3: notebooks through providers, extension API for kernels and more, small fixes

**Small fixes**
- Showing the Chats view puts focus on its list (the current chat), not the search box: toggling
  the side bar doesn't start a search (VS Code's views focus their tree).
- Room past the last item: every tree (Explorer, Search, Outline, Problems, Source control,
  Testing…) has one row of empty space after its last row (VS Code's explorer `paddingBottom`), the
  Timeline the same; settings pages can scroll their last setting up to about the middle (45 % of
  the window). Empty lists don't get it (no scroll bar on nothing).
- A double-click on a control in a Markdown preview (a diagram's zoom, fit, source and copy
  buttons, a diagram you pan, links, fields, code block headers) no longer opens the source; the
  same in notebook Markdown cells (`isMarkdownControl`). Double-clicking text still does.
- `dev.click` takes `double` (two clicks and a dblclick, for tests).

**Notebooks through providers** (preparing the move to a built-in extension:
docs/notebook-extension-plan.md had the inventory and the plan; removed in D204 once done)
- VS Code's split: the IDE keeps one notebook editor; a *notebook type* brings the file format (a
  serializer) and *kernel sources* list and start kernels. `services.notebooks`
  (`core/notebook/providers.ts`, DOM-free, tested) holds both; the editor, the diff view and
  `notebook.new` use only it. The IDE registers its Jupyter format (`jupyter-notebook`, `.ipynb`)
  and kernel source (`jupyter`, for Jupyter notebooks only) the same way an extension does. The
  notebook data stays in nbformat's terms (cells, mime-bundle outputs, kernel events): the format
  every notebook tool speaks, and what the output renderers draw.
- Each type registers its own "default" viewer, so its files open in the notebook editor; the
  static `.ipynb` viewer entry went. A file whose type went away (its extension disabled) says so.
- Kernel options (`KernelOption`: source, id, label, detail, language, data) replace the Jupyter
  choice; remembered kernels saved before are converted. Sources made for a type are listed before
  general ones. A kernel whose source went away is dropped and another is picked.
- `ide://notebook` lists the types and gives the active notebook's type; `notebook.new` takes
  `type`; Export as script works for any file extension; the diff's toggle says "Show text" for
  non-JSON formats.

**`ide.notebooks` for extensions**
- `contributes.notebooks: [{ type, displayName, extensions }]` (the type starts with the
  extension's id or prefix) and `ide.notebooks.registerSerializer(type, { deserialize, serialize })`
  — only for its own types (no taking over `.ipynb`). The worker starts when such a file opens;
  the IDE waits up to 10 s for the serializer.
- `ide.notebooks.registerKernelSource({ id, label, notebookTypes?, find, start })`: `start` returns
  the kernel (`execute(code, run)` with `run.emit(event)` and `run.input(prompt)`, optional
  interrupt, restart, shutdown, complete, inspect, variables, comm) and gets a host
  (`setStatus`, `setInfo` with `mode: "jupyter"` for live widgets, `emit` for outputs of no cell,
  `comm`, `exited`). Without `notebookTypes` a source runs every type, the IDE's Jupyter notebooks
  included (a remote Jupyter server extension).
- Host side `runtimeNotebooks.ts` (`ExtensionKernel` implements `NotebookKernel`); worker side
  `core/extensions/rpcNotebooks.ts` (tested). A cell's `execute` call has no time limit (worker
  calls got an optional timeout); answers are checked and capped (outputs need an `output_type`,
  lists are capped, strings cut). When the extension stops its kernels are dead and running cells
  end with an error.
- Tested end to end by `tests/fixtures/extensions/toybook` (a `.toynb` format and an adder kernel)
  in `tests/scripts/notebook-ext-m7-3.jsonc`.

**General extension API** (for kernel-running extensions and extensions in general)
Context: the Jupyter notebook moves to a built-in extension on the public API (the notebook
editor stays in the core, VS Code's model). A kernel-running extension, and extensions in
general, need more than D102/D176 gave them. Everything below is checked on the host side like
the rest of the API, and everything an extension adds goes when it stops.

- **`ide.process.spawn({ command, args, cwd, env, framing })`** → `{ id, send, onMessage,
  onStderr, onExit, kill }`. *Why:* kernels, linters' servers, tools an extension ships. Built on
  the stdio host the language servers use (`lspIpc`, Rust `lsp` module) with ndjson framing on
  the Rust side; "lines" vs "ndjson" is only how the worker treats a line (string vs parsed
  JSON; a line that isn't JSON arrives as its text). No new Tauri command. *Security:* needs the
  `shell` permission **and** a trusted folder (`services.trust.require`, the same gate as the
  folder's tasks; a restricted folder refuses, an undecided one asks once), and an open folder.
  `cwd` defaults to the open folder and must be inside it or inside the extension's own folder
  (checked in TS; Rust `lsp_start` now also accepts any extension folder, installed or
  unpacked, via `ExtensionStore::folder_within`, canonicalized, UNC refused). Ids on the host are
  `ext:<id>:<n>`, so the MCP `${secret:…}` expansion never applies. *Limits:* 8 at a time per
  extension; killed when the extension stops/is disabled/reloads, when its worker crashes, when
  the folder closes, and when the folder is put in restricted mode (trust taken back). Output is
  batched to the worker (≤ 256 events or 8 ms per call); output before the first listener is
  kept (≤ 1000 lines). `onExit(code, signal)`: `signal` is "SIGKILL" when kill() or the IDE ended
  it (Rust reports no signals). `send` in "lines" mode writes a multi-line string as several
  lines; ≤ 16 MB per send; stderr lines cut at 8 KB.
- **`ide.extension.path`** (absolute folder) and **`ide.env.platform`** ("windows" | "macos" |
  "linux"), passed in the worker's init message. Bundled extensions are already on disk there
  (`seed_bundled` writes every file of `BUNDLED` into `<data>/extensions/<id>`, and rewrites them
  when the app ships different ones), so `node ${ide.extension.path}/kernel.js` works for them.
  No permission (it reveals only the app's data folder).
- **Workspace trust:** `ide.workspace.isTrusted()`, `requireTrust(reason)` (asks when undecided,
  resolves true/false, never throws), `onDidChangeTrust(cb)` (sugar over the event below). No
  permission: knowing whether the folder is trusted isn't sensitive and the dialog is the IDE's.
- **Folder lifecycle events** through `ide.events.on`: `workspace.didOpen`, `workspace.willClose`
  (no veto; `reason` "folder" | "window"; unsaved editors can still cancel the close after it),
  `workspace.didClose`, `workspace.didChangeTrust` ({ trusted }). No permission to subscribe; the
  payload carries `path` only with `fs.read` (a folder's path is about the user's files).
- **Context keys:** `ide.context.set(key, value)` for keys starting with "<extension id>." only
  (so it can't fake `workspaceTrusted`, `editorFocus`… or another extension's keys); strings ≤
  500 chars, numbers, booleans; null removes; ≤ 100 keys; cleared when it stops or its worker
  dies.
- **Dialogs:** `ide.ui.showDialog({ title, message, actions, cancel })` → label | undefined
  (modal, `ui/Dialog`'s `showDialog`). *Security:* the message ends with "Asked by the “<name>”
  extension." so it can't pass for the IDE's own question; 1–4 actions, labels ≤ 60 chars; one
  dialog at a time per extension (queued); an open one is aborted (→ undefined) when it stops.
- **Quick pick** items take `icon` (validated with `safeIcon`, unknown → a dot) and `detail`
  (shown as the row's tooltip: the quick input's rows are fixed-height and virtualized, so no
  second line; `QuickPickItem.detail` added).
- **`readsSettings`** manifest field: setting keys or "prefix.*" its code may read beyond its own
  and editor/workbench/files ones (`settingsAccess.ts`). *Security:* `agent.*`, `ai.*`, `mcp.*`,
  `accounts.*`, `http.*` and any key with a secret-like *word* (token, secret, password, passwd,
  apikey/apiKey, key, credential(s), auth, cookie; split at dots, dashes, underscores and
  camelCase, so "keybindings" or "tokenizer" pass) are refused at parse time (the manifest
  doesn't load) and again at read time, for every key that isn't the extension's own — that also
  newly covers editor/workbench/files keys named like secrets. `settings.onChange` now reports
  own + readsSettings keys (patterns expanded over registered settings, re-evaluated as settings
  register). Shown on the extension page's Permissions tab ("It also reads these settings").
- **`ide.state.register(path, getter)`:** paths under `ide://ext/<extension id>` (any extension;
  its own paths are also readable by it through `state.get`), or a path a *shipped* bundled
  extension declares in `contributes.state` (manager passes `bundled` only for an installed,
  non-customized, registry-bundled one whose id starts with "bundled."; a dev copy can't claim
  core paths) if nothing registered it. The host calls the worker (`CallMessage` kind "state")
  and answers `{ error }` after 2 s; ≤ 20 paths; removed when it stops or its worker dies.
  `contributes.state` entries give the path's description; a non-bundled manifest naming a path
  outside its namespace is refused.
- **Command input schemas:** `contributes.commands[].input`, a small JSON Schema (top level an
  object; string/number/integer/boolean/array/object, `description`, `enum`, `required`,
  `minimum`/`maximum`, `minLength`/`maxLength`, `maxItems`, `additionalProperties` true/false,
  depth ≤ 8, ≤ 100 properties) → the dispatcher's `s.*` schema (`commandInput.ts`), so agents
  see the shape and the dispatcher validates (unknown keys refused unless additionalProperties
  is true, as for built-ins; the palette asks for required fields). Invalid → a warning on the
  extension and `s.unknown()`. The handler's second argument is `{ caller }`: "user" (user and
  test scripts), "agent" (agent, ACP, MCP), "extension", "other"; sent as `CallMessage.context`.
- **Permission text:** `shell` now reads "Run programs (terminals, tasks, its own processes)".
- The stdio host's ndjson reader replaces bytes that aren't UTF-8 (a program printing binary no
  longer ends its stream) and skips the rest of a line over 64 MB.

**Still missing** (for the notebook move and later extensions)
- **Long commands:** a worker call (commands included) times out after 30 s (`CALL_MS` in
  workerHost.ts). Running a long cell through an extension command will fail; the extension
  should answer at once and report progress through its state path/events, or the host needs a
  per-command timeout / progress API.
- **Empty stdout lines are dropped** (ndjson reader skips blank lines), so "lines" mode can't see
  them.
- **No signals other than kill:** no SIGINT/CTRL_BREAK for interrupting a kernel (the current
  notebook kernel interrupts with a message, which works with this API), no closing stdin.
- **Bundled extensions are text only:** `BUNDLED` uses `include_str!`, so a bundled kernel
  extension can't ship binary files; dev copies of a bundled extension can't claim core state
  paths (develop with `ide://ext/<id>` or build the app).
- **Rust cwd check is coarse:** `lsp_start` accepts any extension's folder, not just the caller's
  (the webview can't tell which extension asks; the TS host limits it to the extension's own).
- No `willClose` veto/await (an extension can't flush kernel state before the folder closes), no
  dialog inputs/checkboxes, no process list in `ide://extensions` live info (easy to add), and
  `process.spawn` isn't available without an open folder.
- `workspace.willClose` also fires for the window closing; extensions get it but can't delay it.

**From the change audit**
- An extension kernel's running cells end (error) when it shuts down, exits or its extension
  stops, so the notebook's run queue never waits on a kernel that's gone; a worker crash marks its
  kernels dead and its serializers unregistered.
- The notebook view looks its type up by id on every read and write, and keeps the kernel source
  that made its kernel: after an extension reloads, saving uses the new serializer and a kernel of
  the old one is replaced.
- Switching kernels makes the new one before shutting the old one down; a remembered kernel whose
  source is missing falls back to finding one. A kernel shut down while starting is stopped once
  its start finishes. Restart without the extension's own restart shuts down and starts again.
- A kernel is picked by itself only among kernels made for the notebook's type; one that runs
  every type (an extension's) is the user's pick, and the picker names its extension.
- A file extension belongs to one notebook type (no taking `.ipynb` or another's files); an
  extension's type opens its files by default only with `"default": true`, and only then are its
  files' diffs compared cell by cell.
- Outputs from an extension's notebook data are read like a file's (nbformat line lists joined;
  `core/notebook/nbformat.ts`).
- Processes: one stopped while it started is stopped once it has; a worker crash forgets its
  processes; sends are capped at 100 000 lines.
- Settings: blocked areas are checked before the extension's own keys, `lsp.*` is blocked too,
  and `accounts`, `ai`, `http` are reserved short names. A command's input always allows `path`
  (menus pass it). Kernel option data is capped at 16 KB.
- The stdio host's stderr reader keeps reading through bytes that aren't UTF-8 and cuts lines at
  8 KB (a stopped reader filled the pipe and blocked the program); `//server` paths are refused
  like `\\server` ones in the extension-folder check. The settings page's scroll room is a token
  (`--scroll-past-page`).


### D203 — m7.4: Jupyter as a built-in extension, staged change bars, five gaps

**Change bars and their diff**
- Staged lines show too, dimmed (40 % opacity), beside the unstaged ones, as VS Code draws them:
  with the bars against the index (the default), the file is also compared with HEAD and the lines
  HEAD differs on that the index already has are the staged ones (`stagedMarks`, core/diff,
  tested). Nothing staged (HEAD and the index the same) costs no second diff.
- A click on a staged bar opens the staged diff (HEAD ↔ index); on another bar, the working-tree
  diff (or the bars' base, D202). The diff opens as a tab of its own, not a preview: the file's
  preview (italic) tab you clicked in stays open, so you can go back and forth.

**Usage page**
- OpenRouter's key endpoint reports the API key's own spending limit, not the account balance
  (that needs a management key: `GET /credits` refuses ordinary keys). The row is now "Key limit"
  with a note saying so and pointing to openrouter.ai for the balance; the page's lead says costs
  are estimates and limits are what providers last reported, to check the provider's dashboard
  for exact figures.

**Small UI**
- Menus truncate a long right-hand text (a preset's models) with an ellipsis instead of growing
  past their maximum width and scrolling sideways (`.menu-keybinding`, `.menu-items` no
  horizontal overflow).
- Buttons beside a selector chip in a page header (Agents: New subagent…; AI models: Agent
  settings, Edit in settings.json) have the chip's height, field and edge (`.ai-header-button`).

**Jupyter moves into a built-in extension** (`src-tauri/bundled-extensions/jupyter`, D202's plan)
- `bundled.jupyter`, seeded off like Canvas: its `main.js` registers the `.ipynb` format
  (`jupyter.notebook`, nbformat 4 read and written as before: unknown fields kept, sorted keys,
  one-space indents, lines as lists; tested from the IDE's unit tests by running main.js with a
  stand-in `ide`) and the kernel source `bundled.jupyter/jupyter` (each Python found —
  `jupyter.pythonPath`, then the old `notebook.pythonPath` through `readsSettings`, the folder's
  `.venv` / `venv` / `env` / `.env`, `debug.pythonPath`, `python3` / `python`, `py -3` on Windows —
  probed three at a time with `kernel_host.py --list`, then its Jupyter kernels or plain Python).
  Each kernel is `kernel_host.py` started with `ide.process.spawn` (ndjson), the same protocol as
  before; outputs, input, comms (widgets live: `mode: "jupyter"`), variables, completions, inspect,
  interrupt, restart and shutdown go through `ide.notebooks`. Permissions: "Run programs" and
  "Read files"; finding kernels asks for workspace trust.
- The IDE keeps the notebook editor, the output frame (`notebook_output_origin`), the cell diff and
  the `notebook.*` commands; `kernel.ts`, the ipynb parser/writer and Rust's `notebook_host_path`
  are gone. The type's extra fields (nbformat_minor, unknown top-level and cell fields) travel
  through `NotebookData.extra`, given back to `serialize` unchanged (new in the API).
- Off by default (the owner's choice): `.ipynb` opens as JSON until it's turned on;
  `notebook.new` and a notebook tab say "Jupyter notebooks need the Jupyter extension: turn it on
  in Extensions". A notebook tab restored at startup waits up to 10 s for its format (extensions
  start after the layout). Kernels remembered by D188–D202 (`{ python, kernel }` or source
  `jupyter`) become the extension's (`jupyter.ts`, tested).
- Its icon and the `.ipynb` file icon are an original drawing (a page of two cells,
  `notebook-cells` in the sprite; the extension's own `icon.svg`), not Jupyter's logo, which is a
  trademark; `.ipynb` files get a tint of their own (`--file-icon-notebook`).

**Extension programs and commands**
- `process.closeStdin()` (the program reads end-of-file) and `process.interrupt()` (SIGINT;
  refused on Windows, where a console program without its own console can't be sent Ctrl+C:
  programs there take a message) — Rust `lsp_close_stdin`, `lsp_interrupt` (tested).
- An extension's command runs as long as it takes, as in VS Code (it timed out after 30 s); tree,
  hover, completion and state calls keep their limits.

**Explorer: a folded nest parent takes its nested files along**
- What: delete, cut, copy, duplicate and a drag of a nest parent (explorer.fileNesting) that is
  collapsed act on its nested files too; the delete confirmation counts them ("delete these 3
  items?") and lists their names. An expanded parent acts on itself only: its nested files are rows
  of their own, selected or not.
- Why: VS Code's behaviour. Its explorer context adds a collapsed item's `nestedChildren` to the
  selection (`ExplorerService.getContext`), and its drop handler does the same for dragged items.
  A folded row is visually one item, so acting on part of it surprised people (a moved `a.ts` left
  `a.js` and `a.js.map` behind).
- How: `withNestedFiles(paths, nestedOf, isCollapsed)` in `explorer/nesting.ts` (DOM-free, tested);
  `ExplorerView.withNestedFiles` gives it the parents' nested paths (the view now keeps
  parent → nested paths) and the tree's expansion. The commands apply it to the explorer selection
  by default; with given `path` / `paths` (agents, scripts) only with `withNested: true`, which the
  context menu's Delete (one row) and a drag (explorer.move) pass. New input `withNested` on
  `explorer.delete`, `explorer.cut`, `explorer.copy` and `explorer.move`.
- Limits: what is expanded is read when the command runs (confirm and run see the same tree). Undo,
  import updates and open editors follow each moved file as before (one entry for the group).

**Agent rules: nested `.cursor/rules`, subfolders of the rules folders**
- What: a subfolder's own `.cursor/rules` (`web/.cursor/rules/style.mdc`, Cursor's nested rules)
  holds for files under that subfolder: `alwaysApply` becomes a folder rule (attached on the first
  read or edit of a file under `web/`, like a subfolder's AGENTS.md), `globs` match only under the
  folder (relative to it, or written from the root), a description rule is listed "for files in
  web/". Subfolders inside `.cursor/rules` and `.github/instructions`
  (`.github/instructions/frontend/x.instructions.md`, VS Code reads them) are read as well;
  `applyTo` keeps matching from the root, as Copilot's does.
- Why: monorepos keep rules per package; Cursor and VS Code read them, the IDE read only the root's
  two folders, one level.
- How: `classifyRule` sets `folder` on a nested Cursor rule and `ruleCovers` checks it;
  `nestedRuleFiles` (DOM-free, tested) picks them from two index lookups. The index skips
  gitignored folders and `.git`; the agent's own ignore rules (`.aiignore`, `.cursorignore`,
  agent.ignoreFiles) leave a nested rules file out. Same caching (30 s, invalidated by a rules file
  change), same limits (60 nested files, 40 000 characters a file, 8 000 per rule in the prompt).
  Only with `agent.thirdPartyConfigs`.
- Limits: found through the index, so a folder being indexed shows them a moment later (as nested
  AGENTS.md). `.github/instructions` folders below the root (`web/.github/instructions`) aren't
  read: Copilot doesn't either.

**Slash commands: subfolders, `allowed-tools` narrowing the turn**
- What: `.claude/commands/frontend/test.md` (and the same in the other commands folders) is
  `/frontend:test`, up to three levels (`/a:b:name`), 200 files per folder. A command whose front
  matter lists `allowed-tools` gets, for its own turn, only those tools plus every read-only tool
  (read, list, search, find files, state, update_plan…); the next message has every tool again.
  Claude Code's tool names map to the IDE's (`Bash(…)` → run_command, process_output,
  kill_process; `Read` → read_file; `Edit` / `MultiEdit` → edit_file; `Write` → write_file;
  `Grep` → search; `Glob` / `LS` → find_files, list_dir; `Task` → delegate, explore; `WebSearch` →
  web_search; `TodoWrite` → update_plan); the IDE's own names and `mcp__server` /
  `mcp__server__tool` work as written. A space-separated list is read too (Claude Code takes both).
- Why: the subfolder names are Claude Code's (`/frontend:component`). For `allowed-tools`, Claude
  Code's current docs say the list *pre-approves* tools for the turn and doesn't restrict them. The
  IDE already refuses pre-approval from a project's command file (a cloned repository could run
  anything when its command name is typed, D200 review), so the list is read the other, safe way:
  as the tools the command needs. Read-only tools stay so a command naming only
  `Bash(git diff:*)` can still read the files the diff mentions. The `Bash(…)` patterns still
  pre-approve `!` lines in the user's own command files, as before.
- How: `commandNameFor` / `commandFileFor` / `commandTools` in `core/agent/slash.ts` (tested);
  `promptSlash` returns `allowedTools`, `agent.send` sets `session.nextTurnTools`, which the turn
  takes into `turnAllowedTools` when it starts (like `nextTurnModel`) and drops when it ends;
  `session.tools()` filters by it after the mode's filter (Ask and Plan stay read-only). An
  external agent's turn drops it (its tools can't be narrowed).
- Limits: narrowing changes that turn's tool list, so its prompt prefix isn't cached. A command
  sent while a turn runs is queued with its tools (as with `model`). No `disallowed-tools` yet.

**Task detection two levels deep**
- What: build files are looked for down to `task.autoDetectDepth` folder levels (new setting,
  0–3, default 2: `packages/app/Makefile` gives `make: build - packages/app`). 0 is the root only.
- Why: monorepos keep their packages one level further down (`packages/*`, `apps/*`, `crates/*`).
- How: `foldersToScan` in `tasks/detect.ts` (DOM-free, tested) lists level by level, shallow
  folders first, at most 80 folders in all (was 40 first-level ones), skipping hidden, ignored,
  linked and heavy folders (node_modules, target, build, dist, out, vendor, venv, coverage, bin,
  obj…). A Cargo, Gradle or Maven folder's members aren't detected again at any level. The 4 s
  reuse cache's key includes the depth.
- Limits: a build file added two levels down shows up after the 4 s reuse (the key is the root's
  listing). Makefiles are still read, not run.

**From the full audit** (three read-only reviews: the Rust backend; extensions, notebooks and the
agent; the workbench and editors)
- Windows `.cmd` / `.bat` servers (npx, pip shims) are started by their path: Rust's std runs them
  through cmd.exe and escapes their arguments (refusing ones it can't make safe), where our own
  `cmd /C` broke on quoted paths and let `&`, `|`, `%` in arguments through.
- An extension's `net.fetch` no longer follows redirects in Rust: the IDE follows them (5 at
  most), checking every new address against the extension's network permission (a redirect to
  127.0.0.1 or a LAN host was read with a permission for one public domain).
- `\\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\Mup\…` and `\\.\…` paths count as network paths (only a drive or a
  volume after `\\?\` is local): they reached SMB and the user's NTLM credentials.
- Command output keeps a character split between two reads (it became U+FFFD), and PowerShell
  commands write UTF-8.
- A reload or exit kills the terminals' process trees on Windows (dev servers kept their ports);
  a server replaced by a second start of the same id is killed; accept loops pause on errors
  instead of spinning.
- Secret files (`ai` keys, the MCP info file, the account) are written through a 0600 temporary
  file and the keys file under a lock (two keys saved at once both stay); history ids are
  letters, digits, `_` and `-` only.
- Extension workers can't create code at run time (eval, the function constructors, string
  timers) and code with `import(` is refused: `import()` loads from any URL, a way around the
  network permission. `WebSocketStream` is removed with the other network APIs.
- Only the shipped Jupyter extension may read `.ipynb` files or use the `jupyter.notebook` type;
  `jupyter`, `notebook`, `debug` and `testing` are reserved short names (the IDE's own extensions
  keep theirs). Notebook data from an extension isn't capped (a cap dropped outputs on save);
  files up to 512 MB.
- Jupyter kernels: cells and requests sent during a restart wait for it; a kernel that never says
  hello is stopped; a failed Jupyter restart falls back to a fresh start; a new kernel starts
  before the old one is shut down (a failed switch keeps the old one); stderr from an earlier
  process isn't shown for a later crash; the IDE's shipped extensions may run 32 programs (8 for
  others).
- A slash command's model and `allowed-tools` are dropped when its message goes back to the box
  (send failed, Stop, Take back) instead of applying to the next one.
- The extension viewer closes on a delete reported with other letter case; a notebook with a BOM
  isn't re-read on every change event.
- Checked and not changed: search already prunes symlinks pointing outside the folder (the Rust
  audit's search finding was a false alarm). Left for later (feature-gaps): streaming HTML through
  the preview proxy, git's repo-defined fsmonitor/filters in untrusted folders, the job object's
  spawn race, cookies shared across the local proxies' ports.

**Workbench fixes from the audit**
- **Settings writes refuse a broken settings.json.** `update`, `updateForLanguage` and
  `updateMany` all go through `editableText(scope)`, which calls
  `assertEditableJsoncObject` (`core/settings/jsoncEdit.ts`): a file with a syntax error (or a
  top level that isn't an object) throws "Your user settings.json has a syntax error (line N); fix
  it first so nothing in it is lost." User-run commands show it as a toast. `setJsoncProperty` /
  `setJsoncNestedProperty` throw `JsoncEditError` instead of returning a new one-key object when the
  text has content but no readable top-level object (empty or comment-only text still gets a fresh
  object, comments kept). `mergeSettingsText` returns null for a broken own file, so "Merge into…"
  leaves it alone.
- **Window close with hot exit asks about what has no backup.** The close participant moved into
  `registerHotExit`: on a window close it asks (the same Save / Don't save / Cancel dialog,
  `confirmCloseAll(among)`) about the dirty documents `backupsOf` leaves out (over 2 MB, past the
  10 MB total, no model yet, not a text editor), and skips asking only when every dirty document is
  backed up (`withoutBackup`).
- **No folder open: closing the window asks.** Persistence only saves with a folder, so with no
  workspace root the close falls back to `confirmCloseAll()` (untitled editors were lost before).
- **Autosave skips untitled editors** (`canAutoSave`), as VS Code does: no Save as dialog popping up
  after a pause, on focus change or window change.
- **Keybindings don't run under a modal dialog.** `isModalDialogOpen()` (`ui/Dialog.ts`, a stack of
  open dialogs) is checked first in `KeyboardService.onKeyDown`, whose window capture listener runs
  before the dialog's own. The dialog is focusable (`tabindex="-1"`), so a click on its text keeps
  focus inside it (Esc, Tab still work); Tab from the dialog itself goes to the first (Shift+Tab: the
  last) control; focus that lands outside the topmost dialog is brought back.
- **Git status from a previous folder is dropped.** `GitController.refresh` captures
  `openGeneration` before awaiting and discards a stale status / repo state (and reads again for the
  new repository).
- **Explorer rows' accessible name follows the row.** `setTooltip` replaces an aria-label it set
  itself on the next call, and takes `ariaLabel: false`; recycled rows (explorer, git commit files,
  search folders, extension tree views) pass it, so their text names them instead of the first path
  they showed.
- **Hot-exit restore keeps unapplied backups.** While the restore runs, `save()` returns the
  backups not applied yet along with the current ones (`withPending`), so an early scheduled save no
  longer writes an empty list; a folder switch stops the restore (generation). A backup that can't be
  applied (file deleted, model never came) opens as an untitled editor with its text and a warning
  toast; if even that fails it stays in the saved state.
- **Smaller races.** `editor.openFile` drops a file whose read finished after a folder switch (no old
  folder's file in the new one); `checkDisk` keeps a per-document generation, so an older read that
  finishes last can't flag a deletion or apply stale text. Comments name "the legacy folder name"
  instead of the former product's folder.

### D204 — m7.5: alpha support; the editor, notebooks, git, terminal, debugger, testing, the agent and MCP

Ten areas worked on side by side, each on its own branch, merged for m7.5. Placeholders that
wait for the owner (product.json `issuesUrl`, the beta update endpoint) are listed in
docs/feature-gaps.md; the Windows checks and the owner's release steps are in
docs/windows-pending.md.

#### Workbench

- **Chats side panel like Claude's sidebar** (`chatsView.ts`): the search box on top, then a
  vertical nav of plain rows without backgrounds until hover: New chat, Usage, Configure agents,
  Agent settings; **More** expands to Manage providers, MCP servers, Agent memory and Tidy up
  memory. The old row of buttons under the search box went (and its styles in `agent-usage.css`).
- **Title bar search box:** its background is the header's own (transparent, marked by its
  border) instead of a darker well.
- **Editor info in the main status bar** (VS Code's): the active editor's Ln/Col (with the
  selection's length), indentation (Spaces: N / Tab size: N), encoding, EOL and language, each
  opening its picker (`editor.gotoLine`, the new `editor.selectIndentation`,
  `editor.selectEncoding`, `editor.changeEol`, `editor.setLanguage`).
  `editor.selectIndentation {choice?}`: indent using spaces or tabs, size 2 / 4 / 8, convert
  indentation to spaces or tabs (VS Code's indentation picker). Setting
  `workbench.statusBar.editorInfo` (default on) hides them; people look there even with the
  per-file bar on. `state.ts`, `fileFormat.ts`.
- **Extension logos without a tinted tile:** a logo is drawn as it is (`.ext-avatar.has-image`),
  so any shape looks right, as in VS Code (an icon from the IDE's own set too); extensions with
  neither keep their initials on a tinted tile.
- **Welcome page:** a pinned folder's unpin button shows only on hover or focus, like pin and
  remove.
- `docs/notebook-extension-plan.md` removed: D202's plan for moving Jupyter into an extension is
  done (D203).
- UI test: `tests/scripts/ui-m7-5.jsonc`.

#### Alpha and release support

- **Help → Report a problem…** (`help.reportProblem {title?, description?}`, VS Code's "Report
  issue"): a singleton `report` dock tab with a title, "What happened", and the parts of the
  report, each with a checkbox and its exact text behind a disclosure: System (version, debug
  build, update channel, OS and Windows build, webview, language, window size, extensions on/off,
  the version updated from), Recent errors (the IDE's own errors from the session and the error
  notifications), Session log (its last 80 lines), one part per state path (`ide://workspace`,
  `layout`, `editors`, `extensions`, `lsp`, `update`, `perf`, `safeMode`), and a screenshot of the
  window taken as the report opens (off by default). Below, the full report text as it will be
  used. Ways out: **Open issue in browser** (product.json `issuesUrl` + `/new?title=&body=`; a URL
  is kept under 7 500 characters, which GitHub accepts; a longer body is cut with a note and the
  full text goes to the clipboard), **Copy report**, **Save as zip…** (Rust `report_save_zip`:
  report.md, system.txt, errors.txt, session.log, state.json, screenshot.png for the parts that
  are ticked). The IDE uploads nothing.
  - **Redaction** (`core/diagnostics/redact.ts`, the same text rules in Rust's
    `diagnostics/redact.rs`): known key formats (`sk-…`, `ghp_…`, `github_pat_…`, `xox?-…`,
    `AKIA…`, `AIza…`, `glpat-…`, `hf_…`), `Bearer`/`Basic`/`token <value>`, `key=value` and
    `"key": "value"` for names with api key, access/private key, token, secret, password, pwd,
    authorization, cookie, credential, signature; `user:password@` in URLs; the home folder
    becomes `~`, any other `C:\Users\<name>` / `/home/<name>` / `/Users/<name>` becomes `<user>`.
    State values additionally lose secrets by key name, file contents by key name (text, content,
    body, source, code, selection, preview, output, lines, diff, markdown, prompt, messages…:
    replaced by "<N characters>") and any string over 400 characters.
  - Why our own dialog and not VS Code's issue reporter: VS Code posts through its own GitHub
    integration; we can't use an account or a site (none yet), so the browser does the posting.
  - Limits: a screenshot can't travel in a link: with a folder open, "Open issue" saves it under
    the workspace's screenshots folder and shows it in the file manager to drag into the issue;
    without one, the zip carries it. Redaction is pattern-based: a secret in an unknown format
    and under an innocent name can slip through, which is why every part is shown and can be
    left out.
- **Logs** (`src-tauri/src/diagnostics/log.rs`): a log per session in
  `<data>/logs/sessions/session-<UTC time>-<pid>.log`, the last 10 kept, each capped at 4 MB
  (later lines dropped, with one line saying so), every line redacted on write. It holds the
  start line (version, OS, debug build, extensions off), the frontend's uncaught errors,
  unhandled rejections and `console.error` (the IDE's own code: extensions run in workers and
  frames with their own consoles), failed IPC calls (except the expected NotFound, Cancelled and
  NoWorkspace), failed commands, and Rust panics with a backtrace (`install_panic_hook`, which
  never waits for the log's lock). The frontend batches every 2 s, collapses repeats and caps a
  flood at 120 records a minute (`core/diagnostics/logBuffer.ts`). Help → Open logs folder
  (`help.openLogsFolder`) shows this session's file in the OS file manager (the opener plugin's
  reveal); `help.showLog` opens it read-only; `ide://logs?lines=n` gives the last lines.
- **Starting with extensions off** (VS Code's `--disable-extensions`): `--disable-extensions` on
  the command line, or Help → Restart with extensions off (`help.restartWithExtensionsOff`), which
  writes a one-shot `<data>/next-start-extensions` flag ("off") and restarts (Tauri's restart, after
  the same unsaved-files question as closing the window). While off, the extension manager starts
  no installed or bundled extension (each shows as disabled with the reason; built-in parts of
  the IDE keep working), a status bar item "Extensions off" and a warning notification offer
  "Restart normally" (`help.restartNormally`; for a session started with the flag it writes "on",
  which overrides the flag once since a restart repeats the process's arguments).
  `help.clearNextStart` undoes a pending flag. `ide://safeMode` {extensionsOff, reason, nextStart}.
- **What's new** (`help.showReleaseNotes {release?}`, Help → Release notes): `docs/release-notes.md`
  (bundled, short user-facing notes for m7.0–m7.5) in a `releaseNotes` dock tab. Rust keeps the
  version that ran last (`<data>/last-version`); when it differs from this one the tab opens by
  itself once the folder is restored (`perf.whenMarked("workspaceRestored")`), unless
  `update.showReleaseNotes` (default true) is off. Not on a first start (VS Code does the same).
- **Update channel**: `update.channel` ("stable" | "beta", default stable). Beta checks
  `IDE_UPDATE_BETA_ENDPOINT` (the release workflow passes the repository variable of that name)
  or product.json `updates.betaEndpoint`, through `updater_builder().endpoints(...)`, with the same
  public key; a build without a beta endpoint checks stable and says so when the user asked.
  `ide://update` has the channel; About shows "Update channel: …".
- **product.json** gained `issuesUrl` and `updates.betaEndpoint` (both empty for now; gen.mjs
  validates them).
- No new dependency: the zip writer is ~100 lines over flate2 (already used), dates are computed
  without chrono, redaction uses the `regex` crate already there.

#### Editor and language features

- **Legacy encodings, read and written.** Every WHATWG encoding is listed (UTF-8 / BOM, UTF-16
  LE/BE, 29 single-byte code pages, and Shift JIS, EUC-JP, ISO-2022-JP, GBK, GB 18030, Big5,
  EUC-KR) and can be saved. Decoding stays the webview's `TextDecoder`; the multi-byte ones are
  written by Rust with `encoding_rs` (`src-tauri/src/fs/encoding.rs`, command `encoding_encode`:
  body = the text as UTF-8, header `x-encoding`). It encodes without replacement: characters the
  encoding can't hold stop the save with their names ("Japanese (Shift JIS) can't hold "😀": save as
  UTF-8, or remove them."), so a save never writes `&#NNNN;`. Both sides use the same WHATWG tables,
  so a Shift JIS file opened and saved comes back byte-identical (Rust round-trip tests, UI test).
  Limit: WHATWG decoders fold a few duplicate code points (NEC/IBM extensions in Shift JIS), which
  are then written back with the standard byte sequence, as in VS Code and browsers.
- **Guessing with a real detector.** `files.autoGuessEncoding` now asks `chardetng` (Firefox's
  detector, `encoding_guess`) about text that isn't UTF-8 (no BOM, not binary, not BOM-less
  UTF-16), reading at most 256 KB; the guess wins over `files.encoding` (VS Code's order). Without a
  guess it falls back to `files.encoding`, then Windows-1252. Reopen with encoding lists the
  guessed encoding first ("guessed from content"). jschardet (LGPL) was not used.
- **New dependencies:** `chardetng` 1.0.0 (MIT/Apache-2.0, Mozilla's; about 200 KB of frequency
  tables compiled in; there's no permissive detector in the platform and writing one means
  per-language statistics), `encoding_rs` 0.8 (MIT/Apache-2.0; already compiled for grep-searcher,
  now a direct dependency; browsers have no encoder for these encodings and their tables are
  large).
- **Monaco's keys in the keyboard shortcuts editor.** Once the editor engine has loaded, its default
  keybindings (Ctrl+D, Alt+Up, Ctrl+/, F12, Ctrl+K Ctrl+C…, read from Monaco's keybinding service
  with their `when` clauses and action titles) are rows of the table ("Editor" source), next to
  its unbound actions. keybindings.json takes Monaco's command ids directly (`editor.action.*`,
  `cursorDown`…, as in VS Code); rules for them are handed to Monaco as its own user rules
  (`monaco.editor.addKeybindingRules`), so Monaco checks its `when` contexts and `-command`
  removals apply to its defaults as in VS Code. The IDE's capture listener knows the engine's rules
  and lets their keys through to the editor (behind the IDE's own defaults, as before); the user's
  rules win over both. It also resolves the second key of an engine chord whose first key the IDE
  took and runs it through `editor.runAction`: Monaco's Ctrl+K chords (Ctrl+K Ctrl+C comment,
  Ctrl+K Ctrl+0 fold all…) used to end in "That key combination is not a command". The UI test
  checks the resolution; the edit itself only reliably happened in one test build when the
  keys were synthetic events sent from inside a test command (unexplained: the same
  `editor.runAction` run directly works), so it's a manual test line below and a risk to verify.
- **Shortcuts editor, per binding (VS Code's):** Change keybinding moves that one binding (a user
  entry is changed in place; a default gets a removal rule with its key and `when`, plus the new
  rule) instead of replacing all of the command's keys; Add keybinding; Change when expression (a
  prompt; empty = always); Remove keybinding (that binding); Reset; Show same keybindings; search by
  key in quotes (`"ctrl+d"`, any spelling, or the shown label). Edits keep keybindings.json's
  comments (`setJsoncArrayItem`). Commands `keybindings.changeKey`, `keybindings.changeWhen`,
  `keybindings.add`, `keybindings.remove {key?, when?}`; `ide://keybindings.engineBindings`.
  Conflicts between two of Monaco's own defaults aren't flagged (Monaco sorts them out by `when`);
  an IDE key on a Monaco key is.
- **Semantic tokens: deltas and ranges.** With a server that offers `full.delta`, the client keeps
  the last tokens per document and asks for `textDocument/semanticTokens/full/delta` with their
  result id, applying the edits itself (`core/lsp/semanticTokens.ts`; edits that don't fit fall back
  to a full request). With `range`, Monaco asks for the visible range while a document's full
  tokens are on their way (large files). `workspace/semanticTokens/refresh` re-fetches.
- **Semantic colors actually on.** Monaco's standalone theme never enabled semantic highlighting,
  so D199's semantic tokens weren't requested at all. `editor.semanticHighlighting.enabled` (default
  on, as Dark+ / Light+ have it) turns them on, and token types are colored through VS Code's
  type → TextMate scope table (function → `entity.name.function`, parameter → `variable.parameter`,
  readonly variable → `variable.other.constant`…; `monaco/semanticStyling.ts`). A token whose scopes
  the theme doesn't color keeps its syntax color, instead of turning the default foreground.
- **Workspace pull diagnostics.** A server with `diagnosticProvider.workspaceDiagnostics` is asked
  `workspace/diagnostic` with the previous result ids and a partial result token (results streamed
  through `$/progress` are applied as they come); at start, 1 s after edits (other files' problems
  may follow from one file, `interFileDependencies`), and on `workspace/diagnostic/refresh`; one
  request at a time, no timeout (servers may hold it open). Reports for files that aren't open show
  in Problems (markers of their own owner); an open file's own pull or push wins, and a file that
  closes gets the workspace report back.
- **Language server settings page.** "Language server settings" (palette, the status bar item's
  menu, `lsp.openServerSettings`) lists every server (built-in and `lsp.servers`): its known
  settings as controls (a built-in table for pyright, rust-analyzer, gopls,
  typescript-language-server, clangd, yaml-language-server and lua-language-server: type, choices,
  default, description) and the user's `settings` / `initializationOptions` as JSON. Writes go to
  `lsp.servers.<name>.settings` (or `.initializationOptions`); the user's objects are now merged
  key by key over the server's own (they used to replace them). A settings-only change is sent with
  `workspace/didChangeConfiguration` carrying the merged settings (servers that pull them ask again
  through `workspace/configuration`), with no restart; an initialization option or command change
  restarts the server. After start the client also sends the settings once (servers such as
  typescript-language-server read them only there). Commands `lsp.serverSettings`,
  `lsp.setServerSetting {server, key, value?, target?}`, `lsp.setServerSettingsJson`; state
  `ide://lsp/settings`.
- Test helper: `dev.type` takes `alt`.

#### Notebooks and ghost-text suggestions

- **`.ipynb` without the extension again:** D204 reverses D203's "serializer in the
  extension": the IDE reads and writes `.ipynb` itself again, so a notebook opens as a notebook
  with the Jupyter extension off; the bundled Jupyter extension only provides kernels (see
  "Notebooks out of the box" below).

**Language servers in notebook cells** (`notebook.languageServer.enabled`, default on)
- What: a notebook's code cells go to the language servers of their language (Pyright, pylsp,
  any `lsp.servers` entry for the language) as one document, VS Code's "concatenated document":
  names defined in one cell are known in the next. Diagnostics show as squiggles in the cells and
  in Problems under the notebook with the cell ("[Cell 3, Ln 1, Col 7]"; `problems.list` and
  `problems.copy` carry `cell: { id, index }` / "(cell 3)"); a click opens the notebook at that
  cell's line (`notebook.revealCell`). Hover, completion (with resolve), signature help, go to
  definition (into another cell too), type definition, references, highlights and rename work in
  cells. Opening a notebook starts its language's servers like opening a file does.
- Why: Python notebooks in VS Code get Pylance in every cell; the IDE's cells had only the
  kernel's completions and hovers (which need a running kernel).
- How: `core/notebook/concat.ts` (DOM-free, tested): `ConcatDocument` joins the code cells (one
  newline between cells) and maps positions both ways; Jupyter's magics are masked in Python with
  the first character turned into `#` so no column moves (`%%bash` cells entirely, `%pip` / `!ls`
  lines); `cellDiagnostics` drops problems on masked lines and Pyright's `reportUnusedExpression`
  on a cell's last line (the cell's displayed result, as Pylance does). The joined document is
  opened in the server as `<notebook>.concat.<ext>` beside the notebook (no file is written), so
  relative imports resolve as in the folder. `monaco/notebookLsp.ts` (`NotebookLanguageHub`): one
  session per (server, notebook), the text sent 150 ms after the last edit and before every
  request, pull diagnostics too (D200). The engine contract is `NotebookLanguageSource` /
  `engine.attachNotebook` (engine.ts); the notebook view registers itself (`notebook/language.ts`).
  `diagnostics()` includes every cell's problems, whether its editor exists or not. The file
  servers' rename providers now skip models that aren't theirs (cells).
- Limits: completion edits that land in another cell (an auto-import at the top of the
  notebook) are dropped, the completion itself is kept; rename edits reach the cells and open
  files only; code actions, formatting, semantic tokens and inlay hints aren't mapped into cells;
  a renamed notebook's already-open cells map again after reopening it; IPython-only syntax
  besides magics (`x = !ls`, `obj?`, top-level `await` flagged by Pyright) isn't masked. Kernel
  completions still come alongside the server's (both lists show, as in VS Code with Jupyter).

**Find across cells**
- What: Ctrl+F in a notebook (in a cell's editor too) opens a find bar over the cells' top right:
  every cell's source is searched (Markdown and code), optionally the outputs' text; case, whole
  word and regular expression toggles; "3 of 12"; Enter / Shift+Enter next / previous (wrapping),
  the match is shown and selected (a Markdown cell opens for editing, as VS Code does); Ctrl+H or
  the chevron shows Replace: Replace (the current match, then the next; `$1` in regex mode) and
  Replace all (Ctrl+Alt+Enter), one undo step for every cell it changed. Matches are highlighted
  in the cells' editors (Monaco's find colors) and, by CSS highlights, in rendered Markdown and
  outputs.
- How: `core/notebook/find.ts` (DOM-free, tested), `notebook/findBar.ts`, commands
  `notebook.find` (`query`, `caseSensitive`, `wholeWord`, `regex`, `outputs`, `markdown`, `code`,
  `replace`, `focus`), `findNext`, `findPrevious`, `replace`, `replaceAll`, `closeFind`;
  `ide://notebook` has `active.find`. Undo snapshots now keep the text of several cells.
- Limits: outputs are searched but never replaced; an output's current match is the n-th DOM
  match of that cell's outputs (rendered text can differ from the output's plain text); outputs
  in sandboxed frames (scripted HTML, widgets) aren't highlighted; 5000 matches at most.

**Notebook outline**
- What: the Outline view shows the active notebook: Markdown headings nested by level, code
  cells (their first line) under the heading above them; the selected cell is followed; a click
  reveals the cell (a code cell gets the cursor). `notebook.outline` gives the same to agents;
  `ide://editors/active/outline` too. `notebook.revealCell {cellId|index, line?, column?}`.
- How: `core/notebook/outline.ts` (tested); `OutlineTarget.custom` in `outlineView.ts` lets a
  target bring its own symbols and opening; code cells use the new `cell` symbol kind (code icon).
- Limits: no breadcrumbs for notebooks yet (VS Code shows the cell path above the notebook).

**Kernels beyond Python**
- Verified in code (no R or Julia here): kernelspecs of any language were already listed by
  `kernel_host.py --list` and run through `jupyter_client` (completion, inspect, interrupt,
  restart, comms are protocol-generic; the variables panel says "This kernel doesn't list its
  variables" for non-Python kernels, by design). Fixed: (1) R and Julia cells were plain text —
  the IDE now knows `r` (`.r`) and `julia` (`.jl`) with Shiki grammars and Monaco's language
  configurations (comments, brackets); (2) the kernel option's language kept the kernelspec's
  case ("R"), so the "kernel of the notebook's language" match never hit — the Jupyter extension
  lower-cases it; (3) an R or Julia notebook whose kernelspec name isn't installed fell back to
  the first kernel found, i.e. Python — now the kernel picker opens (agents get an error naming
  IRkernel / IJulia). The saved `kernelspec` keeps the kernel's own `language` ("R") and
  `display_name`, and `language_info.name` the kernel's language, as Jupyter writes them.
- Not verified (no R / Julia in the sandbox): IRkernel's and IJulia's actual startup through
  `kernel_host.py`, their completion replies, rich outputs (R's `text/html` tables, Julia's
  plots), and interrupt on Windows for them.

**Ghost-text suggestions (still off by default: `editor.inlineCompletions.enabled`)**
- What: fill-in-the-middle where the provider has it — Ollama `/api/generate` with `suffix`,
  Mistral's Codestral `/v1/fim/completions`, DeepSeek's `/beta/completions`, and with
  `editor.inlineCompletions.fim: "always"` any OpenAI-compatible `/v1/completions` with `suffix`
  (llama.cpp, LM Studio, vLLM); the chat prompt otherwise, and by itself when a model answers
  that it has no FIM ("does not support insert", 404, a refused `suffix`; remembered for the
  session). Each request carries up to four snippets: the window of another open file most like
  the code before the cursor (Jaccard over identifiers, 20-line windows) and the latest edits
  elsewhere (newest first, fading over 30 minutes), all inside `editor.inlineCompletions.contextTokens`
  (default 1536: the code near the cursor first, 20 % suffix, at most 30 % snippets). One line
  in the middle of a line, up to `editor.inlineCompletions.maxLines` (8) at the end of one; lines
  that run into the file's next line are cut; FIM special tokens are removed. `maxTokens`
  (default 128), `debounceMs` (350) and `context` (on) are settings; each key cancels the request
  in flight (Rust `ai_cancel`). Empty `editor.inlineCompletions.model` now prefers a small local
  FIM-trained code model when one is installed in Ollama (qwen2.5-coder, deepseek-coder,
  starcoder2, codegemma, codellama, codestral…; the smallest of at least ~0.8 GB) over the
  agent's model; `ide://editor/inlineCompletions` says which model and why, and recommends
  `ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:1.5b-base` when none is installed. Commands: Suggest code here
  (`editor.inlineSuggest.trigger`, Alt+\), Accept (Tab), Accept next word (Ctrl+Right),
  Accept next line, Hide (Esc). Suggestions also work in notebook cells.
- Why: Copilot / Cursor Tab quality comes from FIM-trained models seeing both sides of the cursor
  and neighbouring code; the chat prompt with the current file only and 128 tokens was far off.
- How: `editor/ai/fim.ts`, `editor/ai/context.ts`, `core/agent/completionModels.ts` (DOM-free,
  tested in `editor/ai/fim.test.ts`), `editor/ai/completions.ts` (the source, commands, state);
  `LanguageModelService.fill` / `completionInfo` (agent/languageModel.ts); Rust `ai/fim.rs` +
  `ai_fim` (lib.rs, build.rs, capabilities). Recent edits are tracked only while the feature is
  on. Telemetry-free: the usage log records the request locally like every model call (D201).
- Limits: no next-edit-style multi-location prediction from FIM (next-edit suggestions stay a
  separate feature, D193); no caching of suggestions across identical prefixes; the token budget
  is estimated (4 characters a token), not tokenized; other open files are only those open in
  editor tabs (no import-graph context); the Alt+\ key is for file editors (in a notebook cell,
  suggestions come while typing).

#### Notebooks out of the box

**.ipynb is built in again** (VS Code's built-in `ipynb` extension; D203 had moved it into the
Jupyter extension)
- What: Jupyter's `.ipynb` format is the IDE's own (`core/notebook/ipynb.ts`, DOM-free, tested):
  any `.ipynb` opens, edits and saves as a notebook with the Jupyter extension off, as in VS Code
  without the Jupyter extension. The notebook type `jupyter.notebook` is registered by the
  notebook editor (owner "builtin"). Writing is unchanged: nbformat 4, unknown top-level and cell
  fields kept, keys sorted, one-space indents, text as lists of lines, NaN read as null; the
  minor version now lives in `Notebook.nbformatMinor` (D203's `extra.nbformat_minor` still saves).
- Why: the owner's report: in VS Code an .ipynb opens as a notebook out of the box, ours opened as
  JSON while the Jupyter extension was off. VS Code splits it the same way: the format is built in
  (`extensions/ipynb`), kernels come from extensions (ms-toolsai.jupyter finds Python
  environments and starts `ipykernel` in them; it isn't a kernel itself).
- How: `index.ts` registers the type; `bundled.jupyter`'s `main.js` drops its serializer and its
  `contributes.notebooks` (it's a kernel source only, still off by default). No extension may
  contribute `.ipynb` / `jupyter.notebook` now (the shipped Jupyter extension's exception is gone,
  `shippedJupyter` removed); an extension runs Jupyter notebooks with a kernel source
  (`notebookTypes: ["jupyter.notebook"]`).

**Choosing a kernel when nothing runs the notebook** (VS Code's "Select kernel" without Jupyter)
- What: the kernel picker (`kernelPicker.ts`) lists found kernels, then "Kernel sources": each
  kernel source's own actions, extensions' `notebook/kernelSource` commands, "Enable the Jupyter
  extension" (a Jupyter notebook while it's off), and "Browse extensions for kernels…". With
  nothing found the placeholder is "Type to choose a kernel source", as in VS Code. Running a
  cell with nothing to run it opens this picker (a user); an agent gets "turn on the Jupyter
  extension (notebook.enableJupyter), or install an extension with kernels". With the extension on
  but no Python found, a disabled row says to install Python or set `jupyter.pythonPath`.
- `notebook.enableJupyter`: asks the user to allow the extension's permissions first (its own
  dialog, before it starts, so no second prompt), enables it, waits up to 15 s for its kernel
  source, and the picker continues with its kernels. Tests pass `grant`.
- `notebook.browseKernelExtensions`: opens the Extensions view with "kernel" in its filter
  (`extensions.show` takes `query`, `extensionsQuery` in the view) and says other extensions
  install from a folder or a .vsix: **placeholder** until the extension store exists.
- **ipykernel:** a Python without ipykernel still runs cells at once (plain Python, D188); a
  notification offers "Install ipykernel" (once per Python per session). Install runs
  `python -m pip install -U ipykernel` in a new terminal (PowerShell-quoted on Windows, `& 'path'`
  for paths with spaces; `py -3` keeps its argument), waits for it (shell integration), checks the
  Python again and, when its Jupyter kernel is there, the kernel switches to it on its next
  restart ("Restart kernel" in the notification). A remembered plain kernel whose Python got
  ipykernel since starts on its Jupyter kernel directly. Non-blocking on purpose (VS Code asks
  modally before running; a modal would also block scripted runs).

**VS Code's notebook UI, with the IDE's styles**
- Cell toolbar (`cellChrome.ts`), floating at the cell's top right on hover or selection: code:
  run the cells above, run this cell and below, split, extensions' icon buttons, "…", delete;
  Markdown: edit (pencil) or stop editing (✓), split while editing, "…", delete.
- The "…" menu (VS Code's cell menu): cut, copy, paste (off with nothing copied); insert cell
  (code / Markdown, above / below); change cell to (code, Markdown, raw); change cell language…;
  join with previous / next; copy cell down; move up / down; show cell line numbers; collapse /
  clear output; extensions' items without an icon. Key labels from `NOTEBOOK_KEY_LABELS`.
- "+ Code / + Markdown" between cells: a bar over the gap below each cell (and above the first),
  shown on hover, always under the last cell. The cell gap grew to 20 px for it.
- A status row under each code cell: the run's result and time (left), extensions' items, and the
  cell's language at the right, clickable (`notebook.changeCellLanguage`: the kernel's languages,
  Markdown, then every language; a cell's own language is kept as VS Code keeps it,
  `metadata.vscode.languageId`; "markdown" turns the cell into Markdown and a language turns a
  Markdown cell into code). Cells in another language than the notebook's aren't sent to the
  notebook's language server.
- Markdown cells keep the Markdown preview's own classes (`md md-document`, same tokens and
  sizes); no run button on Markdown cells (VS Code has none); double-click or Enter edits, Esc or
  ✓ renders (`notebook.previewCell`).
- New commands, each with keys in `keys.ts`: `notebook.joinCells` (Ctrl/Cmd+Alt+J with the next,
  +Shift with the previous; one undo step; the joined code cell's outputs are cleared),
  `notebook.duplicateCell` (Shift+Alt+Down / Up, with outputs), `notebook.toggleLineNumbers` (L,
  Shift+L for every cell; setting `notebook.lineNumbers` "off"/"on" for new views; engine
  `setLineNumbers` for embedded editors), `notebook.previewCell`, `notebook.changeCellLanguage`,
  `notebook.setMetadata` (notebook or cell, merge, null removes; undoable). `notebook.read`
  takes `metadata: true`. The clipboard of cells is shared by every notebook
  (`notebookClipboard`); paste keeps metadata and outputs.

**Notebook ↔ source toggle (decided: yes)**
- The notebook tab's title bar has "Show source" (`{ }`), the text editor of a notebook file has
  "Show as notebook": `notebook.toggleSource` swaps them in the same tab, like the Markdown
  preview's toggle (VS Code does this with "Reopen editor with…", which stays too). Unsaved
  notebook changes: the user is asked to save first; "Don't save" keeps the notebook's tab open
  beside the JSON. A file that can't be read as a notebook says "Show its source to fix it".
- Why: JSON is sometimes what you need (merge conflicts, a broken file, metadata), and the
  Markdown files already work this way. "Export as script" (`# %%`) stays in the toolbar.

**`ide.notebooks` for notebook extensions (Deepnote, Databricks, Kestra, a Jupyter server…)**
- Compared with VS Code's surfaces: serializer ✓ (D202), controllers ✓ as kernel sources (D202),
  now also: `KernelOption.languages` (supportedLanguages); `run.cell` (the running cell's id,
  index, language, metadata) and `run.clear({ wait })`; kernel source `actions` (VS Code's kernel
  source action providers: picker rows that return a kernel) and `menus` `notebook/kernelSource`;
  `menus` `notebook/toolbar` and `notebook/cell/title` (icon → cell toolbar, else the "…" menu;
  `when` sees `notebookType`, `notebookCellType`, `notebookCellLanguage`);
  `registerCellStatusBarItemProvider(type | "*", provide)` (≤ 4 items per provider and cell, 80
  chars, own commands only, 2 s, asked again 300 ms after a change); output renderers
  (`contributes.notebookRenderers: [{ id, displayName, entrypoint, mimeTypes }]`, VS Code's
  `activate(context) → renderOutputItem(item, element)` API with `item.json/text/data/blob`,
  `context.postMessage/onDidReceiveMessage/getState/setState`) and
  `ide.notebooks.createRendererMessaging(id)`; notebook events (`notebook.didOpen`, `didChange`,
  `didSave`, `didClose`, `didRunCell`, "fs.read"); edits and metadata through the notebook
  commands (`notebook.setMetadata` new). Notebook types may claim compound endings (`.nb.py`:
  the longest ending wins, `NotebookProviders.typeFor` and `ViewerRegistry.for`), and a type
  without `default` is only in Reopen with… (viewer kind "option", no preview button on `.py`).
- Security: renderers run in the existing sandboxed output frame (own origin, no same-origin),
  only in trusted folders, and before their code runs the page gets a content security policy
  allowing only the network the extension was granted (none, its `network:<domain>` hosts, or any
  https host for `network`); messages are JSON, ≤ 8 MB, and a frame's message reaches only its own
  extension. Status item commands and menu commands are the extension's own. The worker lockdown
  is unchanged (a renderer's code never runs in the worker).
- How: worker side `core/extensions/rpcNotebooks.ts` (tested), host side
  `extensions/runtimeNotebooks.ts` (`readOption`, `rendererNetwork`), registry
  `core/notebook/providers.ts` (`registerRenderer`, `rendererFor`, `postToRenderer`,
  `registerCellStatusProvider`, `cellStatusItems`; tested), frame `outputFrame.ts`
  (`RendererBinding`) and `src-tauri/notebook/output/output.js` (renderer runtime: ES module via a
  blob import, else `module.exports`; the CSP meta). Manifest: `contributes.notebookRenderers`
  parsed in `thirdParty.ts`, menus locations in `thirdParty.ts`, `extensionFeatures.ts`,
  `manifestSchema.ts`. Typings in `src/api/index.d.ts`; docs in docs/extensions.md ("Building a
  notebook extension"). The toybook fixture covers all of it.
- view.ts was split (1241 lines): `running.ts` (the kernel and run queue), `toolbar.ts`,
  `cellChrome.ts`, `kernelPicker.ts`, `cellCommands.ts`.

#### Git

**3-way merge editor (VS Code's)**
- `core/diff/merge.ts` (tested): `computeMergeChanges(base, current, incoming)` diffs each side
  against the base (the existing Myers `diffLines`) and groups changes that overlap or insert at
  the same place; a group both sides changed differently is a conflict, the same change on both
  sides is not. `MergeModel` keeps the result as one segment per region (common text or a change):
  `accept(id, "incoming" | "current" | "both" | "bothIncomingFirst" | "base")`, `resetChange`,
  `reset`, counts (`conflictCount`, `unhandledCount`), `nextConflict` (wraps; unhandled only on
  request), `resultSpan`, `mapLine(pane → pane)` for scroll sync. A hand edit of the result
  (`setResultText`) is diffed against the result as it was and the segment boundaries are mapped
  through the edit (text inserted at a boundary joins the change beside it), so Accept keeps
  replacing only its own conflict after the user typed elsewhere; a conflict typed over becomes
  "edited" (handled) unless it now equals one of the choices. Line endings (CRLF) and the final
  newline are kept.
- `editor/mergeView.ts`: the `mergeEditor` dock tab. Incoming (theirs, `git show :3:path`) and
  Current (ours, `:2`) side by side, Base (`:1`) as a toggle (`git.mergeEditor.toggleBase`), the
  Result below. The Result *is* the file's document (shared with its editor tab: dirty dot, undo,
  save): git's file with markers is replaced by the computed result (one undoable edit), as VS
  Code does; a file with no markers left (resolved by hand) is kept as is and read against the
  model, with a notice. Each conflict has actions in a zone above it — in the input panes "Accept
  incoming / current", "Accept both", "Ignore"; in the result "Accept incoming · Accept current ·
  Accept both · Ignore", or its state ("Incoming accepted", "Edited by hand") with Reset. Changes
  are tinted per side (conflicts stronger; unhandled ones amber in the result). The toolbar shows
  "2 of 5 conflicts left" / "All 5 conflicts handled", previous / next conflict, reset, Show base
  and **Complete merge** (asks when conflicts are unhandled; an agent passes `force`), which saves
  the file, runs `git.stage` and closes the tab. The panes' scrolling follows the one being
  scrolled (line mapping through the regions). Narrow tabs stack the input panes.
- Opened from the conflict lenses ("Resolve in merge editor" next to Accept current / incoming /
  both), Source control's conflicted rows (an inline button and the context menu), or
  `git.openMergeEditor {path}`. Commands: `git.mergeEditor.accept {conflict, choice}` (also
  `reset`), `git.mergeEditor.acceptAll`, `git.mergeEditor.nextConflict` / `previousConflict`,
  `git.mergeEditor.reset`, `git.completeMerge`. State: `ide://git/mergeEditors`.
- Rust `git_show` accepts the revisions `:1`, `:2`, `:3` (`cat-file --filters :n:path`, so the
  texts are in working-tree form like the other sides); the git extension serves them as the
  `gitStage:<n>` content source, from the repository the file is in.
- Limits: a conflict where one side deleted the file (no stage 2 or 3) is refused with a message
  (resolve it in Source control). The grouping is our own diff, not git's: it can split or join
  conflicts differently from git's markers (the counts are the merge editor's). No word-level
  highlighting inside changed lines; no "Accept all from left/right" buttons (the command
  `git.mergeEditor.acceptAll` exists); the panes have fixed proportions (no sash).

**Several repositories in one folder**
- Rust `GitService` keeps the workspace's repository plus the ones `git_discover` found
