  (`find_repos`: `git submodule status --recursive` of the workspace's repository, up to 10
  like VS Code's `git.detectSubmodulesLimit`, and folders holding their own `.git` down to
  `git.repositoryScanMaxDepth` levels, default 1, skipping `node_modules`, `.git`, `target`,
  `dist`, `build`, `.venv` and `git.repositoryScanIgnoredFolders`; at most 50; each verified with
  `rev-parse --show-toplevel` so a folder ignored inside its parent repository doesn't count).
  Every git IPC command takes an optional `repo` (a root from that list; any other path is
  refused) and its own watcher per repository. Tests: submodule status parsing, the scan's depth
  and ignores, and a real nested repository found (and the depth-0 case).
- TS: `createGitIpc(root)` / `createGithubIpc(root)`; `GitController` per repository (kind:
  workspace / submodule / nested); `GitRepositories` routes a path to the deepest repository
  holding it (decorations, change bars, hunk staging, blame, file history, the merge editor's
  stages), and keeps a *selected* repository that follows the active editor's file or a click.
  Source control lists the repositories at the top when there are several (name, branch, sync
  counts, pending changes; click selects; right-click: pull, push, fetch, checkout, refresh); the
  commit box, changes, Graph and banner are the selected repository's, each repository with its
  own commit message. The activity badge counts every repository's changes. Commands take
  `repository` (root, folder-relative path or folder name): `git.status`, `git.refresh`,
  `git.stage` / `unstage` / `discard` (paths are grouped per repository when none is named),
  hunk staging (by path), `git.commit`, `git.checkout`, `git.branches`, `git.log`, fetch / pull /
  push and their variants, the stash commands. `git.repositories` (and `ide://git/repositories`)
  lists them; `git.selectRepository`.
- Limits: the other git commands (branches, merge, rebase, tags, worktrees, GitHub, autofetch,
  generate commit message) act on the selected repository rather than asking which one. A new
  nested repository is found on `git init` inside the folder (a `.git` created), a refresh or a
  settings change, not by a background scan. VS Code's "multiple" selection mode (every
  repository's changes at once in one list) isn't there: one repository's view at a time.

**GitLens basics**
- `git/lens.ts` (tested): `parseBlamePorcelain` (commit details once per commit, consecutive
  lines merged into hunks, uncommitted lines), `blameAnnotations` (fixed-width "Author   3 d"
  on a hunk's first line, blank padding on the rest so the code stays aligned; a heat bucket 0–4
  from the file's own oldest–newest dates; a hover with author, mail, date, summary, hash),
  `parseLineLog` (`git log -L` records: hash, parents, author, time, subject, the path at that
  commit, the diff, +/− counts).
- **Toggle file blame** (`git.toggleFileBlame`, `fileBlame.ts`): annotations before every line
  (`EngineEditor.setLineAnnotations`, Monaco injected text at column 1, cursor skips it, hover on
  the line's first character), colored by age (`git.blame.heatmap`, default on). It blames the
  editor's text (`--contents`), again after a save, a pause in typing (1.5 s), a commit or
  checkout. `ide://git/fileBlame`. Drawn through `services.gutterMarks.annotate` (a small
  addition to `workbench/gutterMarks.ts`), so editors opened later get it too.
- **Line history** (`git.lineHistory {path, startLine, endLine, open}`): `git log -L` of the
  selection, in a Source control section; a commit opens its change of the file (parent ↔ commit,
  at the file's path in that commit), Show commit on hover.
- **Compare branches** (`git.compareBranches {left, right, mergeBase, path}`, `git.compareSwap`):
  two refs (pickers of branches and tags from the palette) → the files that differ (Rust
  `git_diff_names`, `git_rev_parse`, `git_merge_base_of`) in a Compare section → each file's diff.
- **Stashes** section: the selected repository's stashes, expand to their files (`git.stashShow`:
  stash^1 ↔ stash per file), hover actions Apply / Pop / Drop, header Stash / Refresh; reloads
  when the refs change. The three sections live under Source control (their ids are in the
  default `workbench.activityBar.hidden`, like Outline and Timeline under the Explorer).
  `ide://git/lens`.
- Limits: no blame of a file's older revision ("blame previous"), no per-author colors, the blame
  hover has no buttons (Show commit is `git.showCommit`); annotations of lines typed since the
  last blame are missing until the next one; line history follows the line range as `git log -L`
  does (no rename-following options); compare lists files only (no commit list between the refs);
  untracked files saved with a stash (`-u`) aren't listed in its files.

**GitHub**
- `githubReview.ts`, through the user's `gh` (no product accounts): `github.pullRequestFiles
  {number}` (default: the current branch's) — a `githubPullRequestFiles` tab with the files
  (status, +/−, thread count) and each file's review threads (author, line, resolved / outdated,
  every comment, **Reply**, **Resolve / Unresolve**, **Go to line**); the pull request tab got a
  **Files changed** button. `github.openPullRequestFile` opens merge base ↔ head (`gh api
  repos/{owner}/{repo}/compare/…` for the merge base; contents from the local repository when it
  has the commit, else `gh api …/contents/<path>?ref=<sha>` raw, cached), read-only.
  `github.replyToReviewThread`, `github.resolveReviewThread` (GraphQL resolve / unresolve
  mutation), `github.addReviewComment` (a comment on a line of the head version). With the pull
  request's branch checked out, each thread marks its line in the editor margin (the hover shows
  the thread). Notifications: `github.notifications {all}` (`gh api notifications`) in a "GitHub
  notifications" section (unread bold, type icon, repository, age; click opens it on GitHub and
  marks it read), `github.markNotificationRead {id | all}`, `github.markAllNotificationsRead`,
  `github.notifications.enabled`. `ide://github/review`.
- Rust `github.rs`: ops `prMeta`, `prFiles`, `compareBase`, `fileAt`, `prThreads`, `prReply`,
  `prComment`, `prResolve`, `notifications`, `notificationRead`, `notificationsReadAll`; hashes,
  repository paths (no `..`, percent-encoded), node ids and comment ids are checked; free text
  goes in `-f body=` fields. `runs_anywhere` (auth, notifications) work without a repository.
  Tests for the argument lists and refusals.
- The fake GitHub CLI (`tests/fixtures/fake-gh/gh.mjs`) serves pull request #7 (the local
  `feature` branch into `main`), its files and contents from the local repository, one review
  thread (reply and resolve persist in `../fake-github/state.json`) and two notifications.
- Limits: review threads are listed in the files tab and marked in the checked-out files, not
  drawn as inline comment widgets inside the diff (no inline reply box: Reply asks in the quick
  input); a pull request with more than 100 files or threads shows the first 100; comments on
  the old side (LEFT) are placed by their line on the new file; no pending reviews (approve /
  request changes) yet.

#### Terminal

- **Terminal profiles** (VS Code's `terminal.integrated.profiles.*` / `defaultProfile.*`, under the
  IDE's names `terminal.profiles.<windows|osx|linux>` and `terminal.defaultProfile.<platform>`;
  VS Code's keys are translated by `core/settings/vscode.ts` when importing). Rust detects the shells
  like VS Code: Windows — PowerShell 7 (PATH, Program Files, preview, the Store alias, a .NET tool),
  Windows PowerShell, Git Bash (registry `HKLM/HKCU\SOFTWARE\GitForWindows InstallPath`, Program
  Files, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Git`, Scoop, next to `git.exe` on PATH), Command Prompt, Cygwin, WSL
  distributions (`wsl.exe -l -q`, Docker's hidden); macOS / Linux — `/etc/shells` (one per name, the
  login shell's path preferred; nologin, false, rbash dropped). Settings entries have VS Code's
  shape (`path` or a list, `source: "PowerShell" | "Git Bash"`, `args`, `env` with null to unset,
  `icon`, `color` like `terminal.ansiGreen`, `overrideName`); null hides a detected profile, an entry
  of a detected name adjusts it. The "+" in the terminal panel has a "▾" (a new `dropdown`
  TabAction) with the profiles, Split terminal, Select default profile, Configure terminal
  settings. Commands: `terminal.newWithProfile { profile }`, `terminal.selectDefaultProfile
  { profile }` (writes the user setting; "" = the IDE's own default), `terminal.profileMenu`,
  `terminal.configureSettings`. `ide://terminals` lists `profiles`, `defaultProfile`, `conpty` and
  each terminal's `profile`; restored tabs start their profile again.
  - Shell integration with a profile: kept when its arguments are ones the scripts can combine with
    (none; bash/zsh/fish `-l`, `--login`, `-i`; PowerShell `-NoLogo`, `-NoProfile`, `-Login`), else
    the shell starts exactly as configured, without integration (VS Code does the same).
    Login flags now make bash source the login files (`IDE_SHELL_LOGIN`), zsh/fish get `-l`.
  - Git Bash: `--init-file` gets a forward-slash path, `CHERE_INVOKING=1` keeps MSYS2's profile from
    going home, `/c/Users/…` folders are read back as `C:\Users\…` (Rust's command records and the
    tab's folder), dropped files are typed as `/c/…` and quoted the POSIX way. WSL's
    `System32\bash.exe` is recognized and gets no scripts. cmd keeps no integration (as before; VS
    Code has none either), its paths are double-quoted.
  - Why IDE names (`terminal.profiles.*`, not `terminal.integrated.*`): every terminal setting here is
    `terminal.*` (D95); the VS Code names are aliases on import / `.vscode/settings.json`.
  - Limits: profiles and the default profile are user settings only (a folder can't make the IDE
    run a program by opening a terminal; VS Code allows them in trusted workspaces). No
    "JavaScript Debug Terminal" profile, no `terminal.integrated.automationProfile` (tasks still
    use the default shell), no profile icons beyond the IDE's terminal icon set. In a WSL folder a
    profile is ignored (the shell runs inside the distribution, as before).
- **Output after a restart** (VS Code's persistent sessions, `terminal.enablePersistentSessions`
  default on, `terminal.persistentSessionScrollback` default 100 lines): each terminal tab's last
  lines are serialized with `@xterm/addon-serialize` (colors kept) into the workspace state
  (`terminal.outputs`, by tab id), saved a few seconds behind output, on folder switches and window
  close, and before Developer: Reload window. A restored tab writes them dim (every SGR gets `;2`),
  then `──── Restored session · <date, time> ────`, then its new shell. On Windows the old lines are
  pushed into the scrollback first (ConPTY thinks it starts on a blank screen and would paint over
  them).
  - Out of scope: process revival (VS Code keeps shells alive in a pty host process across reloads;
    here the shell, and what ran in it, starts again). A full window reload of the test harness
    isn't scriptable (the runner lives in the page), so the UI test reopens the folder, which goes
    through the same save / restore.
- **Command suggestions while typing** (VS Code's terminal IntelliSense; `terminal.suggest.enabled`,
  on, not an AI feature): the renderer keeps the prompt's input (shell integration's prompt-end
  mark to the cursor, VS Code's prompt input model). Typing a word character or a path separator
  opens a list under the cursor: programs on PATH (listed by Rust once and cached two minutes;
  Windows by PATHEXT-like extensions, else the executable bit), shell builtins (bash/zsh, fish,
  PowerShell cmdlets and aliases, cmd), the last commands run that start like this one, files and
  folders (relative to the shell's folder, `~` expanded, hidden ones when the name starts with a
  dot, names only via `pty_list_dir`, only while that terminal lives), git subcommands and branches
  (`git checkout|switch|merge|rebase|…`). Ranking: prefix (exact case first, shorter first), then
  in-order fuzzy from a word start. Tab accepts; Enter accepts once the list was navigated with
  ↑ / ↓ (VS Code's default "partial" selection mode, so typing `ls` + Enter still runs it); Escape
  closes; Ctrl+Space opens it. Accepting types only what's missing (or erases and retypes when the
  case differs); folders end with the separator and keep suggesting inside; quoting per shell
  (POSIX backslashes, PowerShell single quotes, cmd double quotes, inside an open quote as is).
  Commands `terminal.triggerSuggest`, `terminal.acceptSuggestion`, `terminal.hideSuggestWidget`,
  `terminal.selectNextSuggestion` / `PreviousSuggestion`, context keys
  `terminalSuggestWidgetVisible`, `terminalSuggestNavigated`; each terminal's list is in
  `ide://terminals` (`suggest`).
  - Limits: no per-command argument specs (VS Code ships Fig specs for npm, docker…: only git here),
    no PowerShell / zsh completions from the shell itself, no inline (ghost) completion, no
    details pane; aliases and functions of the user's shell aren't listed.
- **Rendering**: `@xterm/addon-webgl` draws terminals when WebGL2 works
  (`terminal.gpuAcceleration` auto / on / off, live). A lost context or a failed start falls back to
  the DOM renderer at once; "auto" then stays on the DOM renderer for the session (VS Code's
  rule), "on" retries once. The sticky command line measures rows without the DOM renderer's row
  elements. `ide://terminals` shows each terminal's `renderer`.
- **Dependencies**: `@xterm/addon-webgl` 0.19.0 (MIT, the xterm.js authors; ≈125 KB minified ESM,
  in the lazy terminal chunk) — WebGL rendering is the point, and writing a GPU renderer isn't
  reasonable; `@xterm/addon-serialize` 0.14.0 (MIT, ≈16 KB) — turns the buffer back into escape
  sequences with colors and wide characters right, which is what VS Code uses for the same
  feature. Both are the releases that match `@xterm/xterm` 6.0.0.
- **Windows 10 ConPTY**: not shipped here (no Windows to test, and it's two Microsoft binaries in
  the installer). portable-pty already prefers a `conpty.dll` found by `LoadLibrary("conpty.dll")`
  (the app's folder first) over kernel32's, so shipping one is packaging only — steps under
  windows-pending. `ide://terminals` `conpty` says "bundled" or "system".
- **Splits in one tab:** not done; splits still open a terminal in a new dock group beside
  it (Ctrl+Shift+5).
- **Seen while testing, not changed**: with zsh the command records (`terminal.runCommand`,
  `ide://terminals/<id>/commands`) end with a stray `#` / `%` line — zsh prints its
  PROMPT_EOL_MARK before the precmd hook that sends D. Older scripts only use `$contains`, so it
  went unnoticed; worth a small fix in `pty/commands.rs` or `scripts/zshrc.zsh`. The sandbox's
  login shell is zsh, so the default terminal in UI tests is zsh, not bash.
- Test helper: `dev.type` takes `inputType` (`"insertText"` is how xterm reads typed text), so UI
  scripts can type into a terminal as a user does.

#### Debugger

- **Several debug sessions at once, and launch.json `compounds`** (VS Code's). The controller
  keeps every session (`RunningSession`: state, threads, frames, scopes, exception, capabilities)
  and which one is *focused*; the toolbar, Variables, Watch, hover, the console's evaluation and
  the stopped-line mark follow the focused one, and a session that stops takes the focus, as in
  VS Code. Starting while sessions run starts another (the configuration picker stays at the top
  of Run and debug while debugging). The call stack becomes a tree when there's more than one
  session or thread: sessions (child sessions under their parent), threads with their state and
  continue / pause buttons, frames; one session with one thread still shows just its frames. The
  toolbar has a session picker when several run. `compounds` (`configurations`, `preLaunchTask`
  run once first, each configuration's own preLaunchTask before it, `stopAll`) show in the picker
  and start side by side; with `stopAll`, stopping one stops all. `debug.stopAll` stops every
  session; `debug.stop` / `restart` / `continue` / `pause` / `step*` / `selectFrame` take
  `{ session, threadId }`. Breakpoints are sent to every session and are "placed" when any
  session placed them. `inDebugMode` is "any session", `debugState` the focused one's.
  - Why: client + server debugging is the most-asked missing piece (feature-gaps L).
  - Limits: one shared debug console (lines carry their session; VS Code has a per-session
    console picker); `presentation` (group/order/hidden) of compounds is ignored; compound entries
    naming another folder (`folder`) are treated as the same folder (one root here).
- **Node child processes, workers, and a JavaScript debug terminal** (js-debug's approach,
  written from scratch). A debugged Node program gets `NODE_OPTIONS=--require <bootloader>`
  (`src-tauri/src/debug/bootloader.js`, written to `<data>/debug-attach/`). In every Node
  process started below it (fork, spawn, `npm run dev`'s server, Jest's workers) the bootloader
  opens the inspector on a free local port, registers by writing `<pid>.json` into a
  registration folder the IDE polls every 250 ms (`debug_autoattach_take`), and waits
  (`inspector.waitForDebugger`) until the IDE has set breakpoints and released it. Each becomes
  a child session (under the session of its parent process, by ppid). It strips `--inspect*`
  from `process.execArgv`, so `fork()` children of the IDE's own `--inspect-brk` program don't
  wait on a port nobody knows. Worker threads come through the parent's inspector (CDP
  `NodeWorker.enable { waitForDebuggerOnStart }`, messages tunnelled) and are child sessions
  too. `"autoAttachChildProcesses": false` turns it off per configuration. "Smart" filter (VS
  Code's default, `debug.javascript.autoAttachFilter`): scripts under node_modules are skipped
  except tools that run your code (jest, jest-worker, mocha, vitest, tinypool, ts-node, tsx,
  vite, next, nodemon, webpack…); `"always"` attaches all. REPLs and `node -e` aren't attached.
  The registration folder has an `alive` file the poll keeps fresh: a bootloader seeing it older
  than 15 s (the IDE gone) runs the program normally. Stopping a child session ends that
  process (`process.exit()` through its inspector), as VS Code's terminate does.
  - **JavaScript debug terminal** (`debug.createJavaScriptDebugTerminal`, "JavaScript debug
    terminal"): an interactive shell with that environment; every Node program run in it is
    debugged as its own session. `pty_spawn` takes `env` for interactive shells now (not saved
    with the tab: a restored one is a plain terminal).
  - **`"runtimeExecutable": "npm"`** (also npx, yarn, pnpm): runs the script in a terminal (through
    the shell, for `npm.cmd` on Windows) as a session with nothing to inspect; its Node processes
    attach as its children ("Launch via npm" snippet).
  - Why: npm scripts, test runners and multi-process servers couldn't be debugged.
  - Limits: the user's own NODE_OPTIONS is kept (`${env:NODE_OPTIONS}`), but a shell profile that
    resets NODE_OPTIONS defeats the debug terminal; bun and deno don't read NODE_OPTIONS (not
    attached); a process registered while the IDE is unresponsive waits for it (it can't time
    out once `waitForDebugger` is called).
- **Function breakpoints** ("+" in Breakpoints, `debug.addFunctionBreakpoint`, condition and hit
  count, kept per folder): DAP `setFunctionBreakpoints` where `supportsFunctionBreakpoints`. For
  Node (js-debug has none), the IDE finds the function's declaration in the loaded scripts
  (`function name(`, `name = (…) =>`, `name: function`, class and object methods; `Cart.total`
  matches the method `total`) and breaks at its body; a name that evaluates globally breaks on
  its calls (`setBreakpointOnFunctionCall`). While any exist, each new script pauses once before
  it runs (`beforeScriptExecution`) so functions in modules loaded later get them too; the stop
  says "function breakpoint". Limits: the declaration search is textual (a function created
  dynamically or renamed by a bundler without a map isn't found); scripts under node_modules are
  searched only for a name containing "node_modules".
- **Data breakpoints** ("Break on value change" in Variables' menu, `debug.addDataBreakpoint`):
  DAP `dataBreakpointInfo` + `setDataBreakpoints`, only where the adapter supports them (lldb-dap,
  GDB…); they belong to the session that made them and go when it ends (VS Code keeps them only
  for adapters that can persist them). Node / browsers can't (V8 has no watchpoints) — the menu
  item isn't offered there.
- **Exception widget** (VS Code's): stopped on an exception, a zone under the line shows
  "Exception has occurred: TypeError" (with "(uncaught)"), the message and up to 12 stack lines
  ("… N more"), with a close button; from DAP `exceptionInfo` (with inner exceptions) or, for
  Node and pages, the paused event's exception object. `debug.exceptionInfo` and
  `ide://debug.exception` give it to agents.
- **The adapter's own exception filters**: Breakpoints lists the focused adapter's
  `exceptionBreakpointFilters` (debugpy's Raised / Uncaught / User uncaught, GDB's…) as
  checkboxes, defaults as the adapter says, a condition ("Edit condition…") where
  `supportsCondition`, sent as `filterOptions` when `supportsExceptionFilterOptions`. Choices
  are kept per filter id; with no session, the last adapter's filters show under Node's two (so
  they can be set before starting). Node and browsers keep caught / uncaught. Note: debugpy's
  "Uncaught exceptions" is on by default now (its default, as in VS Code); before, the IDE only
  turned it on with the checkbox.
- **Threads**: the call stack lists a session's threads (DAP `threads`, kept up to date by
  `thread` events), stopped or running, with per-thread continue / pause; `continued` with
  `allThreadsContinued: false` keeps the others stopped; selecting a thread
  (`debug.selectThread`) shows its stack and variables and the toolbar then acts on it.
- **Launch settings**: `postDebugTask` (runs when a top-level session ends); `serverReadyAction`
  (`pattern`, default VS Code's; `uriFormat`; `openExternally`, `debugWithChrome`,
  `debugWithEdge` — a child browser session, `killOnServerStop` — and `startDebugging` by
  `name`), watched in the terminal output and DAP output, whole lines only; the process picker
  (`${command:pickProcess}`: `debug.listProcesses` / `debug.pickProcess`, `ps -A -ww -o
  pid=,ppid=,args=` or PowerShell's Win32_Process JSON, Node processes and ones with an inspector
  port first; a Node process without `--inspect` is asked to open it with
  `process._debugProcess(pid)`, as VS Code does); "Add configuration…" (`debug.addConfiguration`,
  15 snippets incl. a compound, inserted into the existing launch.json keeping its comments);
  Loaded scripts (a folded section of Run and debug, filterable; DAP `loadedSources`, Node's
  parsed scripts; `debug.loadedScripts`); a disassembly view (`debug.openDisassembly`, DAP
  `disassemble` around the frame's `instructionPointerReference`, in a read-only tab with the
  current instruction marked).
- **Presets**: Go (`"type": "go"`: Delve's `dlv dap --listen=127.0.0.1:<port>` in a terminal, DAP
  over TCP — new Rust `debug_dap_connect`; `mode` defaults to "debug"; `debug.dlvPath`), .NET
  (`"type": "coreclr"`: netcoredbg, MIT, `--interpreter=vscode` over stdio; `stopAtEntry`;
  `debug.netcoredbgPath`). Before starting, a missing adapter program is detected
  (`programs_installed`) and the error says how to install it, with an "Install" action where
  there's a command (`debug.installAdapter`: Delve through `go install`). Java: not built in —
  Microsoft's java-debug is a plugin of the Java language server (JDT LS) that the IDE would have
  to load into jdtls (`bundles`) and drive with `vscode.java.startDebugSession` /
  `resolveClasspath`; `"type": "java"` says so and how to attach a JDWP adapter with
  `debugAdapter` instead.
- **The browser pane as a debug target** (Windows only): `debug.browserPane.debuggingPort`
  (default 0, off; needs a restart) makes the IDE start WebView2 with `--remote-debugging-port`
  (WEBVIEW2_ADDITIONAL_BROWSER_ARGUMENTS for every webview of the process — WebView2 refuses
  environments with different arguments — and removed from terminals and agent commands).
  `debug.attachToBrowserPane` attaches to the pane's frame (the target whose URL starts with the
  pane's proxy origin, never the IDE's own page), with the same page debugging as Edge (script
  mapping, source maps, console). Not possible on Linux (WebKitGTK has no CDP; its Web Inspector
  protocol is different and not exposed to other processes) or macOS (WKWebView: Safari's
  remote inspector only). Security: any local program can drive the IDE's webviews through that
  port while it's on — said in the setting.
- **Tests:** unit: `src/extensions/debug/sessions.test.ts` (compounds parse / resolve / stopAll, the session
  tree and focus, threads after stop / continue, the exception widget from DAP and CDP, filter
  arguments, function / data breakpoint store, Node function-declaration search, ps and
  PowerShell process lists and inspector ports, NODE_OPTIONS quoting and registrations,
  serverReadyAction, Add configuration's insertion, Go / .NET / Java presets, the browser pane's
  target choice, DapSession capabilities / function breakpoints / filters / thread and continued
  events). Rust: `debug::autoattach`, `debug::pane_port`, `debug::dap_frames`.
  UI: `tests/scripts/debug-m7-5.jsonc` (Node: a compound of two sessions, the server's forked
  child and worker as child sessions, a function breakpoint, the exception widget on a thrown
  error; a scripted DAP adapter `tests/fixtures/setup/mock-dap.mjs`: two threads, pausing one,
  exception filters, a data breakpoint, exceptionInfo, loaded scripts, disassembly; the
  JavaScript debug terminal; Add configuration; the process list).

#### Testing

- **Run with coverage** (VS Code's "Run with coverage"): `tests.runWithCoverage` (and on every
  group / file / test row, the view's header, `tests.runAllWithCoverage`). Each framework writes
  its own report into `<root>/<IDE folder>/coverage/<n>/` (git-ignored with a `*` .gitignore,
  replaced each run, since the file scope only reaches the workspace): Vitest
  `--coverage.reporter=json` and Jest `--coverageReporters=json` (Istanbul coverage-final.json),
  node:test `--experimental-test-coverage --test-reporter=lcov` (plus TAP on stdout), Mocha
  through `c8 --reporter=lcovonly`, pytest-cov `--cov=. --cov-branch --cov-report=json:…`,
  unittest through `coverage run --branch … ; coverage json`, `go test -coverprofile`, and
  `cargo llvm-cov --lcov`. DOM-free parsers (lcov, Istanbul, coverage.py JSON, Go profiles;
  `coverage.ts`) give hits per line, branches per line and functions, merged across commands.
  Why: the most asked-for missing piece of the Testing view (feature-gaps "Coverage", M).
  Limits: no per-test coverage ("which tests ran this line"), no inline branch markers (a line
  with an untaken branch is marked "partial"), no function list; Playwright has no coverage.
- **Test coverage tab** (`testCoverage`, bottom dock): files by folder with a bar and the
  covered share (lines + branches, as VS Code's statement coverage), lines / branches /
  functions in the tooltips, totals, what ran and when, a filter, sort by coverage, "Show inline
  coverage", "Run again with coverage", "Clear coverage"; a report missing from a command says
  what to install. **Margin:** covered / uncovered / partly covered lines as a thin bar at the
  right of the glyph margin (so a test's dot on the same line stays visible), with a hover ("Ran
  3 times", "Not run", "1 of 2 branches taken"); `tests.toggleInlineCoverage` and
  `testing.showInlineCoverage` (default on: a new coverage run shows it). **Explorer:** the
  percentage as the file's badge with `testing.showCoverageInExplorer` (default off: the badge
  is the slot git's letter uses).
- **Mocha:** projects found by `.mocharc.{json,jsonc,yml,yaml,js,cjs,mjs}` or package.json
  (`"mocha"` dependency or config key); test files from the config's `spec` (folders and globs;
  a `.js` config can't be read without running it, so Mocha's default `./test/*.{js,cjs,mjs}`);
  run with `npx mocha --reporter json` (`--grep '^full title$'` for one test); results matched
  to discovered tests by file and full title, hook failures listed as their own entries, the
  error's `actual` / `expected` kept.
- **Playwright:** files that import `@playwright/test` (even in a Vitest project); in a trusted
  folder `npx playwright test --list --reporter=json` lists the exact tests and projects
  (`testing.listWithRunner`), several projects becoming the first tree level as in the
  Playwright extension; runs with `--reporter=json`, one test as `file:line --project name`.
- **unittest:** Python files with unittest TestCases in a project not set up for pytest (no
  pytest.ini / conftest.py / `[tool.pytest…]` / `[tool:pytest]` / `[pytest]`, and no pytest
  import) run with `python -m unittest -v` (`testing.pythonRunner`: auto / pytest / unittest).
  Discovery: TestCase subclasses from the text, then (trusted) unittest's own `discover` through
  a small script passed base64-encoded to `python -c` (no file written, nothing for either
  shell to unquote), printing `id`, file and line (decorated methods unwrapped). Results from the
  `-v` lines (docstring lines, older Pythons' `(module.Class)`) and the FAIL / ERROR sections.
- **Compare expected with actual** (`tests.compareExpected`, on a failure's message row and in
  Test results): a diff tab (`editor.openDiff` with two new content sources, `testExpected:` /
  `testActual:`), Expected ↔ Actual. Values come from what the framework reports (Jest's
  `failureDetails.matcherResult`, Mocha's `err`, node:test's TAP YAML `expected:` / `actual:`)
  or from the printed diff (Jest / Vitest / Playwright "- Expected / + Received" and
  "Expected: / Received:", Node's assert "+ actual - expected", pytest's "assert a == b" and
  "Full diff", unittest's "a != b"). `tests.run` returns them with each failure;
  `ide://tests` marks such failures `comparable`. The diff toolbar shows "Expected ↔ Actual"
  (a one-line change in editor/diffView.ts: a labelled `head` that isn't `git:` shows both
  labels instead of "… ↔ commit").
- **Run history** (VS Code's Test Results): the last `testing.resultsHistory` (20) runs, in
  memory, each with what it ran (rerunnable; "failed tests" kept as those test ids), counts,
  duration, commands, coverage flag and each test's result (failures first, messages cut at
  4000). The **Test results** tab (`testResults`, bottom dock; History in the view's header) shows
  them newest first; Run again on a run, Run / Compare on a test. `tests.history {test?}` and
  `tests.rerunFromHistory {run}` for agents; a test's tooltip in the view shows its last results.
- **Debug test** (`tests.debug {test?, file?}`, the bug on test / file rows,
  `tests.debugAtCursor` Ctrl+; Ctrl+C, `tests.debugFile` Ctrl+; Ctrl+F): a launch configuration
  made for the framework (`debugConfig.ts`) started with `debug.start {configuration}` — a new
  optional input of debug.start (the debug area's one small change: `toConfig` on a given
  object). node:test runs the file itself (`node [--import tsx] --test-name-pattern=… file`,
  no `--test` child process), Jest `jest.js --runInBand --runTestsByPath file -t …`, Mocha
  `_mocha --no-timeouts --grep … file` (node_modules found from the project up to the root),
  pytest and unittest as debugpy `module` launches (`pytest file::Class::test`,
  `unittest -v module.Class.test`). Vitest, Playwright (worker processes), cargo and go
  (needs lldb-dap / Delve configurations) say what to do instead.
- `ide://tests` gains `coverage` (totals, least covered files with uncovered ranges, problems)
  and `history` (last 10 runs); failures gain `id` and `comparable`.

#### Agent and MCP

- **Rules for subagents, Claude Code's way.** Claude Code's subagents load CLAUDE.md (its built-in
  Explore and Plan don't; `omitClaudeMd` opts out) and preload what their `skills:` lists. Here:
  custom, general and reviewer subagents get the always-on rules; plan and explore don't;
  `omitClaudeMd` / `omitRules` in a definition leaves them out; `rules:` in a definition preloads
  rules by path or name; a rule's own `subagents:` front matter (names, `*`, `none`) gives it to the
  subagents it names whatever its scope (a rule with `subagents:` and no other scope is for
  subagents only). Claude Code's `.claude/rules/*.md` (`paths` globs) is read too. Why: rules that
  matter for a subagent's work (a reviewer's checklist) reached none of them. Limit: the rules go
  in the subagent's system prompt in full (16 000 characters); folder and glob rules aren't attached
  to a subagent's reads.
- **Rules page** (dock view, ⋯ menu's Rules…, Settings → Agent): every rule with its source, scope
  (always, matching files, by description, a folder's, only when mentioned) and subagents, an
  on/off switch (`agent.rules.disabled`, per folder), edit in place (scope written into the file's
  own front matter: Cursor's alwaysApply/globs/description, Copilot's applyTo, Claude Code's paths;
  the text), delete, and new from a template (Cursor .mdc, a section of AGENTS.md — in a subfolder's
  AGENTS.md for a folder rule —, Copilot .instructions.md, Claude Code .claude/rules). A root
  AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md can't change scope (its place decides). The agent can't call these commands.
- **MCP OAuth** after the 2025-06-18 authorization spec, in Rust (tokens never reach the webview):
  401 → protected resource metadata (header, then well-known with the path, then root) →
  authorization server metadata (RFC 8414, OpenID variants; the 2025-03-26 defaults when there's
  none) → dynamic client registration (public client, loopback redirect) → PKCE S256 + `resource`
  → the browser comes back to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback` (state checked, five minutes) →
  tokens in the secrets file, sent as Bearer, refreshed before expiry and once after a 401; a
  revoked refresh token signs out. Limits: the secrets file, not the OS keychain (same as API
  keys); a server without registration needs `oauth.clientId` in its config; one sign-in per server
  at a time; scopes are what the metadata lists (step-up on 403 `insufficient_scope` isn't done).
- **MCP sampling**: `sampling/createMessage` answered with the user's model after an approval
  (quick input: Allow once / Always allow this server in this window / Deny / Show the whole
  prompt); `agent.mcp.sampling` per server or `*` (allow, deny, ask), set on the MCP servers page.
  Requests from servers wait one at a time; the model is the server's hint if connected, else the
  chat's, else the default; text only (images noted), no tools, maxTokens ≤ 8192, temperature
  passed; stop sequences aren't. The result isn't shown for review before it's sent back (the spec
  says SHOULD); the usage log records it as "MCP sampling".
- **Resource templates and subscriptions**: templates listed with resources (in the @ picker as
  "(fill in)", variables asked at send; `agent.mcpResources` with `values`); RFC 6570 levels 1–3.
  An attached resource is subscribed when the server offers `subscribe`; an update marks it for
  the chats that attached it and their next message carries the new text (`registerSendContext`).
  Limit: updates of a remote server arrive only while a request to it is open (no standing GET
  stream), as list_changed already does.
- **Gallery**: 16 popular servers built in (filesystem, git, fetch, memory, sequential thinking,
  time, Playwright, Chrome DevTools, Context7, DeepWiki, GitHub, Sentry, Linear, Notion, Hugging
  Face, Brave Search), no network to show; Install writes this folder's or the user's mcp.json with
  inputs declared and approves it. The list is static: addresses may move between releases.
- **Tool schemas on demand** (`agent.mcp.toolSchemas`: auto above 30 MCP tools, onDemand, full):
  names and descriptions only, plus `mcp_tool_schema`; a loaded tool carries its schema from the
  next step (per chat). A deferred tool called before loading returns its schema as an error
  instead of running.
- **Worktree agents**: setup step before the window opens (copy `agent.worktree.copyFiles` —
  untracked files, `*` in the last segment — then run `agent.worktree.setupScript` in the worktree
  with the agent's shell; result on the record; a failure warns and the agent starts anyway);
  PORT per worktree (`basePort + n × portStep`, plus WORKTREE_INDEX / WORKTREE_PORT_BASE /
  WORKTREE_PORT_STEP, passed as the new window process's environment, so its terminals, commands
  and dev servers inherit it); best of N (one task to 2–6 models or external agents, a worktree and
  window each, then the compare page); the overview (state from each agent's saved chat — the meta
  now has `status` —, files and lines changed against the start commit from git, elapsed, PORT;
  every 5 s while open); compare (one diff at a time) and Apply this one (`git apply --3way` into
  this folder, staged). Limits: the setup script doesn't see PORT (it runs from the main window);
  windows spawned in UI tests don't exist, so a worktree agent's own turn isn't tested end to end.
- **Per-category auto-approve**: `agent.autoApprove` — one shape for reads and edits (path globs),
  commands (prefix, prefix*, /regex/; chains need every part, redirects and substitutions never
  allowed by a pattern), browser and web (domains, `*.x`), MCP (server, server/tool, wildcards);
  true goes ahead, false always asks even with full access; most specific wins, ask wins a tie.
  `agent.allowedCommands` / `deniedCommands` still count (shown on the page). Reads and edits ask
  through a tool gate before read_file / list_dir / edit_file / write_file; search and find_files
  aren't gated by it (the ignore files hide content there).
- **@docs**: sources in `agent.docs.sources`; the crawler stays within the start URL's folder,
  follows robots.txt (its group or `*`, longest match, Crawl-delay) and noindex/nofollow, waits
  `agent.docs.delayMs` between pages, stops at `maxPages` (60, ≤ 500), and reads through the agent's
  `web_fetch`; pages are chunked under headings and kept in a BM25 index in app data. `@docs:<name>`
  attaches the best passages for the message (or the words after it); `agent.searchDocs` is the
  agent's own lookup. No embeddings; no JavaScript-rendered sites; one crawl per source at a time.
- **Claude Code `/ide`**: `mcp.claudeCode.enabled` (off): the lock file
  `~/.claude/ide/<port>.lock` (pid, workspaceFolders, ideName, transport "ws", authToken), a
  WebSocket MCP server on 127.0.0.1 with the `x-claude-code-ide-authorization` check (pages with an
  Origin refused), `CLAUDE_CODE_SSE_PORT` / `ENABLE_IDE_INTEGRATION` for terminals opened after,
  the tools getCurrentSelection, getLatestSelection, getOpenEditors, getWorkspaceFolders,
  getDiagnostics, openFile, openDiff (Accept writes and answers FILE_SAVED + the text; Reject
  answers DIFF_REJECTED), checkDocumentDirty, saveDocument, close_tab, closeAllDiffTabs, and
  `selection_changed`. Verified against the community protocol write-up (claudecode.nvim
  PROTOCOL.md); not against a live Claude Code here. Limits: `executeCode` and `at_mentioned`
  (sending a selection to Claude Code) aren't offered; diagnostics carry a point, not a range;
  the WebSocket framing is in-house (no extension negotiation, no compression).
- Tests:
  - Unit: `core/agent/ruleEditing.test.ts`, `autoApprove.test.ts`, `docsIndex.test.ts` (robots,
    link filtering, chunks, BM25 ranking, the bounded / rate-limited crawl), `worktrees.test.ts`,
    `core/mcp/features.test.ts` (sampling request/policy/approval gate, client sampling + rejected
    error, templates, subscriptions, schemas on demand, gallery).
  - Rust: `mcp/oauth_tests.rs` (PKCE vectors, WWW-Authenticate, metadata URLs, a full sign-in and
    refresh against a mock authorization server, wrong state / error callback), `mcp/ide_ws_tests.rs`
    (SHA-1, accept key, frames, lock file, token / Origin refusal, MCP over WebSocket, notify),
    `agent/worktree.rs` (copy, diff with new files, apply into the main folder), `agent/docs.rs`.
  - UI: `tests/scripts/agent-m7-5.jsonc` (mock Ollama's docs site and D204 replies,
    `tests/fixtures/sample/tools/mock-mcp-extra.mjs`).

#### After the release review

- **Renderer frames keep to their network.** Besides its CSP, an extension's renderer frame gets
  no popups, no WebRTC (its ICE requests reach any host), no DNS prefetching and no frames of its
  own (a blank child frame would bring fresh globals: `createElement`, the HTML-parsing sinks and
  customized built-ins turn frame tags into inert `x-blocked-*` elements). The frame navigating
  itself elsewhere is refused by the IDE page's `frame-src` (local origins only).
  notebook-ext-m7-3 checks all of it. Messages to the extension are capped at 1 MB; only the user
  enables the Jupyter extension.
- **Small UI fixes:** room above the commit message box for its focus ring; Testing hidden from
  the activity bar by default (like Outline and Timeline; the Testing status item still opens it);
  Manage providers gets the plug icon and MCP servers the server icon used for MCP elsewhere.


### D205 — m7.5.2: Customize, one tab for setting up the agent

**What.** The agent's set-up pages — Models and providers, Agents, Rules, Auto-approve, MCP
servers, Docs — are now sections of one **Customize** tab (`agent.customize`, like Cursor's):
a search box and chips at the top, the section's page below. They are no longer dock view types
of their own; every way in (`agent.showSetup`, `agent.showAgentConfig`, `agent.showRules`,
`agent.showAutoApprove`, `agent.showMcpPage`, `agent.showDocs`, the Chats panel, Settings'
sidebar links, the New tab menu) opens Customize at its section. Settings → Agent shows a
single Customize card instead of seven. Usage stays a tab of its own.

**MCP servers, simplified like Cursor's.** "Connected" lists the IDE's own tools first (a
built-in row with the product name and its tool count; click lists them, `agent.builtinTools`),
then each server as one row: icon with a state dot, name, scope (User, Workspace, or where it's
configured), "N tools enabled" or what's wrong. A row's ⋯ (`agent.mcpServerActions`) signs in or
out, sets sampling, restarts, edits mcp.json or removes it. **New MCP server**
(`agent.newMcpServer`) adds a custom one or one of the popular ones; the gallery is no longer laid
out on the page.

**Why.** Seven tabs and seven settings cards for one job; one place is simpler to find and to
explain. Old layouts that saved one of the removed tabs drop it on restore (unknown view types
are dropped).

**Tests.** ui-m7-5 (sections, every way in, search, the Settings card), agent-m7-5 (the MCP
section's built-in row), agent-m7-2-usage and agent-m6-62 updated.

**Follow-ups (m7.5.3).**
- **Removing a server updates the list at once.** The IDE's own mcp.json writes (install, add,
  remove) bump `mcpConfigVersion`, which the section listens to; before, it waited for a server's
  state to change.
- **A server's Configure dialog**, like Cursor's: its source with an on / off switch
  (`agent.mcp.disabledServers`: listed, never started), sign-in, sampling, and its tools grouped
  into reads and writes (the tool's `readOnlyHint`), each with a switch and "Turn all on / off"
  per group (`agent.mcp.disabledTools`: the agent doesn't see a tool that's off); Reload restarts
  it. Both settings are user scope and guarded from agents. Commands
  `agent.configureMcpServer`, `agent.setMcpServerEnabled`, `agent.setMcpToolEnabled`.
- **The built-in row counts honestly**: the agent's own tools plus the IDE commands it can call
  through call_command (hundreds: git, terminals, editors, layout, settings, extensions), e.g.
  "12 tools and 640 IDE commands enabled"; Cursor's "33 tools" for Origin is one MCP server's
  list. Its dialog lists the tools as reads and writes.
- **Customize → Commands**: the slash command files in User and Workspace groups, "+ New" writes
  a starter file and opens it, a row opens its file, ⋯ deletes it (`agent.newSlashCommand`,
  `agent.deleteSlashCommand`, `agent.showSlashCommands`). A new Rust command `user_file_delete`
  deletes only what `resolve_write_path` lets the IDE write (the user's commands, agents, memory
  files, or the folder's files).
- **Deleting a subagent**: a trash button on your own and the project's subagent cards
  (`agent.deleteSubagent`, asks first); built-in ones can only be turned off.
- **Customize's search and section switch** use the editor's own input and segmented control
  instead of pill shapes.
- Test: customize-m7-5.


### D206 — Agent skills

**What.** The agent uses skills like Claude Code and Cursor (the shared agentskills format): a
folder with a `SKILL.md` whose YAML front matter gives `name` and `description` (Claude Code's
`when_to_use` is appended), then instructions; other files in the folder (references, scripts)
are read only when needed. Found, one level of skill folders each, in the user's folders — the
IDE's own `~/<dataFolderName>/skills`, then `~/.claude/skills`, `~/.cursor/skills`,
`~/.agents/skills` — and the open folder's: `<workspace folder>/skills`, `.claude/skills`,
`.cursor/skills`, `.agents/skills` (other tools' folders only with `agent.thirdPartyConfigs`, as
for rules and commands). One skill per name: **a workspace skill overrides a user skill** (like
settings; Claude Code puts personal ones first, Cursor doesn't say), and within a scope the first
folder wins. A new chat's prompt lists each skill's name, description, `paths` and where it is;
the agent's **use_skill** tool `{ name, file? }` returns SKILL.md's body (with
`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` filled in) and the folder's other files (three levels, 100 files), or one of
those files. A workspace skill's files are also readable with read_file; both ways keep to the
agent's ignore rules (`.aiignore`, secrets) and per-category auto-approve for reads; a SKILL.md
the agent may not see isn't loaded. **`/name args`** runs one (a slash source, so the composer's
/ picker lists skills; `$ARGUMENTS` / `$1`… as for commands, or the arguments appended). A
command file of the same name comes first (Claude Code lets the skill win; changing that would
mean editing the command path for a rare clash). `disable-model-invocation: true` keeps a skill
out of the prompt and use_skill (only /name runs it); `user-invocable: false` keeps it out of the
/ list; `argument-hint` shows in the picker; `allowed-tools` is shown to the agent but doesn't
pre-approve anything (a cloned project's skill could otherwise approve its own commands).
Invalid files (no front matter, no description, a name that isn't lowercase letters, digits and
hyphens) are reported, not loaded; a name that differs from its folder is a warning.

**Customize → Skills** (order 35, like Cursor's): User N and Workspace N groups with + New at the
right of each header, rows with the lightning icon, name, description and folder; Not loaded for
invalid files. A row opens SKILL.md; its ⋯ (on hover) opens, turns off or on, reveals in the file
manager, deletes (asks). Commands: `agent.listSkills`, `agent.showSkills`, `agent.newSkill`
(`<name>/SKILL.md` from a template, then opened), `agent.setSkillEnabled`
(`agent.skills.disabled`, names, user scope), `agent.deleteSkill`, `agent.skillActions`. State:
`ide://agent/skills` (folders, skills, shadowed ones, problems). The list is read again after
any of those commands, on file events under a `skills` folder, when the page opens, when the
window gets focus, and after 30 s.

**Rust.** The fs commands reach the user skills folders through `ipc/skills.rs`: every user
skills folder is readable (the folder itself, a skill folder — which may be a link, as skill
installers make — and anything below it that isn't a link, so a read can't leave it); only the
IDE's own is writable, at `<skill>/…` depth; `skills_delete_user` deletes one of its skill
folders. `dataFolderName` comes from product.json at build time. Claude Code's, Cursor's and
`.agents` user folders stay read-only (as `~/.claude` was in D200): their skills open read-only
and can't be deleted from the IDE, only turned off.

**Limits.** Not yet: nested skills (`<subdir>/.claude/skills`, `/subdir:name`), `paths` deciding
when a skill is offered, `context: fork`, `model` / `effort` overrides, hooks, plugin skills, a
skill as a session-long mode (Cursor), live watching of the user folders. Turning a skill off
holds for new chats (D112 keeps a chat's prompt); use_skill refuses it at once.

**Tests.** `core/agent/skills.test.ts` (front matter with block scalars and lists, fields and
defaults, invalid files, workspace-over-user, the prompt and tool text, paths kept inside the
folder, the template), `ipc::skills` (paths inside a skills folder, links), skills-m7-5 (create,
page, the agent loads one, /name, off, delete); ui-m7-5 counts 7 Customize sections.


### D207 — m7.6: agent gaps closed, ten smaller ones, external agents for commit messages

**What.** The Agent items of feature-gaps section 2 (slash commands, rules for subagents,
auto-approve, worktree agents, the MCP client, Claude Code's `/ide`, @docs), ten smaller gaps in
the editor, keybindings, terminal, git and debugger, and external agents as the model for the
features nobody types against. What's left of each is listed in `docs/feature-gaps.md`.

#### Agent: commands, subagent rules, per-path auto-approve, worktree agents

- **Slash commands.** `disallowed-tools` (or `disallowedTools`) in a command's front matter takes
  whole tools away for its turn (Claude Code's names mapped as for `allowed-tools`); a
  `Bash(prefix:*)` / `Bash(exact line)` entry refuses only the matching lines (any part of a
  chain) and the command's own `!` lines; `Bash` alone refuses every `!` line. It applies to
  project and user files (it only narrows). `allowed-tools` in the **user's own** command files
  (`<config>/commands`, `~/.claude/commands`) now also pre-approves those tools for the turn, as
  Claude Code reads it: like full access for those calls only, so Ask patterns, delete and MCP
  protection, destructive calls and the command denylist still ask. A project's file still only
  narrows: a cloned repository can't approve its own tools. Limits: patterns on non-Bash tools
  (`Read(src/**)`) aren't read; IDE commands through call_command aren't pre-approved; skills'
  `allowed-tools` still doesn't pre-approve (D206).
- **Rules for subagents.** A subagent keeps the always-on rules and those naming it in its prompt
  (16 000 characters, D204), and now gets folder rules and matching-files rules with the result of
  its first read / edit / write of a file they cover, once per run, like the main agent (D200). A
  rule's `subagents:` list still decides; a subagent that omits the project's rules gets only
  those naming it. `subagentRulesForFile` (core/agent/ruleEditing.ts), `RulesService.forSubagentFile`.
- **Auto-approve per path and "Always".** find_files, and `search.run` / `quickOpen.search`
  through call_command, leave out files a reads Ask pattern covers. "Always" on a protected read
  or edit saves that one file as Allow (`/<path>`: a leading `/` now anchors at the folder's root,
  and an exact file beats any glob); on a browser or web page question it saves the domain. The
  chat notes each one. Limits: no Always for a destructive browser command; an IDE command whose
  input names a protected path isn't asked about.
- **Worktree agents.** The setup script gets `PORT`, `WORKTREE_INDEX`, `WORKTREE_PORT_BASE`,
  `WORKTREE_PORT_STEP`. Windows are separate processes with no channel between them, so instead of
  a push each worktree window is started with its chat id as a tag and `app_windows_alive(tags)`
  says whether it still runs (`try_wait`): a window closed mid-turn shows **Stopped**, not "Done
  after 10 minutes". Chats are read every 2 s (was 5 s). Apply with conflicts used to fail with
  git's message (`git apply --3way` exits non-zero) although files changed; now it reports the
  conflicted files, shows Resolve conflicts, and `agent.resolveWorktreeConflicts` opens each in the
  3-way merge editor.
- **Best of N in one window: evaluated, not done.** A chat is tied to the window's folder all the
  way down (tools, changeset, checkpoints, rules, `.aiignore`, the Rust index, language servers,
  the fs scope); a per-chat root through all of that is an L. Best of N keeps one window per model.
- Tests: slash, autoApprove, ruleEditing and worktrees tests in core; Rust `agent::worktree`,
  `ipc::app::windows`; UI agentA-m7-6.

#### MCP client, Claude Code /ide, @docs

- **Secrets in the OS keychain.** `ai/secrets.rs` keeps every secret's value (provider keys, MCP
  inputs, OAuth tokens) in the OS keychain through `keyring` (`ai/keychain.rs`): Credential
  Manager, the macOS Keychain, the Secret Service. One credential per id under product.json's
  `identifier`; a value over Windows' 2560-byte limit is split into parts. `secrets.json` stays as
  the index with a marker in the value's place. The keychain is probed once per run; without one
  (headless Linux, `IDE_NO_KEYCHAIN=1`) or when it refuses a value, the file keeps it as before.
  Plain values move in on first use. No in-memory cache (windows share the file and a rotated
  refresh token must not go stale). Limit: a marker whose entry is gone reads as "not stored".
  **New dependency:** `keyring` 3.6.3 (MIT/Apache-2.0) with the native backends and
  `sync-secret-service` (adds `dbus-secret-service` and RustCrypto crates, all MIT/Apache-2.0; a
  few hundred KB). The webview has no keychain API, and three OS APIs by hand would be more unsafe
  code than the crate.
- **Scope step-up.** A 403 with `error="insufficient_scope"` asks the user to sign in again; the
  OAuth flow asks for the last scopes plus the challenge's (`oauth::merge_scopes`) and the request
  is sent once more. One step-up per server at a time; the D204/D205 checks still apply.
- **Sampling review and images.** A request the user approved by hand shows the model's answer in
  an editable dialog (Reject / Send, `agent.reviewMcpSampling`) before it goes back; "allow" and a
  window's "always" skip it. PNG and JPEG images in user messages go to a vision model; otherwise
  (and for audio) the request is refused with the reason instead of the image being dropped.
- **MCP registry.** New MCP server → Search the MCP registry… (registry.modelcontextprotocol.io,
  `GET /v0.1/servers?search=`), through Rust `web_fetch`. A Streamable HTTP remote is preferred,
  else an npm, PyPI or OCI package with its inputs; the user sees what a server runs before it's
  written (the registry isn't vetted). Offline or with `agent.mcp.registryUrl` empty, the built-in
  list answers.
- **Standing GET stream.** After initialize a remote server gets `GET <url>` (`mcp/stream.rs`), so
  notifications and requests arrive while no request is open. 405 means none; a dropped stream
  reconnects with backoff (1 s to 60 s) and `Last-Event-ID`; 20 failures, a 404 or 401/403 close it.
  Same rules as POST.
- **Claude Code /ide.** `executeCode` runs only in a Jupyter notebook open in the IDE, after the
  user says yes, in a new cell at its end (so what ran stays visible); `at_mentioned` through
  **Send selection to Claude Code** (palette); getDiagnostics gives whole ranges, source, code and
  Hint severity. The D204 lock file token and Origin refusal stay.
- **@docs.** robots.txt's `Sitemap:` lines (or `sitemap.xml`), same origin, at most five files,
  seed the crawl within the start folder. Pages that are almost empty without scripts are skipped
  as "needs JavaScript" and counted (the built-in browser has no headless rendering).
  `agent.docs.refreshDays` (7, 0 = off) reads a source again when its index is older; a failed
  refresh keeps the old index. Embeddings stay out.
- Tests: Rust `ai::secrets`, `ai::keychain`, `mcp::oauth`, `mcp::stream`, `mcp::remote`,
  `ide_ws`; TS registry, sampling, ideTools and docsSitemap tests; UI agentB-m7-6 with a mock
  remote MCP server (`tests/fixtures/mock-remote-mcp.mjs`).

#### Ten smaller gaps

- **Selection count:** `EngineEditor.selectionStatus()` counts from the model's offsets, so the
  status bar no longer copies the selection on each move; several cursors read as VS Code's ("3
  selections (40 characters selected)").
- **A chord's `args`:** the editor-engine path of a chord's second key dropped them;
  `editor.runAction` now passes `args` to actions, provider commands and Monaco commands without
  an action (`cursorMove`, run with `editor.trigger`).
- **Readable titles** for Monaco's plain commands in the keyboard shortcuts editor
  (`keybindings/engineTitles.ts`): a table for the odd ones, else the id in words.
- **Terminal suggestion keys per terminal:** the context keys follow the focused terminal's widget.
- **zsh records:** PROMPT_SP prints `PROMPT_EOL_MARK` before precmd, so the D mark came after it;
  the mark is now prefixed with the D sequence (with `%?`), checked against zsh 5.9.
- **JavaScript debug terminal** in the + ▾ menu and the profile picker, as VS Code lists it.
- **Debugger:** `debug.restart` of a compound's last session keeps the compound and its stopAll;
  the debugger program paths are `"scope": "user"` (a folder can't pick the program debugging
  runs; a launch.json configuration's own `python` still comes from the folder, as in VS Code).
- **launch.json `presentation`:** `hidden`, `group` and `order` order the pickers, with VS Code's
  separator between groups (`presentation.ts`).
- **Merge editor:** Accept all in the Incoming and Current headers, sashes between the input panes,
  word-level highlights against the base (`core/diff/words.ts`, Myers over word tokens).
- **Git repositories:** autofetch fetches every repository, one after another; the pull request
  files tab remembers its repository.

#### External agents for commit messages, Customize polish

- **External agents as a feature's model.** Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and GitHub Copilot
  bring their own sign-in and models, which the IDE can't call as a model API. For the features
  nobody types against (Generate commit message, memory tidy-up) the model picker lists them
  under "Agents" (`acp/<name>`): the agent starts over ACP in the folder, gets one prompt, and its
  answer's text is used; every request it makes (files, commands, questions) is refused, and it's
  stopped afterwards (`acpOneShot.ts`, 2-minute limit). Edit with AI, suggestions and next-edit
  stay on model APIs: an agent takes seconds to start. Test: git-m6-74.
- **Customize polish.** The open section gets the hover background and hover only brightens the
  text; skills from other tools' folders say "From Cursor" / "From Claude Code" instead of a path;
  Settings' sidebar has a Customize link under MCP server, and the MCP server page a "Configure
  MCP servers" card.


### D207 audit — m7.6: the agent, its integrations and the whole IDE

Five audits (agent core; MCP, ACP and providers; editor and languages; terminal, git, debug and
testing; workbench, extensions and the Rust core), each verifying before fixing. The most
important changes, and what the lead added:

- **Restricted mode means it.** Language servers (they run the folder's TypeScript,
  rust-analyzer build scripts and proc macros, gopls) and git (the repository's own
  core.fsmonitor, filters, hooks, sshCommand) start only in a trusted folder, like VS Code; the
  agent's "run commands automatically" asks there too. Tests: git-restricted-m7-6, and the LSP
  scripts trust their folder first.
- **Extensions:** the worker's `import(` check can't be fooled by comments; no FontFace,
  storage or service workers; `fs.write` no longer reaches user-only settings, keybindings.json,
  files outside the folder or anything inside `.git` (its config and hooks run programs).
- **Data safety:** saves refuse to overwrite text changed on disk that the IDE hasn't seen;
  typing during a save is kept; auto save leaves the cursor's line alone; notebooks no longer
  turn `NaN` inside cell code into `null`; two windows merge global state instead of
  overwriting it; keychain entries are per profile (a test run can't touch the user's keys);
  write_file refuses a file changed since the agent read it and keeps CRLF.
- **Robustness:** context overflow is summarized and retried; cut-off streams and cut-off tool
  arguments are errors, not finished answers or empty files; language server messages keep
  their order and crashed servers restart (4 times in 3 minutes); MCP streams back off
  properly and stop on reload; Claude Code's lock file is removed on exit; ACP one-shots fail
  at once when the agent exits.
- **Injection:** task and debug command lines are quoted for their shell (bash, PowerShell
  including its typographic quotes, cmd); registry MCP entries may only use known launchers;
  ACP terminal arguments are single-quoted.
- **Windows:** bare program names in process tasks resolve through PATHEXT (`npm.cmd`);
  taskkill runs off the async runtime; network or relative parents for new folders are refused;
  extension ids that are device names are refused. Not compiled for Windows here (no target):
  in windows-pending.
- **Smaller:** the main window opens where it was closed; quick input is an ARIA combobox;
  restart of one compound session stops only it; nested repositories refresh only for their
  own files; Ctrl+L stays in the browser's address bar.

#### Agent core
- **Context overflow recovery.** The 4-characters-per-token estimate can be off (code, JSON, CJK),
  and a provider's "prompt is too long" / `context_length_exceeded` failed the turn, with Retry
  failing the same way. Now `chat` turns such an error (nothing streamed yet) into
  `ContextOverflowError`; the loop summarizes the older part against half the budget
  (`recoverOverflow`) and tries the step once more (Claude Code's reactive compaction). A second
  overflow, or nothing to summarize, fails the turn as before. `isContextOverflow` in
  `core/agent/loop.ts`.
- **Malformed tool arguments.** A call whose arguments weren't JSON (cut off at the output limit)
  ran with `{}`; write_file then wrote an empty file. Now the call returns "the arguments weren't
  valid JSON" and runs nothing (`toolArguments`), with a hint to write large files in parts.
- **write_file:** no `content` is an error, not an empty file; a CRLF file keeps CRLF
  (`withLineEndingsOf`); and a file changed since the agent last read or wrote it (the user typed,
  a formatter ran) is refused with "read it again" (Claude Code's "modified since read";
  `Changeset.noteSeen` / `lastSeen`, in memory: after a restart nothing is refused).
- **read_file** returns at most 48 000 characters per call (400 lines of long lines were about
  200k tokens), and an offset past the end is an error instead of an empty read.
- **Automatic mode needs a trusted folder (D103).** In a folder that isn't trusted,
  `agent.runCommands: "auto"` asks for commands and IDE commands as "ask" mode does (the card says
  why): the folder's package scripts, Makefile and its own `agent.verifyCommand` (folder-scoped)
  are the folder's programs, and its files can steer the agent to run them. Full access is
  unchanged (it means everything). UI scripts that use auto mode trust their folder first.
- **Protected paths through call_command.** A path agent.autoApprove asks before reading or
  changing (`reads`/`edits` false) now asks too when an IDE command names it
  (`editor.getText`, fs commands…); before, a command was a way around read_file's question.
- **Retry / edit / restore stop background subagents** started for the cut conversation; their
  reports came back afterwards as a turn about a task that was gone.
- **Customize:** a search that matches no section says so; agent.customize's description lists
  skills and commands; Commands → New refuses a built-in name (/review, /compact…) and a name
  already taken where it would be shadowed (the file was written and never showed or ran).

#### Editor and languages
Fixed:
- **Saving over an unseen change on disk.** A save re-reads the file and refuses to overwrite
  text the IDE hasn't seen (the watcher was late, or can't watch: network drives), like VS Code's
  "the file is newer": the "changed on disk" banner shows and the save fails with a message.
  Keep my changes now takes the disk text as the known one, so the next save writes.
  `ide://editors/active` gains `diskState`.
- **Typing during a save marked as saved.** The saved version was read after the (native)
  encoder's await, and a notebook's after serializing and writing: edits made meanwhile were
  marked saved and lost on close. Both now take the version before any await.
- **Saves of one document are queued**, so an auto save and Ctrl+S can't reach the disk in the
  wrong order. Save with encoding passes the encoding to the save (the document takes it once
  written), so its old bytes aren't taken for an outside change.
- **Auto save mid-typing** (afterDelay with `files.trimTrailingWhitespace` /
  `insertFinalNewline`) ate the space just typed. Auto saves now leave the cursors' lines alone,
  and afterDelay runs no `editor.codeActionsOnSave` (VS Code's "always" means explicit and
  focus/window saves).
- **Messages to a language server could be reordered.** Each `lsp_send` is its own async Tauri
  command, run concurrently; two in one tick (didOpen, didChange) could swap. `core/ipc/ordered.ts`
  queues them per server (tested); a restart drops what the old process hadn't been sent.
- **Crashed language servers stayed down.** One that exits while running restarts after 1 s, at
  most 4 times in 3 minutes, then stays failed with a notification (VS Code's policy).
- **LSP programs by relative path** (`./node_modules/.bin/x`) resolve under the folder (Windows
  looked under the IDE's own directory); on Windows an absolute path without extension finds its
  `.cmd` shim.
- **Notebook NaN repair corrupted sources.** Reading Python's bare `NaN`/`Infinity` replaced them
  inside strings too (`print([1, NaN])` became `null` and was saved so); now only outside strings.
- A JSON-RPC notification handler that throws no longer escapes into the transport listener.
- Notebook replace's macOS key (Alt+Cmd+F) no longer fights the explorer's with the sidebar
  focused.

Tests: `core/ipc/ordered.test.ts`, `settings.test.ts` (cursor lines), `notebook.test.ts` (NaN in
strings), `lsp::tests::relative_programs_are_under_the_working_directory`, UI script
`editor-audit-m7-6` (conflict refused then kept, auto-save trim, UTF-8 → Windows-1252).


### D208 — m7.6.1: Git tools as a bundled extension; external agents without a folder, with usage and their changed files

#### GitLens-style features are a bundled extension, on the extension API
The owner: VS Code and Cursor don't build in line history, compare, stashes or GitHub
notifications — those come from extensions (GitLens, GitHub Pull Requests). D204 had put them in
the core; they move into a provided extension so the IDE stays lean, and the extension API grows
so any git extension could do the same.

- **What moved** (`src-tauri/bundled-extensions/gittools`, id `bundled.gittools`, "Git tools",
  original icon): Toggle file blame (`git.toggleFileBlame`, the per-line author/age annotations,
  `git.blame.heatmap`, `ide://git/fileBlame`), Line history (`git.lineHistory`), Compare
  (`git.compareBranches`, `git.compareSwap`, `ide://git/lens`), the Stashes section
  (`git.showStashes`; expand → files, Apply / Pop / Drop on hover) and GitHub notifications
  (`github.notifications`, `github.markNotificationRead`, `github.markAllNotificationsRead`, new
  `github.openNotification`, `github.notifications.enabled`, new `ide://github/notifications`).
  Command, view, setting and state ids are unchanged (no aliases needed); the four views are still
  Source control sections hidden from the activity bar by default
  (`workbench.activityBar.hidden` keeps their ids). Removed from core: `git/lensViews.ts`,
  `git/fileBlame.ts`, the notifications part of `githubReview.ts`, the two settings, the
  `lens-*` CSS; `lens.ts` keeps the porcelain / `log -L` parsers (they serve the API) and the
  review threads.
- **What stayed in core:** Source control and everything from before D204, plus the merge editor,
  several repositories, the stash *commands* (`git.stash*`, `git.stashShow`), GitHub pull
  requests / issues and the D204 pull request files / review threads tab. The status-bar and
  inline blame (D120) are core; only the whole-file blame gutter moved.
- **On by default:** `seed_bundled` seeds ids in `ENABLED_BY_DEFAULT` enabled, with the
  permissions their manifest asks for granted (`git`, `github`, `fs.read`, `fs.write` — the last
  for Apply / Pop, which run `git.stashApply` / `git.stashPop`). Existing users get it on with
  the next start (it's a new bundled id). Disable or uninstall it like any extension: its
  sections and commands disappear; Restore bundled extensions brings it back on.
- **Extension API added (general, documented in docs/extensions.md and src/api/index.d.ts):**
  - `ide.git` ("git", read-only): `repositories()`, `blame(path, { useEditorText })` (parsed
    hunks; the editor's unsaved text by default), `lineLog(path, start, end, { limit ≤ 200 })`,
    `diffNames(left, right?, { mergeBase })`, `revParse`, `mergeBase`, `refs()` (branches, tags),
    `stashes()`, `show(path, rev)`, `onDidChange` (the `git.didChange` event); every call takes
    `{ repository }` and routes like the git commands. Backed by `services.gitAccess`
    (`workbench/gitAccess.ts`), which the git extension provides (`git/access.ts`) over its
    existing Rust commands (`git_blame_file`, `git_log_lines`, `git_diff_names`,
    `git_rev_parse`, `git_merge_base_of`, `git_branches`, `git_repo_state`, `git_stash_list`,
    `git_show`). Writes stay `git.*` commands (permission-checked; destructive ones ask).
  - `ide.github` ("github", a new permission; `github.*` commands now need it too):
    `notifications({ all })`, `markNotificationRead(id)`, `markAllNotificationsRead()` through
    the existing `github_cli` ops.
  - `ide.editor.setLineAnnotations(path, [{ line, text, tone 0–4, hover }] | null)` ("fs.read"):
    `services.gutterMarks.annotate`, generic `.line-annotation-tone-N` styles (were
    `.blame-heat-N`); 80 characters, 20 000 lines, 50 files per extension; cleared on stop.
  - `ide.editor.active()` gains `selection`; the `documents.didChange` event (unsaved edits,
    ≤ every 250 ms per file, "fs.read").
  - Tree views: items' `actions` (≤ 4 hover buttons running commands) and `strong` (bold),
    `registerTreeView(…).setMessage(text)` (VS Code's `TreeView.message`).
  - Manifest: views' `sectionOf` ("scm.view", "explorer.view") and `sectionOrder`; commands'
    `when`; `"namespaces": ["git", "github"]` lets an extension that ships with the IDE keep
    built-in names (any other manifest with it is refused, and the runtime skips such names for
    a copy that isn't the shipped one).
- **Tests:** `gittools.test.ts` (the extension's model loaded as the worker would, the shipped
  manifest parses and declares exactly what main.js registers), `thirdParty.test.ts`
  (namespaces, sections, `when`, `github` permission), `rpc.test.ts` (the new requests),
  `lens.test.ts` (trimmed), Rust `bundled_extensions_are_seeded_once_and_disabled` (Git tools
  seeded on with grants). UI: `git-m7-5` passes through the extension and checks that disabling
  it removes the commands and sections while `git.stashList` stays, then re-enabling brings them
  back; `extensions` / `extensions-api` list it (active).
- **Limits:** the Stashes header lost its "Stash changes…" button (menus may only run the
  extension's own commands; `git.stash` stays in the palette and Git menu). A third-party view
  with `sectionOf` starts on the activity bar (only the IDE's own are hidden by default). A
  grant made at seeding isn't widened when a later version asks for more (it then asks, like any
  extension). Line annotations are one extension's per file.

#### External agents over ACP
- **Chat with no folder.** An external agent (Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Copilot) no longer
  fails with "Open a folder first.": with no folder open it starts in the chat's private folder,
  `<appData>/agent/scratch/<chat id>` (Rust `agent/scratch.rs`, `agent_scratch_dir`; removed with
  the chat). Rust lets a stdio program (`lsp_start`) and a command (`exec_run`) run there without a
  workspace; the agent's `fs/read_text_file` / `fs/write_text_file` go through
  `agent_scratch_read` / `_write`, confined to that one folder (canonical paths, nearest existing
  ancestor, no `..` or links out: `fs::resolve_under`, the workspace's own rule, factored out).
  Nothing else in app data (settings, keys, other chats' folders) is reachable. With a folder open
  the agent's file requests are now also confined to that folder (before, a file the user had
  opened from outside it was readable). Opening a folder later restarts the agent there with a
  recap (`startedFor`). The one-off prompts (commit message, memory tidy-up, D207) use a shared
  `one-off` folder the same way. *Why:* the panel offered "Just chat" but external agents need a
  working directory. *Limits:* the agent's own tools (Codex's shell, Claude Code's Read/Write) are
  the agent's business: they run with its process's cwd in the private folder, but the IDE can't
  stop an agent's own sandbox-less tools from touching other paths — only what goes through ACP is
  confined. A private folder's writes aren't reviewed (nothing of the user's is there).
- **The IDE's own agent with no folder**: checked — it chats; tools that need a folder fail per
  call with "no folder is open" (the model is told to ask the user to open one), nothing blocks the
  chat. Covered by the new UI script.
- **Usage of external agents.** Each turn is one usage-log record (`makeAgentRecord`): provider
  `acp:<agent>`, model `acp:<agent>/<the agent's current model id>`, the tokens from the
  `session/prompt` answer's `usage` (ACP's End-turn token usage RFD, still a draft, but Claude
  Code, Codex and Gemini CLI send it) in the IDE's units (input including cached; Claude Code and
  Codex count `inputTokens` without the cache, Gemini CLI with it — `totalTokens` tells which), and
  a cost only when the agent reports one (`usage_update`'s cumulative `cost`, stable since June
  2026: the turn's cost is the difference). No tokens → still one request, marked `unreported`,
  cost unknown (shown as "—", never $0). No price list is applied to agents' tokens: the IDE can't
  tell whether the agent bills API credits or a subscription. `usage_update`'s `used`/`size` drive
  the chat's context meter. The Usage page lists them as "<agent> (external agent)", the model row
  says "subscription or not reported" or "as the agent reports it", the provider row explains.
  The commit-message / memory one-off prompts are logged under their feature.
- **Codex's Guardian reviews** (its approval-review subagent, streamed by codex-acp as "Guardian
  Review" `think` steps with `toolCallId` `guardian_assessment:<id>`, text Status / Action / Risk /
  Authorization / Rationale and `rawInput.targetItemId`) fold into the step they reviewed: the
  command's row gets a tag "Guardian: approved · low risk", its details start with the rationale.
  A review whose step hasn't appeared yet is a compact row ("Guardian: reviewing…") that goes away
  when the step appears; a denied one (its command never runs) stays as a compact row in the error
  tone, its action and rationale in the details.
- **Commands as typed.** Codex titles a Windows command with PowerShell's full path and quoting;
  the row, the tooltip and the permission card now show `npm run check` with a "PowerShell" tag
  (`prettyCommand`: PowerShell `-Command`/`-c` with its switches, `cmd /c`, `bash -lc`, debug-quoted
  paths with doubled backslashes, a program's full path → its name). Tooltips of external agents'
  rows are the step as shown (plus the shell and the review), not `acp:execute {"title":…}`.
- **Files an external agent writes itself.** Codex (and Claude Code, Gemini CLI) write files with
  their own tools, so no "edited files" showed. Each turn in a folder, `TurnWatch` reads git's
  dirty files (up to 200, ≤ 1 MB each) and HEAD at the start; at the end it compares the dirty files
  then and now (a file clean at the start against HEAD, a new untracked one as created) plus the
  files the agent's steps named (their locations, or a diff's old text). The text changes go into
  the chat's changeset as already-written changes (`Changeset.adopt`: checkpointed first, so the
  review's diff, accept, reject = put back, per-hunk review, the turn's checkpoint restore and
  auto-apply all work as for the IDE's own agent). They show on the step that named the file, else
  on one "Changed files" step. Binary or large files are listed by name only; commits the agent
  made during the turn are noted. Without git: only the files its steps name, read when first
  named (best effort).

**What usage each agent reports.**
| Agent (preset) | Tokens per turn | Cost | Context meter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Codex (`@agentclientprotocol/codex-acp` 2.2.x, TypeScript now) | yes: `PromptResponse.usage` (`inputTokens` without cache, `cachedReadTokens`, `cachedWriteTokens`, `outputTokens` incl. reasoning, `thoughtTokens`, `totalTokens`), also `_meta.quota` | no | `usage_update` `used`/`size` |
| Claude Code (`@agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp` 0.95) | yes: `PromptResponse.usage` (Anthropic counting: input without cache), `_meta.quota` by model | yes: `usage_update.cost` = the SDK's `total_cost_usd`, cumulative, USD, at API prices | `usage_update` (`_meta["_claude/model"]`) |
| Gemini CLI (`gemini --acp`) | yes: `PromptResponse.usage` (`inputTokens` = prompt incl. cache, `cachedReadTokens`, `thoughtTokens`) | no | `usage_update` `used`/`size` |
| GitHub Copilot (`copilot --acp`) | not verified: closed source (a native binary), its ACP docs say nothing about usage; the IDE counts its turns as "not reported" | no | — |

What the IDE shows for each: tokens when reported, cost only from Claude Code (labelled as the
agent's figure), otherwise "—". **Subscriptions:** Codex signed in with ChatGPT and Claude Code
signed in with `claude /login` bill the user's subscription (plan limits, not dollars); with an
API key they bill API credits. The ACP messages don't say which, so the IDE can't know: it shows
the agent's own tokens (and Claude Code's API-price cost, which on a subscription is what the turn
*would* cost on the API, not what was charged), never a price it computed itself. Copilot bills
premium requests per prompt; none of that reaches ACP.

**Also:** tooltips wrap long unbroken text and stop at half the window.


### D209 — m7.6.2: ten features up to VS Code's level, the browser keeps links in the IDE

**What.** Feature-gaps section 2 items in the terminal, debugger, command line and windows,
notebooks, keyboard shortcuts, testing, logs and the merge editor, and the browser pane's links,
redirects, forms and popups, which went to the system browser. What's left of each is in
`docs/feature-gaps.md`.
