  their full definitions in the tool list, so nothing the summary removed is needed to call them).
- **Requests:** the turn's tool list is still fixed for the turn, except that the tools a
  tool_search loads are added at its end from the next step on (`withLoadedTools`; the loop now
  reads `deps.tools()` before each step). Native and text-protocol models both: the text protocol's
  tool prompt is built from the same list each step, and its parser accepts deferred tools' names
  so a call of one gets the error instead of being shown as text.
- **A call of a deferred tool not loaded** doesn't run: "Error: X is a deferred tool and its
  definition isn't loaded… Load it with tool_search {"query": "select:X"}, then call it." (D204
  loaded it as a side effect; now only tool_search loads, so the record stays in one place.)
- **Prompt caching (trade-off):** loading a tool changes the tool list, and the provider's cached
  prefix (tools come first) is re-read once from that request; the note after the system prompt
  changes at the same request. Deferring still wins whenever the deferred definitions are big:
  every request without them is smaller, and a chat typically loads a few tools once. The order
  of the earlier tools never changes, so later requests cache again.
- **Built-in tools are not deferred:** the browser tools are already offered only while a browser
  tab is open (`browserTools`), and the rest are used every turn or are small; deferring them would
  cost a tool_search round trip on common work for little saving.
- **Subagents:** a subagent's tools never include tool_search (its list can't grow mid-run). Tools
  its definition names explicitly come with their full definitions, deferred or not
  (`session.callableTools()`); one that inherits the chat's tools gets what the chat offers now
  (loaded MCP tools included, unloaded ones not).
- `ide://agent/session` has `deferredTools` and `loadedTools` while the chat defers. The rows show
  "Loaded tools <query>".

### D320 — web_search: allowed / blocked domains, extended mode, the Sources rule
- **Parameters:** `query`, `count`, `allowed_domains`, `blocked_domains`, `mode`
  (`standard` | `extended`). `web.search` takes `allowedDomains`, `blockedDomains`, `mode`.
  Domains are normalized (`https://www.docs.rs/x` → `docs.rs`) and match subdomains.
- **Per provider:** Tavily: `include_domains` / `exclude_domains` in the request. Exa:
  `includeDomains`, or `excludeDomains` when no domain is allowed (Exa takes one list; with both,
  the blocked ones are filtered afterwards). Brave and SearXNG: the query syntax, `site:` for one
  allowed domain and `-site:` per blocked one (several allowed domains would need an `OR` that the
  providers parse differently, so those are filtered afterwards). Every provider's results are
  filtered by the domains too, and when filtering afterwards may drop results the search asks for
  twice as many (up to 20).
- **Extended** ("a thorough, fresher search at several times the cost"): twice the results (up to
  20), Tavily's `search_depth: advanced` (its 2-credit search), and the top three results' pages
  read now (3 000 characters each, a page that fails is left out) after the snippets. Standard
  stays one request. The page reads are part of the approved search (they don't ask again or go
  through `WebFetch(domain:…)` rules); `agent.webFetch.enabled` off still stops the whole search.
- **Sources:** the tool's description and every result end with Claude Code's rule: after
  answering from the results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs used, as Markdown links.
- Rust: `ai/search.rs` `SearchOptions { includeDomains, excludeDomains, deep }` (optional
  `options` argument of `web_search`; no new command), `post_body` tested.

### D321 — web_fetch with a question
- **Parameters:** `url`, `prompt` (new, optional), `max_chars`. Without `prompt`, as before.
- **With `prompt`:** web.fetch reads up to 100 000 characters (its maximum), and the page goes to a
  model with the question through `host.subagent` (Claude Code fetches through a subagent too): no
  tools, one step, a system prompt that says the page is untrusted, answer in at most 300 words,
  quote exact text, keep the links, and say "NOT IN THIS PART" when it doesn't answer. The agent
  gets "url — title / Answer to "…", from the page: …", never the page.
- **Huge pages:** parts of 24 000 characters (about 6 000 tokens, so a small local model's context
  takes one), cut at a paragraph or line break; at most four parts. Each part is asked on its own,
  one after another; parts that found nothing are dropped and two or more answers are merged by one
  more call. A page longer than what was read says so ("web_fetch without a prompt and with
  max_chars reads more of it"). Typical pages are one call.
- **The model:** `agent.webFetch.model` (new, empty by default), else the Explore agent's model
  when the user chose one (the cheap helper model they already picked, as Claude Code uses a small
  model for both), else the chat's. A model name that isn't available falls back to the chat's
  (subagents' rule).
- **Failures:** no subagent support (a host without models), an error or an empty answer: the
  page's text, capped at 8 000 characters, with "(The question couldn't be answered by a model:
  …)". Stop between parts ends it.
- **Cost:** the calls are logged like a subagent's (the Usage page, source "subagent"), as the
  Explore tool's are; they aren't added to the turn's cost under the answer (subagents' calls
  aren't either).

### D322 — Monitors: a command's output lines as events in the chat (Claude Code's Monitor)
- New tool `monitor` { command, description, timeout_ms, cwd }. Each output line is an event; lines
  within 200 ms go to the chat as one automatic message (`auto: "monitor"`), which starts a turn
  when the chat is idle or joins the running one at its next step, exactly as a background
  command's end does (D253, `deliverAutoMessage`). The description is in every message.
- It's a background process (`backgroundProcesses`), so it gets a bg id, runs in run_command's
  shell (PowerShell on Windows, with the bash-idiom translation; the description gives a
  PowerShell example there), is listed above the message box ("monitor: …") and in the details
  panel (a radio-tower icon, its description), and `kill_process` / Stop end it. Killing it sends
  nothing (the agent or the user did it).
- It asks as run_command asks: the permission block moved out of run_command into
  `askToRun` (tools.ts) unchanged, so both share it. Not read-only: not in Ask or Plan mode.
- Limits: more than 20 messages or 2000 lines in a minute stops it with one message ("narrow the
  command"); it expires after timeout_ms (default 5 minutes, at most 30, at least 5 s) with one
  message and the event count; when its command exits, its last lines and an end message come.
  Each message carries at most 40 lines / 4000 characters (the rest counted). What it sent is
  marked read for process_output.
- Why not a polling loop in the model: it costs a turn per check; here the IDE watches and the
  model is woken only by real events.

### D323 — Watching a pull request for a chat (Claude Code's app binding a PR to a session)
- Tool `watch_pr` { action: watch | unwatch | status, number }, commands
  `agent.watchPullRequest`, `agent.unwatchPullRequest`, `agent.checkPullRequestNow`, state
  `ide://agent/prWatches`, and a row in the details panel's Background card (Check now, Stop
  watching, the number and title open it on GitHub).
- The IDE polls every 60 s through the user's GitHub CLI (`gh pr view --json …` and the review
  threads GraphQL query the review tab already uses) — never the model, no network beyond gh.
  Errors back off (doubling up to 15 minutes) and show on the row.
- Only actionable changes are sent (`auto: "pr"`): checks that newly fail (a re-run that fails
  again counts), all checks passing, a merge conflict appearing or going away, new conversation
  or unresolved review comments with their text (first 10, 1500 characters each). Merged or
  closed: one message, and the watch ends. The first look is the baseline (the tool's result
  says what's failing already), so the agent isn't woken for the state it just saw.
- One pull request per chat; without `number` the chat's own (the one its agent opened, D227),
  else the current branch's. Watches are saved with the folder and resume when it opens, compared
  with the saved state (comment bodies aren't saved, their ids are). Not started automatically
  when a chat opens a pull request: each wake-up is a turn that uses the model, so it's asked for.

### D324 — delegate with fork: true (Claude Code's subagent_type "fork")
- `fork: true` starts a background subagent from a copy of this conversation instead of a brief;
  `agent` becomes optional (without it, the fork is a copy of the agent: a built-in "fork"
  definition, no file). Named, that subagent's own prompt and tools are used, plus the copy.
- The copy is a transcript in the subagent's system prompt (`forkTranscript`): who said what,
  tool calls with results (the newest 6 up to 2000 characters, older ones 300), notices and the
  running delegate call left out, a summary standing in for what it replaced. Its budget is about
  a third of the context window (`forkBudget`, 8k–240k characters); when it doesn't fit, the first
  request stays and the newest messages that fit follow it, with a note of how many were left
  out. A transcript (not the raw messages) because the fork has fewer tools than the chat had:
  replaying tool calls it can't make breaks some providers and the text protocol.
- Tools: the background subagents' read-only set (as before), unless isolated: true, where the
  transcript opens the helper's task in its worktree.
- The description says when: "a fork for side work that leans on this conversation, a fresh
  subagent with a full brief otherwise".

### D325 — Messages between chats (Claude Code's ListAgents + SendMessage)
- `list_chats`: this folder's chats (saved and loaded, not archived, not this one), newest first:
  id, title, agent, working / waiting for the user / idle.
- `message_chat` { chat, message, notify_when_idle }: the message arrives in that chat as an
  automatic message (`auto: "chat"`) shown with its text and "Message from chat <title>" (the
  title opens the sender), telling that agent it's from another chat's agent and how to answer;
  it starts a turn there or joins the running one. With notify_when_idle, one note comes back
  when the target has taken the message and gone idle, with its answer's first 8 lines (given up
  after 2 hours).
- Permission: asked the first time a chat messages a given chat (it spends the user's tokens);
  "Don't try another way around it" when declined. Not read-only, so Ask and Plan modes don't
  have it; the target works under its own permissions, and the description says never to use it
  to get around what the user denied. At most 20 sends per chat in 10 minutes (two agents can't
  talk forever).

### D326 — A Background tasks view, after Claude Code's app
- What: one dock view (`agent.backgroundTasks`, opened beside the chat) over everything a chat has
  working on its own: its subagent runs (delegate, explore, forks, skills run in a subagent,
  background runs, the automatic review), its worktree helpers (D231), its background commands
  and monitors (D201, D322) and its watched pull request (D323). Sections Running (N) and
  Finished (N) (folds; Show more past 10). Header: title, clear finished (trash), expand
  (`layout.toggleMaximize`), close. Each running task has its live time and Stop.
- A subagent row: its title (the short description `delegate` now takes, else its task's first
  line), its agent, "N tasks" with "1 failed" in the error color, opening to its own tool calls,
  each to its command (or arguments) and output, monospace and scrollable. A command row opens to
  `$ command` and what it printed, live, with Open output (the existing output tab, D286).
- The chip under the conversation ("16 background commands" / "12 completed, 1 failed, 3
  running": an icon, two lines, a chevron) opens the view. It replaces the strip of background
  commands above the message box (D201, D286): the view lists the same commands with their
  output and Stop, and more, so a second list above the composer no longer earned its place
  (Claude Code's app has only the chip). The details panel's Background card stays (quick
  glance) and links to the view.
- Why one view: the details card, the strip, the helpers' rows and the PR row each showed part of
  the picture; the owner wanted Claude Code's single place. Every action is a command
  (`agent.showBackgroundTasks {session?, task?}`, `agent.stopBackgroundTask {session?, id}`,
  `agent.clearBackgroundTasks {session?}`); state `ide://agent/background`.
- Clear hides finished tasks from the view and chip (a per-chat time) and drops finished subagent
  runs; finished commands stay readable with process_output (their own limit of 10 per chat).

### D327 — Subagent transcripts, live and after they finish
- `runSubagent` registers every run in `subagentRuns` (window-wide, not saved): brief, agent,
  model, times, status, a Stop of its own (at its next step; its own model requests are
  cancelled) and its conversation — the loop's own item list while it runs (redrawn at most every
  150 ms), a capped copy once it ends (its brief and its last 400 items; 30 finished per chat).
- The transcript page: back, title, time, Stop, expand, close; the brief in a card folded to four
  lines with Show more; "Model <name>"; then its work laid out exactly as the chat lays out a
  turn (`layoutTurns`, `workSummary`, `renderRow`, `renderItem`) with a quiet item host (no
  message actions, editing or retry). Live while it runs.
- Better than Claude Code: finished subagents open too (there only running ones do), and a helper
  working in this window shows its own chat the same way (one in another window opens its chat).
- A subagent stopped from the view (not the whole turn) returns what it had, marked as stopped
  by the user, so the agent that delegated knows.

### D328 — Monitor over a WebSocket
- The monitor tool takes `ws: { url, protocols? }` instead of `command` (Claude Code's Monitor
  `ws`): each incoming text frame is one event (a multiline frame stays one; one over 2000
  characters is cut), a binary frame is `[binary frame, N bytes]`, an error is an event before
  the close, and the close ends the watch with its code and reason ("closed with code 1000
  (normal closure)"). Same 200 ms batching, flood limit and timeout as a command's; it's a
  background entry like one (bg id, kill_process, the view, `ide://agent/monitors` with the
  address as its command).
- The webview can't open it: the CSP's `connect-src` has no `ws:`/`wss:` and shouldn't (any
  injected script could then reach anywhere). Rust opens it (`src-tauri/src/agent/socket.rs`):
  the handshake through reqwest's HTTP/1.1 upgrade (`Response::upgrade`, already in the crate,
  with its rustls for `wss://`), the frames with the in-house framing (`mcp::ide_ws::read_frame`,
  `debug::encode_frame`). No new dependency. A lifetime (the monitor's timeout plus 10 s) closes
  a socket whose page went away.
- It asks before connecting like a command (a card showing the address) unless
  agent.runCommands is auto in a trusted folder, or full access.
- A normal close (1000, 1001) counts as a clean exit in the lists; others as failed.

### D329 — Hand off a task in flight (hand_off_task)
- Claude Code's hand_off_to_session: `hand_off_task { title (<60), remaining_plan }`. The task
  moves to a new chat that starts working at once (it's the user's task already): its first
  message is the remaining plan; this conversation up to the call goes with it as hidden context
  (the user message's `context`, shown as a chip), built by the fork's transcript builder (D324,
  `forkTranscript` / `forkBudget`). Same agent (chat mode) and model as this chat. The new chat
  isn't opened: the call draws a "Moved to a new chat" card with Open chat, and the result tells
  the agent to stop that task and answer the new message, no recap.
- Not read-only (it starts work that edits files): offered in Agent mode only, like
  enter_plan_mode. A turn tool: subagents never get it (`TURN_TOOL_NAMES`).
- Interplay with propose_task (D303): that one offers separate follow-up work the user may start;
  this one moves the work in progress, without asking (Claude Code doesn't ask either). Files the
  task already changed stay on disk and in this chat's review.
- Core: `core/agent/handOff.ts` (arguments, texts, the card's chat), tested.

### D330 — Plan mode's plan as an editable document
- Claude Code's plan file + ExitPlanMode, without a new tool: a Plan turn's answer is the plan
  (the Plan rules now say the final answer is the plan document, Markdown with a # title), and
  the IDE saves it when the turn ends, where the "Plan ready" notice is added. Every model and
  every planner agent (read-only agents included, whose tool list a write_plan tool wouldn't pass)
  gets it, and no tool description is added to every request.
- Where: `<user config>/plans/<chat id>.md`, next to settings.json (like Claude Code's
  ~/.claude/plans): no file in the project (nothing to ignore or commit), works without a folder,
  and editable in an editor tab (the config folder is in the app's file scope).
- The latest plan notice draws as a card: title, step count, "edited" once the file differs from
  the agent's answer; folded by default (the answer is right above it), opened it shows the
  file's Markdown. Build / Open to edit / Keep planning while it's the chat's last item. Saving
  the file (`files.didSave`) redraws it.
- Build (`agent.build`) sends the file as it is: unchanged, "carry out the plan above (saved as
  …)"; edited, the edited text, which wins where it differs. Keep planning shows the chat; in
  Plan mode, the next message carries the edited file once, so the revised plan starts from the
  user's version. A new Plan turn overwrites the file (the user's edits went with the message).
- Commands `agent.openPlan`, `agent.keepPlanning`; state `ide://agent/planDoc`. Core:
  `core/agent/planDoc.ts`, tested.

### D331 — Search other chats (search_chats)
- Claude Code's search_session_transcripts: `search_chats { query, limit? (5, at most 20) }`,
  read-only, no permission ask. Over this folder's chats: saved ones read from the transcript
  store once per saved version (cached by the store's stamp; at most the newest 400), loaded ones
  as they are now; the asking chat left out. Searched: titles, the user's messages and other
  chats' messages, the agent's answers; not tool output (cheap enough to leave out, and noisy).
- Ranking (`core/agent/chatSearch.ts`, tested, DOM-free): query words (common words dropped),
  each found word scores 1 + log(count), times the share of words found squared, doubled for the
  whole phrase; a chat ranks by its title (×3), its best message and a quarter of the next two;
  newer first on a tie. Each hit: chat id, title, date, up to three snippets with the message
  number (#n, 1 = the first message).
- Opening: `agent.openChatMessage { session, message }` (a number or an item id → agent.showMessage),
  discoverable so the agent can show the user a hit; `agent.searchChats` (palette: "Search
  chats…": a box, then the hits; picking one opens it at the message).
- The same scoring ranks the user guide for read_guide (D333).

### D332 — A self-paced loop (/loop, schedule_wakeup)
- Claude Code's /loop + ScheduleWakeup. `/loop <prompt>` (self-paced) or `/loop 5m <prompt>` /
  `/loop <prompt> every 2 hours` (fixed, 1 minute to 1 day). The /loop message is the first check;
  it carries the loop's rules. Built-in slash commands with their own module register in
  `builtinSlash` (slashCommands.ts), so /loop's code stays in chatLoops.ts.
- Timing reuses the schedules (D253): each next check is a one-off scheduled message to the chat,
  whose text opens with "Loop check N (/loop, …)" and asks for schedule_wakeup. One-offs rather
  than a repeating schedule, so a fixed loop can be shorter than the schedules' 5-minute repeat
  minimum (the 1-minute one-off minimum holds) and a self-paced one needs no special case. A fixed
  loop sets its next check as soon as one is sent; a self-paced one when the agent calls
  `schedule_wakeup { delay_seconds (clamped to 60–3600), prompt, reason, noop?, stop? }`. A
  self-paced turn that ends without it ends the loop (as in Claude Code). A check cancelled from
  the schedules list, or a deleted chat, ends it too. Every loop ends after 7 days.
- schedule_wakeup is offered only in a chat with a loop (extraTools by session), read-only (works
  in Plan and Ask), a turn tool (no subagent gets it). In a fixed loop its delay is ignored; noop
  and stop still count.
- The chat: a strip above the box (the background commands' shape: pace, next check or "the
  agent is choosing", checks and quiet ones, the reason and prompt on hover, Stop =
  `agent.stopLoop`); each check a quiet line ("Loop check 3: …"); runs of quiet checks (a done
  schedule_wakeup with noop, no stop, no file changed) fold into one line "N quiet checks"
  (`collapseQuietTicks`, applied before the layout; the transcript is unchanged).
- Saved with the folder (`agent.loops`); restored, a fixed loop whose check is gone sets the next,
  a self-paced one ends. Commands `agent.startLoop`, `agent.stopLoop`; state `ide://agent/loops`
  (with the pending check's `scheduleId`, which `agent.runScheduleNow` sends now). Core:
  `core/agent/chatLoop.ts`, tested.

### D333 — The guide subagent
- Like Claude Code's claude-code-guide agent: a built-in read-only subagent `guide` (Plan, Review,
  General's list) that answers how-to questions about the IDE from its user guide and cites the
  page, so the main conversation stays small. Tools: read_guide, find_commands (to check a
  command's id), get_state. context.ts: questions about the IDE itself go to it; read_guide for a
  quick look (the prompt used to point at call_command help.readDocs).
- The guide is reachable in an installed build: docs/guide/*.md are already bundled as text by the
  help extension (`?raw` imports in extensions/help/pages.ts, its `help.readDocs` command), so no
  build change was needed. read_guide reads the pages through that command (once per window) and
  ranks their sections (`core/agent/guideSearch.ts`: split at headings, outside code fences,
  scored with the chat search's scoring, heading matches weighted; tested); `page` returns one
  whole (30 000 characters at most).
- read_guide is a chat tool (subagents only get tools the chat has), kept out of READ_TOOLS (that
  list is what "Read only" means in agent files: changing it would change existing files' access
  level); `GUIDE_TOOLS` lets read-only and background subagents keep it.

### D334 — Inline widgets (Claude Code's show_widget and read_me)
- `show_widget` { title (snake_case id, also the saved file's name), widget_code, loading_messages
  (1–4 short lines) }: an SVG picture (the code starts with `<svg`, after blank space, an XML
  declaration or comments) or a small HTML page (anything else) drawn as a card in the chat. A
  whole page sent anyway (DOCTYPE, `<html>`, `<head>`, `<body>`) keeps its head's styles and
  scripts and its body; a Markdown fence around the code is dropped; 200 000 characters at most.
  The model gets "Shown to the user as an SVG / HTML widget (title)".
- `widget_guide` (no parameters): the design rules, like Claude Code's read_me: where it draws
  (the chat column, 320px and up, height follows the content to 900px), the theme's CSS
  variables by group (surfaces, controls, text, accent, borders, status, series `--label-1…6`,
  type, shape), typography (inherit, sentence case), the quiet style (DESIGN.md), what code can
  do (no network, no storage, sendPrompt on a click). A tool of its own, not in the description:
  it's long, and every request carries the descriptions while few turns draw a widget. Both go
  with the display tools (`agent.richBlocks`, not for a small model).
- The frame: `src-tauri/notebook/output/widget.html` + `widget.js` on the notebook outputs' local
  origin (`notebook_output_origin`, the same static server; two more files in its list), not a
  srcdoc frame: a srcdoc or blob frame inherits the IDE page's policy (`script-src 'self'`), which
  blocks inline scripts. Sandboxed with `allow-scripts` only (no same-origin: it can't reach the
  IDE; no popups, forms or top navigation). The page's own policy allows no network at all
  (`default-src 'none'`; scripts inline or the origin's own, pictures and fonts `data:`/`blob:`,
  `connect-src 'none'`, no frames or workers), and `harden.js`'s `harden()` takes away WebRTC and
  nested frames, as for an extension's renderer (D204).
- Theme: the IDE's tokens (the pages' THEME_TOKENS plus the guide's: `--bg-input`, `--bg-chip`,
  `--space-*`…) are set on the page's root when it draws and again when the theme changes, with an
  `is-dark` / `is-light` class. No `color-scheme` on the page: the frame's and the page's must
  match or the frame paints an opaque backdrop instead of the chat's color. Buttons, inputs
  (`--bg-input`), tables and links have a native look by default.
- Size: the page posts its content's height (ResizeObserver); the frame takes it, between 24 and
  900px; taller content scrolls inside. A tab fills its slot.
- A chat re-renders its items often, and an iframe that's moved or rebuilt reloads: the card is
  made once per chat view (cached by the view's item host and the call) and returned as the same
  element, so `morph` leaves it alone; a frame that does reload (a moved tab, another window)
  is drawn again from its code. Frames listen through one message listener per window.
- `sendPrompt(text)` sends the text as the user's message (`agent.sendFromWidget`): shown with a
  "From <widget>" chip and told to the model as sent from the widget; it joins a running turn, or
  answers a waiting ask_user card, like a typed message. Checked three times, since the code is
  the model's: in the frame, only during the user's activation (getters captured before the
  widget's code runs; a widget can still post raw messages, so this only stops honest mistakes
  like a call on load); in the IDE, only while the frame has focus (the user clicked in it) and
  one per 1.5 s, six a minute; and the command keeps the same limit per widget. The IDE can't see
  clicks inside the frame, so a widget the user clicked keeps that focus until they click
  elsewhere: the limit is what bounds it, and every message shows where it came from. Links go to
  `agent.openLink` under the same focus check (https only).
- The card: the title (the id as a sentence) and quiet actions: **Open in a tab** (`agent.openWidget`,
  dock view `agent.widget`, one tab per widget; sendPrompt still goes to its chat; restored after a
  restart up to 50 000 characters), **Copy code** (`agent.copyWidgetCode`), **Save as file…**
  (`agent.saveWidget`: an SVG as .svg with its namespace, an HTML widget as a whole .html page with
  the theme's colors as they are and a sendPrompt that logs). The loading lines turn while it draws;
  a script error shows under it. Saved with the chat (the call's arguments).
- State: `ide://agent/widgets` (the active chat's widgets: title, mode, drawn, height, script
  errors, messages sent; the widget tabs). `dev.clickInWidget` (dev builds) clicks inside a frame
  for UI tests, which `dev.click` can't reach (another origin).
- Not done: a widget that navigates its own frame to another local address can't be stopped
  (the IDE page's `frame-src` allows local origins for the browser and notebook frames); it gets
  nothing from the IDE by doing so. Streaming the code into the frame while the model writes it
  (Claude Code draws as it streams): the IDE draws once the call is complete.

### D335 — ask_user's card as Claude Code's AskUserQuestion: rows, Skip, Ctrl+Enter
- The card is a raised card: the question in a header area, the options as quiet rows with a
  radio (a checkbox for several picks) and the description under the label, the number key at
  the end, the picked row highlighted (`--bg-selected`), and a last "Other" row with its radio
  and the field to type in (on `--bg-input`). A footer: a hint with **Ctrl+Enter**, **Skip** and
  **Submit**. Header chips as tabs, previews and keys 1–9 / ↑↓ / ←→ stay (D312); ↓ from the last
  option goes to the Other field.
- One question: a single pick still answers on click; Submit sends several picks or the typed
  answer; Skip answers at once with "The user skipped this question" (`SKIPPED`), and the model
  reads "The user skipped this question. Go on with your own judgment, and say what you chose."
- Several questions: Skip skips the question on screen (its tab shows a dash) and moves on; a
  pick or typing un-skips it; Submit (enabled once each is answered or skipped) sends them, the
  skipped ones as "(skipped)" in the result ("…for a skipped one, use your own judgment"); all
  skipped reads "The user skipped these questions". The answered card shows "Skipped" on them.
- Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter) submits from anywhere in the card, the Other field too, when Submit
  would. `agent.answer { skip: true }` skips a whole card (agents and tests).
- The classes the D171 / D292 / D312 UI tests use stay (`rb-choice`, `rb-choices-hint`,
  `rb-choices-send` on a one-question Submit, `rb-ask-submit`, `rb-ask-other`, `is-selected`,
  `is-chosen`).

### D336 — run_command in the operating system's sandbox

- **Opt-in (the lead's change at merge):** `agent.sandbox` defaults to `off`. On Windows the first
  sandboxed command marks the whole folder low integrity, inheritable, and the mark stays (seconds
  per 20 000 files; undone only by hand with icacls), so it's the owner's choice, not a default.
- **What:** with `agent.sandbox` `auto`, the agent's commands (`run_command`, in the
  foreground and the background, and `monitor`) run inside the operating system's sandbox where
  there is one, after the usual permission check. `run_command { sandbox: false }` runs one outside
  it and **always asks** (even with full access, never "always allow"); the card says "Outside the
  sandbox, with your full rights". A sandboxed run's result ends with `[sandboxed: …]` and its row
  summary with "· sandboxed"; when it fails in a way the sandbox may have caused (access denied,
  EPERM/EACCES, read-only file system, no network…), the result tells the model it may retry with
  `sandbox: false` only for that, and that the user is asked. A sandbox that can't start returns
  an error (the command never ran) with the same hint. `off` runs everything as before.
  `ide://agent/sandbox` says what the system's sandbox does (`exec_sandbox_info`).
- **Windows (verified, `cargo test` runs a real one):** no AppContainer and no restricted token —
  both make most developer tools fail (AppContainer can't even read the user profile, where node,
  npm, git configs and caches live). Instead **mandatory integrity control**: the shell runs at
  **low integrity**. Windows then refuses it write access to every object labelled medium, which is
  every file, folder and registry key of the user's that isn't explicitly marked lower; what it
  starts inherits the low token. To let it write its folder, the folder (and, for a linked
  worktree or a subfolder of a repository, the repository's git folder, so commits work) gets an
  inheritable low label (`S:(ML;OICI;NW;;;LW)`, `SetNamedSecurityInfoW`, which carries it down to
  what's inside: ~4 s per 20 000 files, once per folder; the folder's DACL isn't touched). TEMP
  and TMP point to `<LocalLow>\<data folder name>\sandbox-temp`.
  - How it starts: `job::spawn_then` creates cmd suspended (in the IDE's job), lowers its token
    (`SetTokenInformation(TokenIntegrityLevel)`) and resumes it; cmd then starts PowerShell, which
    is low from its creation. PowerShell lowered after its own start fails fast (0x80131623: it
    opens its own process, whose object stays medium). The script travels in an environment
    variable (`AGENT_SANDBOX_SCRIPT`) that a short `-Command` stub runs in the global scope, so cmd
    never sees `&`, `|` or quotes (`-EncodedCommand` was tried: 5.1 then prints errors as CLIXML).
  - **Protected:** writes (create, change, delete, rename) anywhere outside the folder, its git
    folder and the sandbox's temp folder: the rest of the user's files, other projects, the IDE's
    own settings and data, `%APPDATA%`/`%LOCALAPPDATA%` (so `npm install -g`, the npm cache, pip
    and cargo installs fail: retry outside), HKCU registry keys; and it can't send input to or open
    medium processes for writing (UIPI, process DACLs).
  - **Not protected:** reading (it can read every file the user can, secrets included), the
    network (no limit at all), writes to anything already labelled low (`%USERPROFILE%\AppData\
    LocalLow`, `HKCU\Software\AppDataLow`), and volumes without ACLs (FAT/exFAT USB drives, some
    network shares). The marked folder stays writable for every low-integrity program on the
    machine afterwards (rare: sandboxed browser processes use stricter tokens). A file moved into
    the folder from outside keeps its own (medium) label, so a sandboxed command can't change it.
    To unmark a folder: `icacls <folder> /setintegritylevel (OI)(CI)medium`.
- **macOS (written, not run here):** `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec -p <profile> $SHELL -lc <command>`,
  profile: allow by default, deny `file-write*` except the folder, its git folder, `/dev`, `/private/
  tmp`, `/private/var/folders` and `$TMPDIR`; deny `network-outbound` except to `localhost`. Reads
  aren't limited. (sandbox-exec is deprecated by Apple but present on current macOS.)
- **Linux (written, not run here):** bubblewrap when installed: `bwrap --ro-bind / / --dev-bind
  /dev /dev --bind /tmp /tmp --bind <folder> <folder> [--bind <git folder>] --unshare-net
  --die-with-parent -- $SHELL -lc <command>`. Without bwrap: **no sandbox**, and the card and
  `ide://agent/sandbox` say so (Landlock would need no install but couldn't be tested here).
- Remote and WSL folders run as before (the command runs on the other side); hooks, `!` lines,
  the worktree setup script and terminals are not sandboxed.
- **Why default `auto`:** Claude Code's model (the brief): commands that only touch the project run
  as before, and anything reaching outside it is a visible, asked decision. The cost: the first
  sandboxed command in a folder marks it (Windows), and installs into the user profile need an
  approval each time. The skills UI test (agent-skills-m7-7) writes into the user skills folder
  and turns the sandbox off for that step.

### D337 — the chat itself in a git worktree (enter_worktree / exit_worktree)

- **What:** `enter_worktree { name?, path? }` moves the chat into a git worktree, only when the user
  asks for one (its description says so): a new branch `agent/<name>` (default `agent/chat-<id>`)
  and folder made the worktree agents' way (D193/D204: next to the repository as
  `<repo>.agent-<name>`, the setup step — copy `agent.worktree.copyFiles`, run
  `agent.worktree.setupScript` in a trusted folder — and the worktree's PORT), or an existing
  linked worktree of this repository by `path`. From then on the chat's file tools, searches and
  commands work there (`toolRoots.ts`, exactly as a headless helper's, D246); the open folder isn't
  touched, IDE commands acting on the window's folder are refused, and each message carries a line
  saying where the chat works. `exit_worktree { action: keep | remove }` leaves: keep leaves the
  branch and folder; remove (only a worktree enter_worktree made) deletes both, stops the chat's
  background commands first, and **asks first** (even with full access) when there are uncommitted
  changes or commits beyond where it started (or git can't tell).
- Where the worktree lives: not `.claude/worktrees/` (Claude Code's): the IDE's own worktree
  agents and helpers put theirs next to the repository, and review, merge and delete already work
  on those; one place for all of them.
- Review and merge: the worktree gets a record in the worktree agents' list (`headless`, by the
  chat's id; a second worktree after a kept one gets an id of its own), so **Review** (the compare
  page, `agent.compareWorktrees`), **Merge** (`agent.applyWorktree`, which asks) and Delete
  (`agent.worktrees`) work as for helpers. The chat header shows the branch as a chip; clicking it
  runs `agent.chatWorktree` (review, merge, leave, leave and remove). State
  `ide://agent/chatWorktrees`.
- The chat remembers its worktree (`meta.worktree` in its saved file) and goes on there after a
  reload; the helpers' tool gate lets the folder into Rust's scope again before its next tool call
  (and says when it's gone). A record deleted elsewhere brings the chat back to the folder.
- Nothing is linked into the worktree (no node_modules junction: removing a worktree once deleted
  the main checkout's node_modules through one); the setup step copies files only.

### D338 — Workflow scripts (run_workflow), after Claude Code's Workflow tool

- **What:** a `run_workflow { script | path, args?, resume_from? }` tool. The script is plain
  JavaScript that begins with `export const meta = { name, description, phases? }` and uses
  `agent(prompt, { label, phase, schema, model, tools, agentType })`, `parallel(thunks, { limit })`,
  `pipeline(items, ...stages)`, `phase()`, `log()` and `args`, with Claude Code's semantics
  (parallel is a barrier and a throwing thunk is null; pipeline has no barrier, stages get
  (previous, item, index), a throwing stage drops the item; agent() is null when it fails). It
  runs in the background: the tool returns a run id at once, the chat shows a progress card, and
  the result comes back as an automatic message (D253's path, `auto: "workflow"`).
- **meta is parsed, never run** (`core/agent/workflow.ts` `readLiteral`): objects, arrays,
  strings, numbers, true/false/null, comments, trailing commas; a variable, call, spread,
  computed key, shorthand property or `${}` is refused with its line. The user is asked with the
  description and phases before any of the script runs; the script itself is shown as the card's
  code. "Always" covers the chat until the window closes. Full access (`agent.runCommands: full`)
  doesn't ask, as for every other tool (the user said they're away).
- **Isolation:** the script runs in a Web Worker of its own (`src/workers/workflow.worker.ts`),
  locked down exactly as an extension's worker (the lockdown moved to `src/workers/lockdown.ts`,
  now shared, not copied): no DOM, IPC, network, storage, nested workers, `import()` or code
  generation after the script's function exists. `Date.now()`, `Math.random()` and `new Date()`
  throw, as in Claude Code: a resumed run must make the same calls. Values cross as JSON. The
  window ends the worker when the run ends, fails, is stopped or times out.
- **Agents are the chat's background subagents** (`startBackground` through the turn's
  `background`, as delegate's background runs): the subagent (`general`, or `agentType`), its
  rules, its model (`opts.model`, else the phase's `model`, else the subagent's own), the
  read-only tools (`subagentTools(…, background)`, narrowed by `opts.tools`). Two small hooks on
  `SubagentSpec` make that reusable: `onReport` (the report comes back to the runner instead of
  the chat, and no notice is shown) and `onUsage` (each request's tokens and cost, from
  `subChat`). Nothing about running a subagent is duplicated.
- **Read-only agents:** Claude Code's workflow agents can edit (with worktree isolation for
  parallel edits). Here every background subagent is read-only (D195): edits from several agents
  at once, with permission cards for each, while the chat goes on would be a mess. Workflows are
  for research, review and verification fan-outs; the agent makes the changes afterwards. A
  worktree option can come later through the isolated helpers (D231). `opts.effort` is accepted
  and ignored for now (a background subagent has no per-run effort).
- **Schemas:** `agent()` with a JSON Schema appends an instruction to answer with only JSON for
  it, parses the answer (whole, fenced or the outer braces) and checks it (`schemaIssues`: type,
  properties, required, additionalProperties: false, items, enum, const, anyOf/oneOf, bounds);
  an invalid answer is asked once more with what was wrong, then null. The IDE's `core/schema`
  builds schemas from code and doesn't validate arbitrary JSON Schema, so a small checker was
  written (its `JsonSchema` shape is the same subset). As in Claude Code, the root must be an
  object schema, and `required` must name properties (else agent() throws).
- **Limits:** `agent.workflows.maxAgents` (10, the brief's and Claude Code's guideline; a call past
  it throws in the script), `agent.workflows.concurrency` (4 at once: Claude Code allows ~10, but
  most of the IDE's users run local or rate-limited models), `agent.workflows.timeoutMinutes`
  (30; past it the run and its agents stop and the agent is told). Usage: each agent's tokens and
  cost, shown on the card, in `ide://agent/workflows` and in the end message; the requests are
  logged as subagent usage as before.
- **Resume:** results are cached per run by the call's prompt and the options that change its
  answer (schema, model, tools, agentType, effort; not label or phase), each result used once in
  order, so an edited script re-runs only the calls that changed — finer than Claude Code's
  "longest unchanged prefix". Runs live in the window's memory (the last 20); scripts can also be
  run from a workspace file (`path`, read through the review queue so a proposed file works).
  Claude Code persists every script to a file; here the agent's file tools are confined to the
  workspace, so a persisted copy outside it couldn't be edited, and writing into the project
  unasked would leave files behind. resume_from without a script re-runs the earlier one.
- **Stopping:** the card's Stop and `agent.stopWorkflow` stop the script and its agents; the run is
  one of the chat's background jobs, so the chat's Stop and deleting the chat stop it too (as
  background subagents, D195). A run the user stopped sends no message (no turn starts after
  Stop); a run that finished, failed or ran out of time does.
- **Opt-in (AGENTS.md rule 8):** this is inside the agent's chat, so `agent.workflows.enabled`
  defaults to on, like delegate. The tool's description says to call it only when the user asked
  for a workflow or to fan out agents, every run asks first, and it's off with
  `agent.delegate` off too. Subagents never get it (`subagentTools`).
- **UI:** a card under the latest message (after the plan, D300): the run's name, status, agents
  finished, tokens and Stop; its agents grouped by phase (meta's phases, then ones phase()
  started), each with a spinner, a waiting ring, a check or an x. It stays after the run ends
  until the user's next message; the end message is a quiet line in the conversation.
- **State and commands:** `ide://agent/workflows` (each run's id, chat, name, status, phases,
  agents with status, tokens and cost, usage, log, result); `agent.listWorkflows`,
  `agent.stopWorkflow { id?, session? }`.

### D339 — Files into a page: browser_act upload (Claude in Chrome's file_upload and upload_image)

- `browser_act upload` with `files` (workspace paths) and/or `screenshot` (an id the `screenshot`
  tool now gives with each page shot, "(id shot3)"; a chat's last 8 are kept), onto a target by
  `ref` / `selector` / `name` or `coordinate`. An action of browser_act, not a new tool: two
  parameters cost less context than a tool, and it is a page action like the others (it asks the
  same way, batches, records).
- Paths go through the agent's sandbox (`sandboxPath` over the workspace folders) and its ignore
  rules (.aiignore and the like): a path outside the workspace or an excluded file is refused
  before anything is read. The command `browser.upload` checks again (`workspace.contains`), and
  Rust's fs access is scoped to the workspace anyway.
- Two steps through the bridge: `input.fileTarget` says what the target is (a file input itself or
  the one a label is for → "input", with `multiple`, `accept`, `disabled`; anything else →
  "drop"); `planTransfer` (core, tested) decides: a single-file input refuses two files, a disabled
  one refuses, a file the input's `accept` doesn't list still goes with a note (browsers don't
  enforce `accept` for scripts either, and the page may check), at most 20 files and 10 MB (the
  bytes travel to the page as base64: postMessage to the frame, an eval to a site's window).
- `input.files` builds `File` objects (name, MIME type from the extension, bytes), puts them in a
  `DataTransfer`, and either assigns `input.files` and fires `input` and `change` (bubbling), or
  dispatches dragenter, dragover and — only if the page cancelled dragover, as a real drop from the
  desktop requires — drop, at the element's center or the point. A drop zone that didn't accept
  says so (the result is an error for the agent, with what to try).
- Not done: Claude in Chrome's `upload_image` also takes images the user attached to the chat;
  here a screenshot or a workspace file (an attachment can be added to the project first).

### D340 — Recordings: browser_act start_recording / stop_recording as an animated GIF

- Claude in Chrome's gif_creator as two actions of browser_act (cheaper than a tool): while a chat
  records, a frame is taken after each of its browser actions (a ring where it pointed — the
  coordinate, or the element's center from `browser.locate` before the action — a dashed line for
  a drag, and its `action_summary` as a caption band) and every second, from the screenshots the
  IDE already takes (`browser.screenshot inline`). Frames are taken only while the page is on
  screen (`ifShown`): a recording never brings a tab forward or takes the user's view away.
- GIF, not animated WebP or APNG: every viewer, chat app and issue tracker plays GIF, the IDE's
  webview shows it in an `<img>`, and an encoder of either other format would be as big. The
  encoder is ours (`core/image/gif.ts`, ~350 lines, tested byte for byte on a 2×2 image and with an
  LZW decoder round trip): a median-cut palette per frame (exact when a frame has ≤ 256 colors),
  LZW with variable code sizes and clear codes, each frame cropped to the rectangle that changed
  since the previous one (disposal "keep"), identical frames skipped (the previous one stays
  longer), delays in hundredths (at least 2), looping. Frames are encoded as they come, so only
  the last frame's pixels stay in memory; the GIF is at most 960 px on its long side.
- Stop makes the GIF and the call is drawn in the chat as a card (`view/recordingCard.ts`): the
  animation, "12 frames · 8.4 s · 960×600 · 1.2 MB", Save to project… and Download…
  (`agent.saveRecording`, `to: project | file`; never overwrites). Nothing is written until the
  user saves. Recordings stay in memory (object URLs) until the IDE closes, the last 10; a chat
  reopened later says the recording is no longer kept. `ide://agent/recordings` lists them and the
  chats recording now.
- Limits: a recording ends by itself after 5 minutes, 300 frames or 30 MB (the next stop_recording
  reports it); the interval frame is skipped while another is being taken.
- The GIF isn't sent to the model (it would cost image tokens for frames it already saw); the
  result says frames, length and size.

### D341 — The user's own browser: an "external" target over the DevTools protocol

- Feasible without a dependency: the IDE already speaks the Chrome DevTools Protocol for page
  debugging (D196: Rust's local-only WebSocket client `debug_socket_*`, `/json/list`, finding
  Chrome or Edge). A browser extension (Claude in Chrome's way) would need packaging and a store
  listing for two browsers: out of scope.
- `browser.launchExternal {browser: chrome | edge, port = 9222, url?}` starts the installed browser
  as a task terminal's process with `--remote-debugging-port`, a profile of its own in the
  workspace's IDE folder (`external-browser-profile`, git-ignored: the everyday profile can't take
  a debugging port while it runs, and its cookies shouldn't be open to the port) and no first-run
  pages, waits for the port, connects. `browser.connectExternal {port, url?}` attaches to a browser
  the user started with the flag. `browser.disconnectExternal` lets go (the browser stays).
- On connect the IDE installs the same bridge as the tabs' (new Rust command
  `browser_bridge_source`) with `Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument` and now, in "external" mode
  posting through a `Runtime.addBinding` binding with an unguessable name; calls go in with
  `Runtime.evaluate`. So a plain `Page` drives it, and the page commands (snapshot, find, text,
  click, hover, type, press, select, scroll, wait, eval, console, input, upload, locate, navigate,
  back, forward, reload, screenshot via `Page.captureScreenshot`) take `tab: "external"`; after
  `browser.selectTab external` (the agent's `browser_act select_tab`) they act on it by default
  until another browser tab comes forward. `browser.list` / `ide://browser` list it; the agent's
  browser tools are offered while it's connected.
- In the user's browser the bridge leaves the page's links, popups, shortcut keys (F12, Ctrl+R…)
  and scrollbars alone; it only reports and answers calls.
- Permissions are the tabs' (page actions ask; browser_eval on a site that isn't local asks first
  and only runs in a tab the chat worked on). Input stays synthesized through the bridge, as in the
  tabs, rather than `Input.dispatchMouseEvent` (trusted events would be a later step).
- Not done: DevTools panels and the data commands (dom, styles, storage, network, requests) for
  the external page; one page at a time (the one connected to, or picked by `url`); new tabs the
  user opens there aren't followed.

### D342 — suggest_skill: skills the user can add, as a card

- `suggest_skill { keywords, reason }`, the IDE's take on Claude Code's SearchSkills /
  SuggestSkills / ListSkills: the agent searches the skills the user could add and shows up to
  three as a card (name, where it comes from, what it does, **Add** or **Turn on**). The agent
  never adds one; the click runs `agent.addSuggestedSkill` and marks the card.
- **Where skills come from.** The IDE had no skills source beyond the folders it reads and one
  built-in skill (D255), which is always on. Added: a **skill catalog**, seven in-house skills
  bundled as `src/extensions/agent/catalogSkills/*.md` (review-checklist, release-notes,
  write-tests, pr-description, debug-systematically, docs-style, dependency-update) that are not
  active until added. Adding one writes its SKILL.md into the user's own skills folder
  (`~/<data folder>/skills/<name>`), so it behaves and can be edited like any skill, and a later
  release changing the catalog doesn't change a skill the user already has. The second source is
  skills found on disk but turned off (`agent.skills.disabled`): **Turn on** turns one on again.
- No network: no skills marketplace exists in the IDE. Claude Code's plugin marketplaces cloned
  under `~/.claude/plugins` were considered as a third source and left out: Rust lets the webview
  read only the skills folders (`ipc/skills.rs`), and widening that scope for a suggestion card
  isn't worth it now.
- Ranking (`core/agent/skillSuggest.ts`, tested): keywords are stemmed words; a keyword in the
  skill's name scores 4, in its tags 3 (catalog skills carry tags), in its description 2, a
  description word starting with it 1; at least 2 to be shown; a tie goes to the catalog.
- Rules, in the description and enforced: when the task is one a skill could make repeatable and
  nothing enabled covers it; not for one-off questions; once per conversation unless the user
  took it up (added one, or wrote about skills since) — D314's rule, now `oncePerConversation`
  in `core/agent/extensionSuggest.ts`, shared by the three suggestion tools.
- Commands: `agent.skillCatalog { keywords? }` (the list, plus `userDir`), `agent.addSkillFromCatalog
  { name? }` (palette: **Add an agent skill from the catalog…**, a pick without a name),
  `agent.addSuggestedSkill { item?, name }` (the card's button; `item` defaults to the latest card).
- Off with the display tools (`agent.richBlocks: false`) and for small models, like the other
  cards; not given to subagents.

### D343 — suggest_mcp_server and mcp_status: finding, adding and checking MCP servers

- `suggest_mcp_server { query, reason }`, the IDE's take on Claude Code's mcp-registry
  (search_mcp_registry, suggest_connectors): the built-in gallery (D204) and the official MCP
  registry (D207's `agent.searchMcpRegistry` path, `agent.mcp.registryUrl`) are searched and up to
  three servers shown as a card: name (opens its page), how it runs (npx, uvx, Docker, Remote),
  where it's from ("Popular servers", or "MCP registry (not reviewed)"), what it runs, what it
  needs, a field per input (a password box for keys, a list for choices) and **Add**.
- **The catalog decision.** Both: the gallery answers offline and wins ties (it's vetted); the
  registry finds the long tail. The registry is the D207 search the user can already run from
  New MCP server; here the agent's call triggers it during a turn the user started. AGENTS.md
  rule 4 forbids loading code or assets at runtime, not a catalog search: nothing found is run or
  loaded until the user clicks Add (Open VSX's search for suggest_extension, D314, is the
  precedent). With `agent.mcp.registryUrl` empty, or offline, only the gallery is searched and
  the result says so.
- The registry's search matches names only, so the tool asks it for the whole query and then its
  longest words (at most three requests, `registryQueries`) and ranks everything itself
  (`rankServers`, tested on a saved registry answer, `core/mcp/registrySample.ts`): a word in the
  id, title or registry name scores 3, in the description or category 2, a prefix 1; ties go to
  the gallery, then to a server needing nothing typed in, then to a remote one. The same server
  twice (by what it runs, versions aside) is kept once.
- **Add** runs `agent.addSuggestedMcpServer`, which runs `agent.installMcpServer` as the user's
  click: a registry server shows what it runs before it's written, and the user picks this folder
  or every folder. The values typed in the card are then stored as the server's inputs
  (`McpClients.presetInputs`: a key as its secret, keyed by the server's identity as the hidden
  box would; other values for the window). An empty field is asked in the hidden box when the
  server starts. The fields reach the command through `stashCardValues`, not its input, because
  the dispatcher logs command inputs (the audit log): a key typed in the card never lands there.
  `values` in the input exists for scripts only.
- `mcp_status { name? }`: the servers from `ide://agent/mcp` (state, tools, where configured,
  error, sign-in needed), one line each for the model and a card for the user with **Reconnect**
  on failed, waiting or running servers (`agent.reconnectMcpServer`: restarts it like
  `agent.mcpServers { restart }`, then redraws the row with the state it reached). Claude Code's
  connector "enable" maps to Add (and the MCP servers page's on/off), "reconnect" to Reconnect.
- Same once-per-conversation rule as D314 for suggest_mcp_server; mcp_status may be called any
  time. None of the three are given to subagents.

### D344 — "Don't show again" on notices that come back every start

- The owner saw "Pyright is off while the ms-python.python extension provides its languages…" on
  every start. VS Code gives notices like that a "Don't Show Again" action it remembers
  (neverShowAgain storage), and most informational ones show once.
- `showDismissible(services, key, kind, message)` (workbench/notices.ts) adds the button and keeps
  the choice in the global state (`hiddenNotices`, every window, at most 200 keys). The LSP yield
  notice uses it (keyed by server and extension). Every hidden notice comes back with
  `notifications.resetHidden` ("Show hidden notices again"); `ide://notifications` lists them.

### D345 — The chat's cards reviewed: quieter cards, one toast per notice, no mode chip

From the owner's look through every card (tests/scripts/agent-card-gallery.jsonc):

- **No mode chip on a message:** a message sent in Plan or Ask mode no longer shows a "Plan" /
  "Ask" chip above it (the composer shows the mode). The message keeps its `mode` in data.
- **The same notice once, with a count:** a notice whose kind, title and text match one showing
  now (or the newest in the bell's list) bumps a "×N" on it and restarts its timer, instead of a
  new toast or list entry; that call's own buttons aren't added (an extension's promise resolves
  undefined, as for a repeat within a second). `dev.notify` shows one for tests.
- **An MCP server that exits** says why with the line that names the error (core/mcp/exitReason.ts),
  not the last three lines, which for a Node crash were "}", a blank line and "Node.js v24…".
- **The folder card and the "Started in …" strip** look like the wrap-up box: the chat's own
  background (not the raised surface or the info blue), a quiet border, the larger radius; the
  folder card's Open folder… / Just chat are secondary buttons and Create and start primary;
  the strip's Open is primary, Continue here secondary.
- **The card gallery** (`agent-card-gallery`, `"manual": true`) puts every card in one chat
  and keeps the window open for an hour. The UI test runner skips manual scripts in batches and
  filters; only naming one in full runs it.

### D346 — Trusted input: a person's events through the DevTools protocol

- **Why:** the bridge synthesizes events (`dispatchEvent`), so `event.isTrusted` is false and pages
  that check it (anti-bot guards, some editors, payment and sign-in widgets, `requestFullscreen`,
  clipboard and popup gestures) ignore the agent's clicks and keys. Claude Code's browser tools
  send real input; the IDE now does where it can.
- **What goes trusted:** `browser.input` (click with button and count, hover, drag, wheel, keys
  with modifiers and repeat, typing at the focus) and the element actions `browser.click`,
  `browser.hover`, `browser.press`, `browser.type` — so every pointer and keyboard action of
  `browser_act` (and `browser_batch`). `select` (a native popup) and `scroll` by ref / `to`
  (scrolling isn't a gesture pages check) stay with the bridge.
- **How:** the bridge's new `input.prepare` says where the events land (CSS pixels of the
  viewport, after scrolling a ref into view, the same `targetOf` the bridge uses, so points from a
  screenshot's coordinate frame mean the same thing), focuses the element for keys, selects a
  field's text for `browser.type` (so typing replaces it; `clear: false` types at its end);
  `core/browser/trustedInput.ts` (tested) turns the action into `Input.dispatchMouseEvent`
  (moved / pressed / released with `clickCount`, `mouseWheel`, a drag in 8 steps a frame apart),
  `Input.dispatchKeyEvent` (US-layout key definitions with `code` and Windows virtual key codes;
  chords press their modifiers down and up around the key; Ctrl/Alt/Meta never type text) and
  `Input.insertText` (characters no US key types; `browser.type` into an element in one insertion;
  text over 300 characters in one insertion); `input.report` gives the result (focus, a field's
  value, scroll, address), with the same fields as the bridge's results plus
  `input: "trusted" | "synthesized"` and, when synthesized, `inputNote` with why.
- **The user's own browser** (D341): over its socket, points as they are. HTML drag and drop
  (a `draggable` source, an image, a link) uses Chrome's drag interception
  (`Input.setInterceptDrags`, press and moves, `Input.dragIntercepted` hands the drag data,
  `Input.dispatchDragEvent` dragEnter / dragOver / drop at the target): the browser's own drag
  starts an OS drag loop that protocol mouse events can't finish.
- **The built-in tab (Windows):** no debugging port is opened (the IDE's own page would be
  reachable on it). WebView2's in-process `ICoreWebView2::CallDevToolsProtocolMethod` is reachable
  cleanly: Tauri's `with_webview` gives the controller, and `webview2-com` (already a direct
  dependency, in Cargo.lock through wry) has `CallDevToolsProtocolMethodCompletedHandler`. Rust
  `browser/trusted_input.rs` (`browser_trusted_input`) passes on only `Input.dispatchMouseEvent`,
  `Input.dispatchKeyEvent` and `Input.insertText`, to `main`, an auxiliary window or a site's
  webview (`browser-*`); the main-window-only capability is unchanged (site webviews can't call
  it). It works with DevTools disabled (`AreDevToolsEnabled` governs the UI, not the protocol).
  - A local page shows in an iframe of the IDE's own webview, so its events go to the IDE's
    webview at the frame's place (`hostPoint`: the frame's box, scaled in device mode). Before
    any pointer event the IDE checks `elementFromPoint` there is the frame itself; if a menu, a
    dialog or a toast of the IDE covers it, the bridge does it instead (never a click on the IDE).
  - Keys go to the focused frame, so the IDE focuses the page's frame first (if it can't, the
    bridge). After the action, focus goes back to the IDE text field the user was in (chat box,
    editor), so the user's typing doesn't land in the page; the page then sees its window blur,
    as when a person clicks back into the IDE. Trade-off accepted over leaving the user's keys
    going to the page.
  - A site in its own window or shown inside the tab (`browser.embedSites`): its own webview,
    points as they are.
  - HTML drag and drop stays synthesized there: `CallDevToolsProtocolMethod` has no events
    without a protocol event receiver per event, and drag interception needs one; pointer drags
    (sliders, canvases) are trusted.
- **macOS / Linux:** WebKit has no in-process protocol entry; the built-in tab's input is
  synthesized as before, the result's `inputNote` says so, and `browser_act`'s row reads
  "click (synthesized)". The user's own browser is trusted on every system.
- **Fallbacks:** anything the protocol can't do before the first event is sent (not Windows,
  covered, no focus, an unknown key name, a refused call) goes to the bridge with the reason;
  a failure after some events were sent is an error ("Input stopped after N events"), never a
  second, doubled action.
- **Setting** `browser.trustedInput` (default on): off sends everything through the bridge. Not
  AI-specific (it applies to the user's browser commands too), so not under AGENTS.md rule 8.
- **Permissions:** unchanged. Page actions ask as before (Claude Code's browser asks per site:
  `agent.autoApprove` / Always on a page's question allows a site for the chat).
- **State:** `ide://browser` entries say `input: "trusted" | "synthesized"`.
- Not done: Cmd+A and other macOS editing shortcuts in the user's own Chrome on a Mac (Chrome
  needs protocol `commands` there; Ctrl shortcuts work on Windows and Linux).

### D347 — DevTools data of the user's own browser over the protocol

- `browser_inspect` (`browser.network`, `request`, `dom`, `styles`, `storage`, `setStorage`,
  `highlight`, `resize`) and `browser_console` answer for tab `external` over the DevTools
  protocol, with the outputs the built-in tab gives (`externalDevtools.ts`; message mapping in
  `core/browser/cdpDevtools.ts`, tested, no real browser in tests):
  - **network / request:** `Network.enable` at connect; requestWillBeSent / responseReceived
    (with the headers really sent) / loadingFinished / loadingFailed / webSocketCreated into the
    same request records (a redirect becomes a finished hop `id:1`, the next under the id);
    bodies on demand with `Network.getResponseBody` / `getRequestPostData` (base64 decoded, cut at
    `maxChars`). The bridge's own request reports are skipped (as for proxied pages). The main
    document's request, which can arrive before the page says it's loading, is kept in the new
    page's log.
  - **dom:** the bridge's element (ref, selector or name, `window.__ideBridge.internal.find`)
    as a protocol object, `DOM.getOuterHTML`; `all` keeps the bridge's `dom.query`.
  - **styles:** `CSS.getMatchedStylesForNode` (rules last-applied first, the browser's own
    defaults left out as in the built-in tab, each with its file **and line** — rules from other
    origins' sheets included, which the bridge can't read), `getComputedStyleForNode`,
    `DOM.getBoxModel` for the size; margin / border / padding from the computed values.
  - **storage:** `DOMStorage.getDOMStorageItems` for the origin, `Network.getCookies` for the
    page's URL — `cookies` pairs as before plus `cookieAttributes` (domain, path, expires,
    HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite), HttpOnly cookies included. `setStorage`: DOMStorage set / remove /
    clear, `Network.setCookie` / `deleteCookies`.
  - **highlight:** `Overlay.highlightNode` with Chrome DevTools' colors; none clears.
  - **resize:** `Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride` (narrower than 1024: mobile) or
    `clearDeviceMetricsOverride`; `colorScheme` by `Emulation.setEmulatedMedia` (real media
    emulation, not D318's rewriting). Both hold across the page's loads.
  - **console:** the bridge keeps reporting `console.*` calls (with expandable arguments and
    element refs, which `Runtime.consoleAPICalled` previews lack, so that event isn't used);
    `Log.entryAdded` adds what page script can't see — failed loads, security, interventions —
    and failed non-fetch requests (images, scripts) join `failedRequests`.
- The built-in tab's DevTools panels stay with the tabs; their element hover now names its own
  tab, so it never highlights in the user's browser while that is the selected target.
- **Permissions:** unchanged: `browser_inspect` is read-only (Claude in Chrome's reads don't ask
  either); `browser.setStorage` is a write command as before.
- **UI test:** none for D347. The UI tests have no Chrome, and a fake DevTools endpoint would
  need a page running the bridge behind it — a browser. Unit tests cover the message building and
  result mapping (`cdpDevtools.test.ts`) and the command layer against a fake protocol
  (`externalDevtools.test.ts`); manual steps below.

### D348 — The command sandbox's network on Windows: a filtering proxy, honestly limited

- **What was tried (real APIs, `src-tauri/src/exec/sandbox_win_tests.rs`):** the Windows Filtering
  Platform with a *dynamic* session (filters that vanish with the session, the least a firewall
  change can be): `FwpmEngineOpen0` succeeds for a normal (not elevated) user, `FwpmFilterAdd0`
  returns `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` (0x5), even for a filter on port 1. A filter scoped to an app id or
  a security descriptor goes through the same call, so it's out too. The Windows Firewall API
  (`INetFwPolicy2`) needs an administrator as well. **AppContainer** without `internetClient`
  blocks the network, but loopback too (the exemption, `NetworkIsolationSetAppContainerConfig` /
  `CheckNetIsolation LoopbackExempt`, is documented as needing an administrator; not run here: a
  successful call replaces the machine's whole exemption list) and it can't read the user profile,
  where node, npm, git and their caches live — D336 rejected it for that, and a dev server on
  localhost would be unreachable. A Job Object has no network limit. So **nothing a normal user
  can do makes Windows refuse a low-integrity program's connections.**
- **What's built:** a small filtering HTTP proxy per sandboxed command (`exec/sandbox_net.rs`, std
  sockets and threads, no dependency) on 127.0.0.1, set through `HTTP(S)_PROXY`, `ALL_PROXY` (both
  cases), `NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1,::1` and `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1`. It speaks CONNECT (any
  TLS) and absolute-form HTTP (one upstream connection per request, `Connection: close`, so an
  allowed request can't carry another host's). Loopback is always allowed; other hosts only when
  `agent.sandbox.allowHosts` / the project's allowances list them (`example.com`, `*.example.com`,
  `*`). Refused hosts get a 403 that says why and are recorded: the run's result names them
  (`ExecResult.blockedHosts`) and points the model at `suggest_sandbox_allowance` (D350).
- **What that protects, per system** (`SandboxInfo.network`, the card and `ide://agent/sandbox`
  say it):
  - **Windows (`proxy`):** tools that honor the proxy variables — npm, pnpm, yarn, pip, git over
    HTTPS, curl, cargo, Go, Python's urllib/requests, .NET's HttpClient, Node 24+'s fetch — reach
    localhost and the allowed hosts only. **Not protected:** anything that opens its own sockets
    (a malicious script, ssh, PowerShell 5.1's `Invoke-WebRequest`, which uses the system proxy, a
    raw `net.connect`). `limitsNetwork` stays false. It stops honest tools from fetching, and makes
    the agent ask before a project's commands talk to new hosts; it is not a wall.
  - **macOS (`blocked`):** sandbox-exec already refuses every connection but to localhost, so the
    proxy is the only way out: the allowlist is enforced (written, not run here).
  - **Linux (`blocked`):** bubblewrap's own network namespace can't reach the host's loopback, so
    with no allowed hosts it stays `--unshare-net` (no network at all, as D336); with allowed hosts
    the network is shared and the proxy set, i.e. Windows' guarantee (`networkMode` says `proxy`
    then). A bridge into the namespace (as Claude Code's socat) is left for later (written, not run
    here).
- Verified on Windows (cargo): the WFP refusal; a sandboxed `curl.exe https://example.com/` refused
  by the filter with `example.com` recorded and nothing leaving the machine; the proxy's own
  tunnel to an allowed (loopback) host and refusal of others. Behavior change: on Windows a
  sandboxed `npm install` now fails until the registry is allowed (as on macOS/Linux already).

### D349 — Secrets hidden from sandboxed commands (agent.sandbox.denyRead)

- **Setting:** `agent.sandbox.denyRead` (user scope; a folder's settings can't shrink it): paths
  (`~/` is home) and placeholders expanded per system in `exec/sandbox_read.rs`: `${secrets}` (the
  IDE's `<data>/secrets.json`), `${keychains}`, `${browserProfiles}`, `${envFiles}` (`.env*`
  outside the command's folders). Default: `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, `~/.azure`, `~/.config/gcloud`,
  `~/.config/gh`, `~/.docker/config.json`, `~/.kube`, `~/.gnupg`, `~/.netrc`,
  `~/.git-credentials`, and the four placeholders. A path that holds one of the command's own
  folders (`~` with the project inside it) is skipped: it would hide the work.
- **macOS:** `(deny file-read* (subpath …))` per path after the write rules; `.env*` by regex,
  re-allowed inside the writable folders. Keychains' files are hidden, but a program can still ask
  the Keychain service (it may prompt). Written, not run here.
- **Linux:** after the binds, `--tmpfs <dir>` over a folder, `--ro-bind /dev/null <file>` over a
  file (existing ones). `.env*`: those in home and the folder's parents, found per run. Written,
  not run here.
- **Windows (verified, cargo test runs a real one):** low integrity can't be denied reads by
  integrity alone, but a **mandatory label with no-read-up** does it: each existing path gets an
  explicit `S:(ML;OICI;NRNW;;;ME)` (a file `S:(ML;;NRNW;;;ME)`), set by `SetNamedSecurityInfoW`
  with `LABEL_SECURITY_INFORMATION` only — a normal user may (it's the owner's object, at its own
  level). Medium programs (the user's own, the IDE) read and write as before; the low-integrity
  command and what it starts can't read, and files made in the folder later inherit it. An
  explicit label beats an inherited low one (a secret inside the marked folder stays hidden).
  Protecting the label from inheritance (`PROTECTED_SACL_…`) needs the security privilege (error
  1314), so it isn't used. The label before is recorded in `<data>/sandbox-hidden.json`;
  **Let sandboxed commands read my secrets again** (`agent.sandboxUnhideSecrets`,
  `exec_sandbox_unhide`) puts it back (explicit ones restored, inherited ones re-inherit); the
  test checks both ways. Consequences: the label stays (like D336's folder mark) and also hides
  those paths from every other low-integrity program — which is why **browser profiles aren't
  labelled on Windows** (Chrome's and Edge's sandboxed network/utility processes run at low
  integrity and read the profile) and keychains have no files there (Credential Manager is a
  service: not covered). `.env*` outside the folder: those in home and the folder's parents, found
  per run. The atomic-write of `secrets.json` replaces the file, so it's labelled again on the next
  sandboxed run.
- What couldn't be hidden comes back as a line in the result (`sandboxNotes`), never silently.

### D350 — Per-project sandbox allowances, and the agent's card to ask for one

- **Where they live:** `agent.sandbox.projects` (user scope): `{ "<folder>": { allowWrite, allowHosts
  } }`, plus `agent.sandbox.allowWrite` / `agent.sandbox.allowHosts` for every project. Not
  `.<IDE folder>/sandbox.json` nor folder-scope settings (the brief's options): those are the
  repository's files, and a cloned repository could then widen its own sandbox (allow `*`, or
  writes to the home folder) — the sandbox exists for exactly that code. Kept by folder in the
  user's settings, a project's allowance is still "set once per project".
- **Folders:** absolute or `~/…`, existing; a drive's root or one holding the home folder is
  refused (Rust). On Windows each is marked low (D336) when first used.
- **Hosts:** go to the proxy (D348): enforced on macOS, proxy-aware tools only on Windows and on
  Linux (shared network then).
- **The card:** tool `suggest_sandbox_allowance { hosts?, folders?, reason }`, offered only while
  `agent.sandbox` is `auto` and not to subagents. It refuses `*`, non-hosts, relative or too-wide
  folders and folders inside the project. The card (`view/sandboxCard.ts`, the discovery cards'
  style, D345) lists what it allows and has **Allow** (`button-primary`; then "Allowed"), which
  runs `agent.allowSandboxSuggestion` — hidden from the agent: only the user's click widens the
  sandbox. The run's result tells the model to use it when the filter refused a host, or when a
  write outside the folder failed.
- **Permission default (Claude Code's):** Claude Code asks when a sandboxed command reaches a new
  domain and can remember it for the project; here the agent shows the card and the user's Allow
  remembers it for the project. Running one command outside the sandbox still asks every time
  (D336).
- **The permission card** shows the policy: "In the sandbox: writes only in the folder, D:/cache
  and a temp folder; secrets hidden (~/.ssh, ~/.aws and 12 more); tools that use the proxy
  settings reach only localhost and pypi.org; other programs' connections aren't limited."
  `ide://agent/sandbox` adds `limitsReads`, `network` and the `policy`.

### D351 — Workflow agents that edit, each in a worktree of its own

- Claude Code's Workflow `agent()` takes `isolation: 'worktree'`; ours does too. Such a call runs as
  one of the IDE's worktree helpers (D231/D246, headless always: a window per script agent would
  be a crowd) through `IsolatedHelpers.startForWorkflow`, which reuses `startNow` but asks
  nothing, adds no line to the chat and sends no notification: its end goes to the run through a
  waiter instead of a message. Its tools are the chat's (D232), like a delegated helper's.
- agent() then returns `{ result, branch, folder, changes, files }` (the answer, or the parsed
  object with a schema, plus where it worked and what it changed). With a schema it gets one try:
  asked again it would start over in a second worktree.
- The permission card names the editing agents before any of the script runs: `editingCalls`
  finds `isolation: 'worktree'` in the script's text (with the call's label). A run whose text has
  none refuses such a call at run time (options built some other way would edit without the user
  having been told). "Always" for workflows with editing agents is its own allowance; the
  read-only one doesn't cover them. Permission default: asked per run, as Claude Code asks for a
  workflow (and as starting a helper asks).
- Limits: at most `agent.workflows.maxEditingAgents` (default 3, 1–10) per run; they don't count
  against `agent.isolatedHelpers.max` (the run's own cap and concurrency bound them). `files:
  [...]` claims paths (`FileClaims`: a glob claims its folder; equal or nested paths overlap), so
  two editing agents never work on the same files at once when the script says which; without
  `files` the IDE can't tell, so the end message names branches that changed the same files
  instead (merging both may conflict).
- Refused up front when the chat can't edit (Ask/Plan), it isn't a git repository, or helpers
  aren't available. Stop (the card's, the chat's, the time limit) stops the run's helpers; their
  worktrees and changes stay for review.
- The run's card lists each editing agent's branch and changes under its row, with Review
  (primary) and Merge (`agent.helpers` review / merge: the compare page, and the merge that asks
  first). Nothing is ever merged without the user. `ide://agent/workflows` has each agent's
  `worktree`; `ide://agent/helpers` marks them `workflow: true`.
- Worktrees are made by `git.createWorktree` next to the repository, copying files as the
  existing setup does; nothing is linked (no node_modules junctions).

### D352 — Auto-merge a watched pull request

- Claude Code's app has set_auto_merge, used only when the user asked. Ours: `watch_pr {
  action: "auto_merge", method?: merge|squash|rebase }` (watching it first when needed) and
  `auto_merge_off`; the description says only when the user asked, and a confirmation card shows
  the first time per pull request (per window). Permission default: once per pull request.
- The user's way: `agent.autoMergePullRequest { session?, method?, off? }` (no method → a pick),
  a merge button on the pull request's row in the chat's details and in Background tasks (the
  same button turns it off). The agent calling that command is sent to watch_pr instead, so the
  card can't be skipped.
- Where the repository allows auto-merge (`gh repo view --json autoMergeAllowed`), GitHub's own:
  `gh pr merge <n> --auto --<method>` (new gh ops `prAutoMerge`, `prAutoMergeOff`,
  `repoAutoMerge`). Otherwise, or when that call fails, the IDE merges it itself at a look where
  `mergeDecision` says ready: open, not a draft, every check passed (no checks: nothing to wait
  for, as GitHub does), approved when reviews are required (`reviewDecision` not REVIEW_REQUIRED
  or CHANGES_REQUESTED), MERGEABLE and not BLOCKED/DIRTY (`prView` now also asks for
  `autoMergeRequest` and `mergeStateStatus`). It then ends the watch and says so in the chat
  ("Pull request #7 (…): merged by auto-merge (squash)", why it was ready). A failed merge turns
  auto-merge off and says why, so it doesn't fail at every look.
- With GitHub's auto-merge, the usual "merged" message gets a line saying auto-merge did it.
- Auto-merge is saved with the watch (`agent.prWatches`) and resumes with the folder.
